phases.name: Operating rules
phases.aim: Study habits. These do not count toward progress.

sections.title: The weekly shape
sections.guide: The fixed layout of each week. Keep the days in this order so new material (Mon-Thu) is consolidated by building and testing (Fri), then checked without help (Sat). Plan the coming week on Sunday evening or first thing Monday.

items.text: Mon–Thu: learn and build.
items.how: On each of these days, study one topic from the current phase, then build something with it the same day. Write the day's topic and the program you built in your log.
items.done: Your log shows four weekday entries, each naming a topic and a program that uses it.

items.text: Fri: build, debug, write tests.
items.how: Spend Friday on the week's code, not new topics: fix known bugs, add pytest tests for the functions you wrote, and tidy names. Run the whole suite before you stop.
items.done: The week's project has a test file and pytest passes on Friday evening.

items.text: Sat: independent challenge — no tutorial open.
items.how: Pick a problem you have not seen, such as a CS50P problem set, and solve it with only the official docs open. Note each point where you wanted a tutorial and what you did instead.
items.done: You have a working solution written with no tutorial or AI answer open, and a list of where you got stuck.

items.text: Sun: rest, or light review only.
items.how: Either take the day off, or do at most an hour of review: reread the week's log and rewrite one earlier small function from memory. No new topics.
items.done: Monday starts with a written plan for the week and no backlog of half-read new material.

items.text: Target 4–6 focused hours a day, six days a week.
items.how: Time focused work with a timer and pause it for every break or distraction. Record the total each day. If you are regularly under 4 hours, cut the plan rather than the rest day.
items.done: Your log has a daily hours figure for the last two weeks and the weekly totals fall between 24 and 36.

sections.title: The daily protocol
sections.guide: The order of a working day. Run the blocks top to bottom; a short day (about 4 hours) uses the low end of each range and a long day (about 6 hours) the high end. Never drop the last block: the commit and log entry are how you see progress later.

items.text: 10 min — write down the outcome for today in one sentence.
items.how: Before opening any material, write one sentence of the form 'By tonight I can ...' naming a concrete result, e.g. 'By tonight my todo manager saves to JSON and reloads it'.
items.done: At the end of the day you can mark the sentence met or not met without arguing with yourself.

items.text: 45–75 min — study the course, video, or docs.
items.how: Work through one section of the course, video, or docs for today's topic. Type every example into the REPL or a file and change one value to see what happens, rather than reading passively.
items.done: You can explain the topic in three sentences without looking at the material.

items.text: 90–150 min — implement it without copy-pasting.
items.how: Close the material and write today's program from a blank file. When stuck, look up the one fact you need in the docs, then close them again. Never paste example code.
items.done: The program runs, and you typed and can explain every line of it.

items.text: 30–60 min — deliberate problem solving.
items.how: Solve one or two small problems unrelated to your project, such as a CS50P problem. Write your plan as comments before any code, then implement it.
items.done: You solved at least one problem and your written plan matches what the code does.

items.text: 30–60 min — push the current project forward.
items.how: Take the next task off your current project's list and finish it, error handling included. If it is too big for this block, split it into smaller tasks first and do the first one.
items.done: One project task moved from open to done and is committed.

items.text: 15–30 min — tests, cleanup, commit, log entry.
items.how: Run the tests, delete dead code and debug prints, then commit with a message saying what changed. Write a log entry: hours, what you learned, what broke, tomorrow's first task.
items.done: git status is clean, the tests pass, and today's log entry exists.

sections.title: The 20-minute debugging rule
sections.guide: A fixed procedure for any bug that has held you for 20 minutes. Work the five steps in order and write down what each one produced before moving to the next. Searching or asking for help comes last, not first.

items.text: Reproduce the failure on demand before touching anything.
items.how: Find the smallest input and command that trigger the bug every time. Save them as a script or a failing test so you can rerun the exact failure with one command.
items.done: You can make the failure happen on demand with one command.

items.text: Read the whole traceback, bottom line first.
items.how: Read the last line first: the exception type and message. Then read the frames upwards and find the deepest frame in your own code rather than in the standard library.
items.done: You can name the exception, the file and line in your code where it happened, and the calls that led there.

items.text: Inspect actual state — print, breakpoint, or pdb.
items.how: Put breakpoint() on the line before the failure and run the reproduction. In pdb, use p to print a variable, n to step over, s to step in and w to show the stack.
items.done: You have written down the actual values of the variables involved, not the values you assumed.

items.text: Form one hypothesis and write it down.
items.how: Write one sentence of the form 'X fails because Y, so if I change Z the result will be W'. One hypothesis at a time, in your log or a comment.
items.done: There is a written hypothesis that predicts a specific, checkable result.

items.text: Test the hypothesis. Only then search for help.
items.how: Make only the change the hypothesis names and rerun the reproduction. If the result differs from the prediction, record why and form a new hypothesis. Search or ask only after that.
items.done: The bug is fixed with a known cause, or your help request includes the reproduction and the hypotheses you ruled out.

sections.title: The AI ladder — climb in order
sections.guide: How to use an AI assistant without letting it do the learning for you. Start at rung 1 and move down a rung only when the one above has not unblocked you. Rungs 4 and 5 come after your own code works.

items.text: 1. Explain the concept to me.
items.how: Ask for an explanation of the concept with one small example, then ask it to quiz you with two questions. Check what it told you against the official docs page for the topic.
items.done: You can answer the quiz questions and the docs agree with the explanation.

items.text: 2. Give me a hint, not the answer.
items.how: Paste the problem and your current attempt and ask for one hint with no code. Apply the hint yourself before asking for another.
items.done: You solved the problem and the final code contains no lines written by the assistant.

items.text: 3. Diagnose my reasoning, not my code.
items.how: Describe in prose what you think your code does step by step, and ask the assistant to find the wrong step in that reasoning without rewriting the code.
items.done: You can state which of your assumptions was wrong, and you fixed the code yourself.

items.text: 4. Review my implementation after it works.
items.how: Once the code works and tests pass, ask for a review of naming, error handling and structure, with PEP 8 as the style reference. Apply the changes you agree with by hand, one at a time.
items.done: You can say which review points you applied and why you rejected the others.

items.text: 5. Generate adversarial test cases against it.
items.how: Ask for inputs likely to break your function: empty, huge, malformed, unicode, boundary values. Turn each into a pytest.mark.parametrize case and run the suite.
items.done: The new cases are in your test file, and each one either passes or led to a fix.

items.text: 6. Show an implementation — only after I've attempted it.
items.how: Only after your version works, or after a full 20-minute debugging cycle, ask for a reference implementation. Compare it with yours line by line and write down each difference.
items.done: You have a written list of differences and can say which version is better on each point.

sections.title: Non-negotiables
sections.guide: Rules that apply to every phase and project. Reread them at the start of each phase, and check every finished project against all six before calling it done.

items.text: Never copy a whole tutorial project and call it finished.
items.how: If you follow a tutorial, treat it as practice, then build a second version with different requirements from a blank file. Only the second version goes in your portfolio.
items.done: Each portfolio project has features that no tutorial you followed had.

items.text: When a concept lands, modify it immediately into something else.
items.how: As soon as an example works, change it: a new input type, a new output format, or an extra feature. For example, turn a word counter into a counter of letter pairs.
items.done: For each topic in your log there is a modified version, not only the original example.

items.text: Break your own code on purpose so you learn what failure looks like.
items.how: In a working program, delete a return, pass the wrong type, rename a file it reads, or divide by zero. Predict the traceback before each run, then compare.
items.done: You can predict the exception type for common mistakes before running the code.

items.text: Every serious project gets Git, tests, a README, and a real commit history.
items.how: Start each project with git init, a README and a tests/ folder before any features. Commit after each small working change, not once at the end.
items.done: git log shows many small commits, and the repo has a README and passing tests.

items.text: Measure performance. Never guess at it.
items.how: Before calling code fast or slow, time snippets with timeit and profile whole programs with python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py. Record the numbers next to the claim.
items.done: Every performance claim in your notes or README has a measured number beside it.

items.text: 80% doing, 20% studying. Early phases 60/40, later phases 90/10.
items.how: Log study time and build time separately each day. At the end of the week, work out the split and move time between the two if you are off the target for your phase.
items.done: Your weekly log shows the doing/studying split, within 10 percentage points of the target.

phases.name: Environment & Git
phases.aim: Set up your tools. Every project from here on uses Git from its first commit.

resources.name: Git & GitHub Crash Course — freeCodeCamp
resources.why: Beginner to working workflow in one sitting

resources.name: GitHub Skills — Introduction to Git
resources.why: Repos, commits, history, branches — hands on

resources.name: GitHub Skills — Introduction to GitHub
resources.why: Branch → commit → PR → merge

resources.name: Git documentation
resources.why: The command reference you'll live in

sections.title: Set up
sections.guide: One-time installation and configuration. Do the steps in order in one sitting (about 1 to 2 hours), and open a fresh terminal after each install so PATH changes take effect. Everything later in the course assumes these commands work.

items.text: Install Python 3.13+ and confirm python --version in a fresh terminal.
items.how: Install from python.org (on Windows tick 'Add python.exe to PATH', or use the py launcher). Close all terminals, open a new one and run python --version and py -0 to list installed versions.
items.done: A new terminal prints Python 3.13 or later for python --version.

items.text: Install uv, then run uv init scratch && cd scratch && uv run python -c "print(1)".
items.how: Install uv with the standalone installer from its docs, open a new terminal, run the command, then list the scratch folder: note pyproject.toml, main.py and the .venv created by uv run.
items.done: The command prints 1, and you can say what pyproject.toml and .venv are for.

items.text: Install VS Code with the Python and Pylance extensions.
items.how: Install VS Code, add the Python extension (Pylance comes with it), open the scratch folder and choose its .venv interpreter with 'Python: Select Interpreter'. Run main.py with F5.
items.done: The status bar shows the .venv interpreter and F5 runs the file with the debugger.

items.text: Create a GitHub account and add an SSH key.
items.how: Create the account, run ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com", add the public key (.pub file) in GitHub settings, then run ssh -T git@github.com.

where.name: GitHub: Generating a new SSH key

items.done: ssh -T git@github.com greets you by your GitHub username.

items.text: Set git config --global user.name and user.email.
items.how: Set both values, using the email on your GitHub account (or GitHub's noreply address) so commits link to your profile. Check with git config --global --list.
items.done: git config user.name and git config user.email print the values you set.

items.text: Set git config --global init.defaultBranch main.
items.how: Run the command (needs Git 2.28 or later; check with git --version), then run git init in an empty folder and git status.
items.done: git status in a new repository reports 'On branch main'.

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The Git model and commands you will use every day. Read each topic, then try it in a throwaway repository straight away. Spend most time on the index/HEAD model (s1.1) and on revert/reset/rebase (s1.5); the rest follows from those.

items.text: What a commit is: a snapshot, not a diff.
items.how: Read how Git stores data, then in a test repo run git cat-file -p HEAD and follow the tree hash with git cat-file -p to see the full file listing stored in one commit.
items.done: You can explain why git diff output is computed from two snapshots rather than stored.

items.text: Local vs remote: working tree, index, HEAD, origin.
items.how: Read the three trees section. Edit a file, then compare git diff, git diff --staged and git status before and after git add. Run git remote -v in a cloned repo to see origin.
items.done: You can draw working tree, index, HEAD and origin and say which command moves changes between each pair.

items.text: init · status · add · commit · log · diff
items.how: In a new repo run each command in the order listed, with git status between them. Make three commits, then read them with git log --oneline and git log -p.

where.name: Pro Git: Viewing the commit history

items.done: From memory you can create a repo, make a commit and show what changed in it.

items.text: Branching, switching, merging, resolving a conflict by hand.
items.how: Create a branch with git switch -c, commit on it and on main to the same line of one file, then git merge. Edit out the conflict markers by hand, git add the file and commit.

where.name: Pro Git: Basic branching and merging
Pro Git: Branches in a nutshell

items.done: You resolved a conflict without a GUI and git log --graph shows the merge commit.

items.text: push · fetch · pull · restore · stash
items.how: Push a repo to GitHub, edit a file on the GitHub website, then compare git fetch plus git log origin/main with git pull. Discard a local edit with git restore and park one with git stash.
items.done: You can say the difference between fetch and pull, and between restore and stash.

items.text: revert vs reset vs rebase — and when each is safe.
items.how: Read Reset Demystified and the Rebasing chapter, including 'The Perils of Rebasing'. In a test repo undo one commit with git revert, then with git reset --soft HEAD~1, and compare git log.
items.done: You can explain why revert is safe on pushed commits and reset and rebase are not.

items.text: Pull requests and reviewing someone else's diff.
items.how: Complete the Introduction to GitHub course. Then open a pull request against your own repo from a branch, leave line comments on the diff, and merge it.
items.done: You have a merged pull request with at least one review comment on a changed line.

sections.title: Drill
sections.guide: A drill in one repository that exercises everything from Learn. Do the steps in order in the same git-training repo, running git status and git log --oneline --graph --all after each one. Repeat the whole drill from scratch until it takes under 30 minutes.

items.text: Create git-training, commit a README and an app.py.
items.how: Run git init git-training, write a short README.md and an app.py that prints a greeting, and commit them as two separate commits with clear messages.

where.name: Pro Git: Getting a Git repository

items.done: git log --oneline shows two commits and git status is clean.

items.text: Branch to feature/calculator, change app.py, commit.
items.how: Run git switch -c feature/calculator, add an add(a, b) function to app.py, commit, then switch back to main and confirm the function is absent there.

where.name: Pro Git: Basic branching and merging

items.done: git log --oneline --all --graph shows the feature branch one commit ahead of main.

items.text: Make a conflicting change on main, then merge and resolve it.
items.how: On main, edit the same lines of app.py differently and commit. Run git merge feature/calculator, resolve the markers by hand, run python app.py, then git add and commit.

where.name: Pro Git: Basic branching and merging

items.done: The merge commit exists, app.py has no conflict markers, and the program runs.

items.text: Stash uncommitted work, switch branch, pop it back.
items.how: Edit app.py without committing, run git stash, switch to the other branch and back, then git stash pop. Check git stash list before and after.
items.done: Your uncommitted edit reappears after pop and git stash list is empty.

items.text: Break the branch on purpose, then recover it with reflog.
items.how: On the feature branch run git reset --hard HEAD~1, or delete the branch with git branch -D. Find the lost commit in git reflog and restore it with git reset --hard or git branch and its hash.
items.done: The branch points at the lost commit again and you can do the recovery without notes.

phases.snippet:
mkdir git-training && cd git-training
git init
# create README.md and app.py
git add . && git commit -m "Initial project"
git switch -c feature/calculator
# edit app.py, commit
git switch main
# make a conflicting change, then:
git merge feature/calculator

gate.note: Do all seven from memory, in one sitting, without notes.

items.text: Create a repo, clone it, make and inspect three commits.
Create two branches and merge them.
Cause a merge conflict and resolve it correctly.
Push and pull against GitHub.
Use stash, restore, and revert without losing work.
Recover a commit you 'lost' using git reflog.
Explain merge vs revert vs reset vs rebase in plain English to someone else.

phases.name: Python foundations
phases.aim: Learn the language by writing a working program every day.

resources.name: CS50P — Introduction to Programming with Python
resources.why: Your primary curriculum for weeks 1–4

resources.name: Python Tutorial (official)
resources.why: The language, explained by the people who built it

resources.name: Python Standard Library
resources.why: Look up modules while you build, not before

resources.name: Corey Schafer — Python tutorials
resources.why: When a specific CS50P topic doesn't click

resources.why: Deep single-topic articles when you need one

sections.title: Week 1 — one program a day, no exceptions
sections.guide: Seven small programs, one per day, each built around one language feature. Spend the first hour on the feature in the tutorial, the rest writing the program from a blank file. Commit each day's program to Git; Day 7 has no tutorial open at all.

items.text: Day 1 · variables + functions → calculator with history and error handling.
items.how: Write one function per operation and a loop that reads 'number operator number'. Catch ValueError for bad numbers and ZeroDivisionError separately. Keep past results in a list and add a history command.
items.done: Typing 'abc', '5 / 0' and 'history' each gives a clear message and the program keeps running.

items.text: Day 2 · conditionals → guessing game with difficulty, scoring, replay.
items.how: Use random.randint for the secret number and if/elif/else for too high, too low and correct. Difficulty sets the range and attempt limit; score depends on attempts left; ask to replay at the end.
items.done: You can play three rounds on different difficulties without restarting, and invalid guesses do not crash it.

items.text: Day 3 · loops → password generator with charsets and strength scoring.
items.how: Build the character pool from string.ascii_letters, digits and punctuation as chosen, and pick with secrets.choice in a loop. Score strength from length and the number of character classes used.
items.done: You can explain why secrets and not random is used for passwords.

items.text: Day 4 · strings → text analyzer: words, sentences, frequency, averages.
items.how: Read a text file, split words with str.split after lower-casing and stripping punctuation, split sentences on full stops, question marks and exclamation marks, and count words with collections.Counter. Print the top 10 and the average word and sentence length.
items.done: Word counts on a short paragraph match a count you did by hand.

items.text: Day 5 · lists and tuples → CLI todo manager (add, remove, complete, list).
items.how: Store each task as a tuple (title, done) in a list, and replace the tuple to mark it complete, since tuples are immutable. Implement add, remove by number, complete and list as commands in a loop.
items.done: You can explain why marking a task complete replaces the tuple instead of changing it.

items.text: Day 6 · dicts and sets → contact manager with search and tags.
items.how: Store contacts in a dict keyed by name, each with a phone, an email and a set of tags. Search by partial name, and find contacts sharing tags with set intersection (&).
items.done: Adding a duplicate tag has no effect, and a tag search returns exactly the contacts you expect.

items.text: Day 7 · independent → one small app with no project-specific tutorial open.
items.how: Choose a small app you have not built (unit converter, quiz, expense log). Write the requirements in five lines first, then build it with only the Python docs open.
items.done: The app meets all five written requirements and no tutorial was open while you built it.

sections.title: Week 2 — the standard library
sections.guide: The standard-library modules every real script uses. Study one module per day (s1.0 to s1.5) with a short script for each, then spend the last two days on the File Organizer, which uses all of them together.

items.text: Modules, imports, __name__, and how Python finds things.
items.how: Split a script into two modules and import one from the other. Print __name__ in both, add an if __name__ == "__main__": block, and print sys.path to see where imports are searched.
items.done: You can say what __name__ is when a file is run directly and when it is imported.

items.text: Exceptions: raising, catching narrowly, custom exception classes.
items.how: Define class ValidationError(Exception), raise it with a message from a validation function, and catch only that type at the call site. Use raise ... from err when re-raising.
items.done: You can explain why except Exception around a whole function hides bugs.

items.text: Files with pathlib, instead of joining path strings.
items.how: Rewrite a script that uses string paths with Path: build paths with /, list files with iterdir and glob, read with read_text, and create folders with mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True).
items.done: The script has no os.path.join or string concatenation for paths and runs on your machine.

items.text: JSON and CSV round-trips.
items.how: Save your contact manager to JSON with json.dump and load it back; convert sets to lists first. Export the same data with csv.DictWriter, opening the file with newline="", and read it back.
items.done: Saving and reloading gives data equal to the original, checked with ==.

items.text: argparse for a real CLI interface.
items.how: Work through the argparse HOWTO, then give one of your programs positional arguments, a --dry-run flag with action="store_true", and typed options. Run it with --help.
items.done: --help prints usage for every option and bad arguments give an error, not a traceback.

items.text: logging instead of print for anything that runs unattended.
items.how: Replace the prints in a script with logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) calls at the right levels. Configure basicConfig once in main to write to a file with timestamps, and log errors with logger.exception.
items.done: The log file shows timestamp, level and message for each run, including a traceback for a forced error.

items.text: Build: File Organizer with dry-run, undo, duplicate detection, logs.
items.how: Order: plan moves by extension, apply them with shutil.move and record each in a JSON journal, add --dry-run to print the plan only, --undo to replay the journal backwards, and SHA-256 hashing for duplicates.
items.done: On a test folder, organise then undo returns every file to its original path, and dry-run changes nothing.

sections.title: Week 3 — testing
sections.guide: Automated testing with pytest. Learn the tool (s2.0 to s2.3) in the first half of the week on small examples, then spend the second half retrofitting tests onto your own projects and proving they catch bugs.

items.text: pytest basics: test discovery, assertions, running a suite.
items.how: Install with uv add --dev pytest. Write test_*.py files with test_* functions using plain assert, run uv run pytest -q, then try -k to select tests and -x to stop at the first failure.
items.done: You can say which files and functions pytest collects and read a failing assertion's output.

items.text: Arrange–act–assert, and one behaviour per test.
items.how: Rewrite three tests so each has three blocks separated by blank lines: arrange the inputs, act with one call, assert on the result. Split any test that checks two behaviours into two tests.
items.done: Each test name describes one behaviour, and when a test fails the name tells you what broke.

items.text: Edge cases: empty, huge, malformed, unicode, permission denied.
items.how: For one function, list inputs for each category and turn them into pytest.mark.parametrize cases. Use pytest.raises for expected errors, and monkeypatch to raise PermissionError, since Windows file permissions are hard to fake.
items.done: Your tests cover all five categories and each one passes or led to a fix.

items.text: Fixtures and tmp_path for filesystem tests.
items.how: Write a fixture that builds a small folder tree inside tmp_path, then use it in tests of your file code. Never touch real folders in tests; tmp_path gives each test its own new directory.
items.done: Your filesystem tests pass in any order and leave nothing behind in your project folder.

items.text: Retrofit tests onto the calculator and File Organizer.
items.how: Start with the pure functions (calculator operations, move planning), then the file-touching parts using tmp_path, then dry-run and undo. Commit after each group passes.
items.done: Both projects have a test suite that passes with pytest, including a dry-run test and an undo test.

items.text: Introduce three bugs deliberately and confirm the suite catches all three.
items.how: Introduce one bug at a time (off-by-one, wrong comparison operator, a swallowed exception), run the suite, then git restore the file. Write a new test for any bug that got through.
items.done: Each of the three bugs makes at least one test fail, and the suite passes again after restoring.

sections.title: Week 4 — objects
sections.guide: Classes and the data model. Take the concepts in order (s3.0 to s3.4), about a day each with small examples, then build the Inventory Engine with tests and refactor it once it works.

items.text: Classes, instances, __init__, and attribute lookup.
items.how: Write a small class with a class attribute and instance attributes set in __init__. Inspect vars(obj) and type(obj).__dict__, then shadow the class attribute on one instance and see which value each instance reads.
items.done: You can say the lookup order: instance, then class, then base classes.

items.text: Composition first; inheritance only for a true is-a relationship.
items.how: Model a Warehouse twice: once inheriting from list, once holding a list as an attribute. Note which list methods the first version exposes that a warehouse should not have.
items.done: For any two of your classes you can say whether the relation is is-a or has-a, and justify it.

items.text: Properties, class methods, static methods.
items.how: Add a @property with a setter that rejects negative prices, a @classmethod from_dict as an alternative constructor, and a @staticmethod helper that uses neither the class nor an instance.
items.done: Setting a negative price raises ValueError, and you can say when to use each of the three decorators.

items.text: dataclasses for data-shaped objects.
items.how: Rewrite a plain class as @dataclass and compare the generated __repr__ and __eq__. Try frozen=True, and use field(default_factory=list) for a mutable default.
items.done: You can explain why a mutable default like items: list = [] is rejected by dataclasses.

items.text: Dunder methods: __repr__ __eq__ __len__ __iter__.
items.how: Give a Category class __repr__, __eq__ that returns NotImplemented for other types, __len__ and __iter__. Then test len(), ==, a for loop, and whether instances still work in a set.
items.done: You can explain why defining __eq__ alone makes instances unhashable.

items.text: Build: Inventory Engine — Product, Category, Warehouse, Order, Customer.
items.how: Order: Product and Category as dataclasses, Warehouse holding stock counts, Customer, then Order with lines that reserves stock and fails cleanly when stock runs out. Write tests for each class as you go.
items.done: Tests pass for placing an order, rejecting one that exceeds stock, and stock totals after both.

items.text: Refactor it once, after the first version works.
items.how: With the tests passing, list the three worst parts (long methods, duplicated logic, unclear names) and fix one at a time, running the tests and committing after each change.
items.done: The tests pass unchanged after the refactor, and git log shows separate commits for each change.

sections.title: Standing requirements for every project
sections.guide: A checklist applied to every project from here on, not a week of work. Check each project against all five items before you call it finished, and fix any that fail.

items.text: No blanket except: pass anywhere.
items.how: Search each project for except: and pass inside except blocks. Replace each with the specific exception type and a real action: log it, re-raise it, or return an error value.
items.done: No search hits remain, and every except block names an exception type and does something with it.

items.text: Config lives outside business logic.
items.how: Move paths, limits and other settings into a config.toml read once with tomllib at startup, or into environment variables via os.environ. Pass the values into functions as arguments.
items.done: You can change a setting without editing any file that contains business logic.

items.text: Logs are detailed enough to diagnose a failure you didn't witness.
items.how: Log the start and end of each operation with its inputs and IDs, log decisions at INFO, and use logger.exception in except blocks. Then break an input and diagnose it from the log alone.
items.done: Someone reading only the log file can say what the program was doing when it failed and with which input.

items.text: README covers install, usage, design decisions, limitations.
items.how: Write four headed sections: install (exact commands), usage (example commands and output), design decisions (why, not what), and limitations (what it does not handle). Follow the install steps in a fresh clone.
items.done: A fresh clone installs and runs using only the README's commands.

items.text: Meaningful commit messages, committed as you go.
items.how: Commit after each working change. Write the subject in the imperative, under about 50 characters ('Add undo to organiser'), and a body for the why when it is not obvious. Stage related changes together with git add -p.

where.name: How to write a Git commit message
Pro Git: Contributing to a project

items.done: Reading git log --oneline alone tells you how the project was built, step by step.

gate.note: Start from an empty file. No tutorial, template or AI-written code.

items.text: Build a working CLI program from a blank file in under two hours.
It uses functions, a collection type, file I/O, and exception handling.
It has a pytest suite covering normal and edge cases.
Explain the difference between a list, tuple, set, and dict — and when you'd pick each.
Explain what happens when you mutate a default argument.

sections.title: Week 5 — iteration and the object model
sections.guide: Work in order: iterators, then generators, lazy pipelines and itertools, then the object-model traps (identity, hashing, default arguments). Spend about three days on the reading and REPL exercises and two on the multi-GB file build, which uses everything before it.

items.text: The iterator protocol: __iter__ and __next__, by hand.
items.how: Write a class Countdown whose __iter__ returns self and whose __next__ counts n down to 1, then raises StopIteration. Drive it by hand with iter() and next(), then with a for loop. Then write an iterable whose __iter__ returns a new iterator each time.
items.done: You can explain the difference between an iterable and an iterator, and why a second for loop over the same iterator prints nothing.

items.text: Generators, yield, generator expressions, yield from.
items.how: Rewrite Countdown as a generator function and compare the line count. Write the same thing as a generator expression, then a generator that delegates to two sub-generators with yield from. Put a print before each yield to see when the body actually runs.
items.done: You can say why a generator object can only be iterated once and at what moment its body code runs.

items.text: Lazy pipelines: chain generators instead of building lists.
items.how: Build a chain of generator functions, read_lines then parse then keep_errors then count_by_key, each taking an iterable and yielding. Run it on a large log file, then write a version that builds a list at every stage and compare peak memory.
items.done: Each stage can be tested alone on a three-item list, and the full pipeline holds about one line in memory at a time.

items.text: itertools — at minimum islice, chain, groupby, tee.
items.how: Try islice, chain, groupby and tee in the REPL on small lists. Run groupby on unsorted input to see it only groups consecutive keys, then sort first. Take the first 10 lines of a file with islice instead of reading it into a list.
items.done: You can predict the output of groupby on unsorted data and explain why tee can use a lot of memory.

items.text: Identity vs equality; hashability; why dict keys must be immutable.
items.how: In the REPL compare is and == on lists, small ints and strings, and check id(). Write a class with __eq__ but no __hash__ and try to add it to a set. Then use a tuple that contains a list as a dict key and read the error.
items.done: You can explain why a key that changes after insertion breaks dict lookup, and why defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None.

items.text: Mutable default arguments and other shared-state traps.
items.how: Write def add(item, bucket=[]), call it three times and print the result. Fix it with a None sentinel. Then reproduce two more shared-state traps: a list as a class attribute shared by all instances, and a grid built with [[0] * 3] * 3.
items.done: You can explain that default values are evaluated once, when def runs, and spot the bug in someone else's code.

items.text: Build: process a multi-GB file with flat memory usage. Prove it with a memory profile.
items.how: Generate a test file of several GB. Write a one-pass generator pipeline that aggregates it. Measure peak memory with tracemalloc.get_traced_memory() (or the process peak in Task Manager) on a 100 MB and a multi-GB input, then write the list-based version and measure it too.
items.done: Peak memory is about the same for the 100 MB and multi-GB inputs, and both numbers are written down next to the list version's.

sections.title: Week 6 — protocols, decorators, typing
sections.guide: Do decorators and context managers first (about two days), then type hints and a full type-checker run (two days), and finish with the module refactor. The refactored project is a good base for the engineering challenge that follows.

items.text: Write decorators from scratch: timer, retry with backoff, logger, cache.
items.how: Write each decorator as a function returning a wrapper: timer using time.perf_counter, retry that re-calls on an exception with doubling sleeps, logger that logs arguments and return value, cache that stores results in a dict keyed on the arguments. Test each one.
items.done: You can write timer from a blank file and explain that @timer means f = timer(f).

items.text: functools.wraps, and decorators that take arguments.
items.how: Print __name__ and __doc__ of a decorated function with and without @functools.wraps. Then turn retry into retry(times=3, delay=0.5), which needs three nested functions: the factory, the decorator and the wrapper.
items.done: You can explain why a decorator that takes arguments needs one more level of nesting than one that does not.

items.text: Write a context manager as a class, then again with @contextmanager.
items.how: Write a Timer class with __enter__ and __exit__ that records elapsed time, then the same with @contextlib.contextmanager using try/finally around yield. Raise an exception inside the with block and check that cleanup still runs in both.
items.done: Cleanup runs when the body raises, and you can say what returning True from __exit__ does to the exception.

items.text: Type hints: X | None over Optional, unions, Protocol, Self, @override, TypedDict, and PEP 695 generics (def first[T](xs: list[T]), type Row = dict[str, int]).
items.how: Annotate one small module using each feature at least once: X | None returns, a Protocol argument, Self on a builder method, @override in a subclass, a TypedDict record, a PEP 695 generic function and a type alias. Run a type checker on it.
items.done: The module type-checks clean, and a deliberately wrong call against each annotation is reported by the checker.

items.text: Run a type checker over an old project and fix what it finds.
items.how: Install mypy and run it on a project from an earlier phase. Start with default settings, fix errors one file at a time, then turn on --strict for one module. Keep a list of real bugs found versus missing-annotation noise.
items.done: The checker exits with zero errors on the project, and you can name at least one real bug it caught.

items.text: Refactor one earlier project into clean module boundaries.
items.how: Pick an earlier project and draw its modules and which imports which. Move code so that I/O, core logic and the CLI sit in separate modules and the core imports neither of the others. Import each module on its own to check for cycles.
items.done: Each module has one stated job, nothing has an import cycle, and the core module imports nothing from the CLI or I/O code.

sections.title: Engineering challenge
sections.guide: One refactor of File Organizer, done in this order: split the four layers, share one code path for dry-run and execute, then write the disk-free tests, which prove the redesign worked. Plan about a week; most of it goes on the split.

items.text: Redesign File Organizer so classification logic is testable without touching a disk.
items.how: Write classify() as a pure function that takes plain data (name, suffix, size, modified time) and returns a destination, with no os, shutil or Path I/O calls. The scanner builds that data and a separate mover acts on the result.
items.done: You can call classify() in the REPL with hand-made inputs while no test directory exists anywhere.

items.text: Separate: pure decision logic / filesystem effects / configuration / logging.
items.how: Make four modules: rules.py (pure decisions), fs.py (scan, move, mkdir), config.py (load and validate settings into a dataclass) and cli.py, which wires them together. Only cli.py configures logging; the others call logging.getLogger(__name__).
items.done: rules.py imports nothing from the other three modules and contains no open(, shutil or os calls.

items.text: Add dry-run and execute modes sharing one code path.
items.how: Make the planner return a list of planned moves (source, destination). Execute mode hands that list to an executor that moves files; dry-run hands it to one that only logs. Add a --dry-run flag with argparse.
items.done: Dry-run and execute log the same plan for the same folder, and after a dry-run the folder is unchanged.

items.text: Test the decision logic with zero filesystem access.
items.how: Write pytest tests that feed the planner lists of fake file records and assert on the returned moves: name clashes, unknown suffixes, duplicates, empty input. Add a fixture that uses monkeypatch to make shutil.move and Path.iterdir raise, so any disk access fails the test.
items.done: The decision tests pass with the disk-access guard active and the whole file runs in under a second.

gate.note: Explain each one. Reproducing syntax does not count.

items.text: Implement an iterator class and an equivalent generator, and say why you'd choose each.
Write a caching decorator from a blank file, with functools.wraps applied correctly.
Write a context manager both ways and explain what __exit__ returning True does.
Explain when a generator saves memory and when it saves nothing.
Type-check a project cleanly and explain one error the checker caught.

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Read in order: environments and lockfiles, then pyproject.toml and layout, then entry points, then lint, type-check and release habits. Allow about two days, and try each idea in a throwaway project as you read, because the build section applies all of it to a real tool.

items.text: Virtual environments and why global installs eventually break you.
items.how: Create a venv with python -m venv .venv, activate it, and compare sys.prefix and pip list inside and outside it. Install two packages, delete the folder, and rebuild it from a requirements.txt. Run where python to see which interpreter your shell finds.
items.done: You can explain what activation changes (PATH) and why two projects needing different versions of one library cannot share a global install.

items.text: Dependency resolution, lockfiles, and reproducible installs.
items.how: Start a project with uv init, add two dependencies with uv add, and open uv.lock to see exact versions and hashes for every transitive dependency. Delete .venv, run uv sync and confirm the same versions come back.
items.done: You can explain the difference between a version range in pyproject.toml and a pin in the lockfile.

items.text: pyproject.toml: metadata, dependencies, optional groups, tool config.
items.how: Write a pyproject.toml by hand with [build-system], [project] (name, version, requires-python, dependencies), a dev extra under [project.optional-dependencies] and a [tool.ruff] table. Install it with pip install -e . and check pip show.
items.done: The project installs in editable mode and you can say which table the build backend, the installer and Ruff each read.

items.text: src-layout vs flat layout — and why src-layout catches import bugs.
items.how: Make a flat-layout package and run its tests from the project root: they pass without installing. Move it under src/ and watch the tests fail until you install it. That failure is the point: tests now run against the installed package, not the working directory.
items.done: You can explain how the current directory on sys.path hides files missing from the built wheel in a flat layout.

items.text: Console-script entry points so your-tool works from any directory.
items.how: Add [project.scripts] with your-tool = "your_package.cli:main", reinstall, and run your-tool --help from another directory. Find the generated launcher in .venv/Scripts (Windows) or .venv/bin.
items.done: your-tool runs from any directory while the venv is active, and you can name the function it calls.

items.text: Linting and formatting as a pre-commit hook, not a manual chore.
items.how: Install pre-commit, write a .pre-commit-config.yaml using the ruff-pre-commit hooks for ruff check --fix and ruff format, run pre-commit install, then commit a badly formatted file and watch the hook stop the commit.
items.done: A commit containing a lint error is rejected locally without you running any check by hand.

items.text: Static type checking in CI.
items.how: Write a GitHub Actions workflow that installs the project and runs mypy on every push and pull request. Push a commit with a deliberate type error, confirm the run fails, then fix it.
items.done: A pushed type error turns the CI run red, and the fix turns it green.

items.text: Semantic versioning and writing a changelog.
items.how: Read the SemVer spec and Keep a Changelog. Decide the version bump for three changes: a bug fix, a new option, a removed flag. Start a CHANGELOG.md with an Unreleased section and Added, Changed, Fixed and Removed headings.
items.done: You can say whether a change needs a major, minor or patch bump, and what a 0.x version does and does not promise.

sections.title: Build — promote one tool to a real package
sections.guide: Choose one earlier tool and do the steps in order; each depends on the one before. Budget about a week: a day for the restructure and pyproject.toml, a day for tooling, and the rest on fixtures, property tests and the README. Finish by installing from a clean venv.

items.text: Restructure into src/your_package/ with a tests/ sibling.
items.how: Move the code into src/your_package/ with an __init__.py, put tests in tests/ beside src/, and change every import to use the package name. Install with pip install -e . and run pytest from the project root.
items.done: pytest passes after installation, and import your_package works from any other directory.

items.text: Write a complete pyproject.toml including the CLI entry point.
items.how: Fill in name, version, description, readme, requires-python, license, dependencies, a dev extra and [project.scripts]. Build with python -m build or uv build, install the wheel into a fresh venv, and run the command there.
items.done: The wheel installs into a clean venv and the CLI command runs there with no source checkout on the path.

items.text: Configure Ruff and a type checker in that same file.
items.how: Add [tool.ruff] with line-length and target-version, [tool.ruff.lint] with a select list (start with E, F, I, B, UP), and [tool.mypy] with strict = true or a stated subset. Run both and fix or explicitly ignore every finding.
items.done: ruff check ., ruff format --check . and mypy all exit 0 using settings from pyproject.toml only.

items.text: Add a conftest.py with shared fixtures.
items.how: Find setup repeated across test files (sample config, fake data, temp folders) and move it into fixtures in tests/conftest.py. Use the built-in tmp_path for files and choose each fixture's scope on purpose. Run pytest --fixtures to list them.
items.done: No test file carries its own copy of shared setup, and pytest --fixtures lists yours with docstrings.

items.text: Add at least one Hypothesis property test.
items.how: Pick a function with a clear invariant, such as a round trip (parse(format(x)) == x) or output that is always sorted. Write a @given test using hypothesis.strategies, run it, and read the shrunk example if it fails.
items.done: The property test runs in your normal pytest run and you can state its invariant in one sentence.

items.text: Write a README with install, usage, configuration, limitations.
items.how: Write four sections: install (exact commands from a clean machine), usage (real command lines and their output), configuration (every option and its default), limitations (what the tool does not handle). Then follow the README word for word in a new venv.
items.done: Someone following only the README in a fresh environment can install, configure and run the tool.

pytest -q
your-tool --help

Explain what belongs in pyproject.toml versus what belongs in code.

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Go in order: C and memory first, since everything after depends on it, then linear structures, hashing, trees, heaps, tries and graphs, then the notation and memory-management topics. For each, watch or read the explanation, then step through the VisuAlgo animation. About a week in total.

items.text: Enough C to understand pointers, memory, and why Python costs what it costs.
items.how: Watch CS50 week 4 (Memory) and do its problems, or write small C programs that print addresses with %p, allocate with malloc and free, and walk an array with pointer arithmetic. Then compare sys.getsizeof(1) and a list of ints with the C sizes.
items.done: You can explain why a Python list of a million ints uses several times more memory than a C int array of the same length.

items.text: Arrays vs linked lists — cache behaviour, not just Big O.
items.how: Use timeit to compare summing a million numbers stored in a list with walking a million nodes of a small linked-list class. Read about locality of reference and explain the gap in terms of contiguous memory and cache lines, not operation counts.
items.done: You have a measured ratio and can explain why a linked list is slower to traverse even though both walks are O(n).

items.text: Stacks and queues, and where each shows up in real systems.
items.how: Use a list as a stack and collections.deque as a queue, and time list.pop(0) against deque.popleft() at 100,000 items. Write down real uses of each: call stack, undo history, bracket matching; print spoolers, BFS, job queues.

where.name: Tutorial: lists as stacks and queues

items.done: You can say why list.pop(0) is O(n) and name a real system that relies on each structure.

items.text: Hash tables: hashing, collisions, load factor, resizing.
items.how: Watch the hash table part of CS50 week 5, then insert keys on VisuAlgo's hash table page under linear probing and separate chaining. Work out the load factor after each insert, note when a resize would trigger, and why it has to rehash every key.
items.done: You can explain how collisions push lookup towards O(n) and why resizing keeps average lookup O(1).

items.text: Trees, binary search trees, balancing, traversals.
items.how: On VisuAlgo, insert the same keys into a BST in sorted order and in shuffled order and compare the heights. Write pre-order, in-order and post-order for a small tree by hand, and step through AVL rotations to see how balance is restored.
items.done: You can give all three traversals of a 7-node tree from memory and explain why sorted input turns a plain BST into a list.

items.text: Heaps and priority queues.
items.how: On VisuAlgo's heap page, insert and extract-max and watch sift-up and sift-down. Then use heapq to keep the 10 smallest items of a stream and to merge sorted lists. Draw the array-to-tree mapping: children of index i sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2.
items.done: You can state the heap invariant, the index formulas, and why push and pop are O(log n).

items.text: Tries and prefix problems.
items.how: Draw a trie for ten words by hand and mark which nodes a prefix search for 'ca' visits. Compare that with filtering the word list using str.startswith, and note how each cost changes as the list grows.
items.done: You can explain why a trie prefix lookup depends on the prefix length, not on how many words are stored.

items.text: Graphs: adjacency list vs matrix, directed vs weighted.
items.how: Represent one small directed, weighted graph as a dict of lists and as a 2D matrix. For each, work out the cost of listing a node's neighbours and of checking one edge, and the memory needed for a sparse graph with 10,000 nodes.
items.done: You can choose adjacency list or matrix for a given graph density and justify the choice with numbers.

items.text: Big O, Θ, Ω — and the difference between them.
items.how: Read the formal definitions of O, Omega and Theta. Write one function whose running time is Theta(n) and one whose best and worst cases differ (linear search). Then classify the loops in five of your own functions.
items.done: You can explain that O is an upper bound, Omega a lower bound and Theta both, and that none of them means worst case on its own.

items.text: Stack vs heap, allocation, and what garbage collection buys you.
items.how: Read how stack frames and heap allocation work (CS50 week 4), then how CPython frees memory: reference counting plus a cycle collector. Build a reference cycle, delete the names, and check the return value of gc.collect().
items.done: You can explain what reference counting frees at once, what needs the cycle collector, and what garbage collection costs.

sections.title: Build — pystructures
sections.guide: Build a pystructures package with one module per structure, in the order listed, because later ones reuse earlier ones: the stack sits on your array, the queue on your linked list, BFS on your queue. Write tests and the benchmark with each structure, not at the end. Allow one to two days per structure.

items.text: Implement dynamic array with amortized growth.
items.how: Write DynamicArray on a preallocated list ([None] * capacity) using only index reads and writes, with append, pop, __getitem__ and __len__. Double the capacity when full and copy. Count total copies over a million appends.
items.done: Total copies over n appends stay below 2n, and you can explain why doubling gives amortised O(1) append.

items.text: Implement singly and doubly linked list.
items.how: Write SinglyLinkedList with push_front, append (keep a tail pointer), pop_front, find and remove, and DoublyLinkedList with O(1) removal of a known node. Add __iter__ and __len__. Test empty lists, one node, and removing the tail.
items.done: Tests pass for empty, one-node and tail-removal cases, and you can say which operations are O(1) in each list.

items.text: Implement stack and queue on top of your own primitives.
items.how: Build Stack on your DynamicArray and Queue on your linked list (enqueue at the tail, dequeue at the head), without using list methods or deque inside them. Raise a clear exception when popping from an empty one.
items.done: Push, pop, enqueue and dequeue are O(1) (amortised for the stack), and tests cover the empty case.

items.text: Implement hash table with collision handling and resizing.
items.how: Write HashTable with __setitem__, __getitem__, __delitem__ and __len__, using separate chaining. Index with hash(key) % capacity, resize when the load factor passes 0.75, and test with a key class whose __hash__ always returns 1.
items.done: Tests pass with all keys colliding, and every key is still retrievable after several resizes.

items.text: Implement binary search tree with insert, search, delete, traversals.
items.how: Write a BST with insert, search and delete covering all three delete cases: leaf, one child, two children (replace with the in-order successor). Add pre-order, in-order, post-order and level-order traversals as generators.
items.done: In-order traversal matches sorted() after any random mix of inserts and deletes.

items.text: Implement min-heap with sift-up and sift-down.
items.how: Store the heap in a list. Write push (append, then sift-up), pop (swap root with last, remove it, sift-down) and heapify in O(n) by sifting down from the last parent to the root. Check results against heapq on random inputs.
items.done: Popping everything returns items in sorted order and matches heapq on thousands of random lists.

items.text: Implement graph with BFS and DFS.
items.how: Write Graph with an adjacency dict and add_edge for directed or undirected edges. Add bfs using your Queue and dfs both recursively and with your Stack. Return the visit order and, from BFS, the shortest path by edge count.
items.done: BFS returns shortest edge-count paths on test graphs, and iterative DFS walks a 100,000-node chain without a RecursionError.

items.text: Implement trie with insert, search, prefix search.
items.how: Write Trie with nodes that hold a dict of children and an end-of-word flag. Implement insert, search for whole words, and starts_with that yields every word under a prefix. Load a word list and test prefixes with zero, one and many matches.
items.done: starts_with returns the same set as filtering the word list with str.startswith, for every prefix you test.

items.text: Every structure gets tests and a benchmark against the stdlib equivalent.
items.how: For each structure write pytest tests with edge cases, and a timeit benchmark against its stdlib counterpart: list, collections.deque, dict, heapq, bisect on a sorted list. Record the ratios in a table in the README.
items.done: Every structure has passing tests and a recorded speed ratio, and you can explain why the stdlib version is faster.
