sections.title: Study in this order
sections.guide: Take the topics in the listed order, since each builds on earlier ones. For each topic, read or watch the explanation, then solve three to five problems in that category before moving on. Expect roughly two or three topics a week alongside the daily routine.

items.text: Complexity analysis — estimate before you code.
items.how: Before coding each problem, write down the input limit and the complexity it allows, assuming roughly 10^7 simple Python operations per second. Then time your solution on the largest input and compare with the estimate.
items.done: Your estimate and the measured time on the largest input agree within a factor of ten.

items.text: Binary search, including on answers rather than arrays.
items.how: Write binary search from scratch with a stated loop invariant and compare it with bisect_left and bisect_right. Then solve a search-on-the-answer problem, such as the smallest ship capacity that delivers all packages in D days, using a feasibility check.
items.done: You write binary search without off-by-one errors and can state the monotonic condition that makes searching the answer valid.

items.text: Sorting: what the stdlib does and when you'd ever write your own.
items.how: Read the sorting HOWTO and practise key=, multi-key sorts and stability. Implement merge sort and counting sort once each and time them against sorted(). Note when a custom approach wins: a small integer range, or top-k with heapq.nsmallest.
items.done: You can say that sorted() is stable and O(n log n), and name one case where counting sort beats it.

items.text: Recursion, and converting recursion to iteration.
items.how: Write a recursive function for tree depth or permutations, then rewrite it with an explicit stack. Feed the recursive version an input deep enough to raise RecursionError, check sys.getrecursionlimit(), and confirm the iterative version succeeds.
items.done: You can convert a recursive DFS into a loop with an explicit stack and explain what the call stack was holding.

items.text: Divide and conquer.
items.how: Implement merge sort and use it to count inversions, then solve maximum subarray by divide and conquer. For each, write the recurrence and solve it with the master theorem.
items.done: You can write the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) for merge sort and explain why it solves to O(n log n).

items.text: Greedy — and how to prove a greedy choice is safe.
items.how: Solve interval scheduling (most non-overlapping intervals) by picking the earliest end time. Then break a greedy: coin change with coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6 gives 4+1+1 instead of 3+3. Write an exchange argument for why the interval greedy is safe.
items.done: You can give a counterexample to a wrong greedy and a short exchange argument for a correct one.

items.text: BFS and DFS on grids and graphs.
items.how: Solve a grid problem (count islands, shortest path through a maze) with BFS on collections.deque, and a connectivity or cycle problem with DFS. Write a neighbours helper for grid moves and mark cells visited when you enqueue them.
items.done: You can explain why BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs and why marking on enqueue avoids duplicate work.

items.text: Heaps and priority queues in anger.
items.how: Solve three problems with heapq: k-th largest element, merge k sorted lists, and a running median with two heaps. Push tuples (priority, counter, item) so ties never compare the items themselves.
items.done: You can solve k-th largest in O(n log k) and explain the invariant that keeps the two median heaps balanced.

items.text: Dynamic programming: memoize first, tabulate second.
items.how: For climbing stairs, coin change and longest common subsequence: write the plain recursion, add @functools.cache, then turn it into a bottom-up table. Write the subproblem and recurrence in one line before coding each.
items.done: You can write the state, recurrence and base case for coin change and derive the table version from the memoised one.

items.text: Shortest paths: Dijkstra, and when BFS is enough.
items.how: Implement Dijkstra with heapq, skipping stale heap entries. Solve one unweighted problem with BFS and one with 0/1 weights using a deque. Run your Dijkstra on a graph with a negative edge and find the wrong answer it gives.
items.done: You can say when BFS, 0-1 BFS and Dijkstra each apply, and why a negative edge breaks Dijkstra.

items.text: Backtracking and pruning.
items.how: Solve N-Queens, subsets and combination sum with one recursive choose, explore, unchoose template. Count the calls made with and without a pruning rule, for example stopping once the running sum exceeds the target.
items.done: You have call counts showing your pruning cuts the search, and you can write the template from memory.

sections.title: Daily problem routine
sections.guide: Run these seven steps on one problem a day, in order. Spend 20 to 30 minutes on the attempt, about 20 on the implementation and tests, and 10 on the write-up. Keep the 48-hour re-solves on a list and do them first each day.

items.text: Attempt for 20–30 minutes before reading anything.
items.how: Set a timer. Read the problem twice, work two examples by hand on paper, and try an approach before opening hints, solutions or a search engine. When the timer ends, write down where you got stuck.
items.done: Your notes for each problem record what you tried before you looked anything up.

items.text: Write the brute force first, even if it's obviously too slow.
items.how: Code the most direct solution, such as trying every pair or every subset, and run it on the examples. Keep it as the reference implementation that the fast version is checked against later.
items.done: You have a correct brute force for the problem, even if it only handles small inputs.

items.text: State its complexity, then state your target complexity.
items.how: Write the brute force's time and space complexity in a comment. Then read the input limits and write the complexity they require, for example n up to 10^5 needs O(n log n) or better.
items.done: Each problem has the brute-force and target complexities written down before you start the fast version.

items.text: Look for a data structure or invariant that closes the gap.
items.how: Ask what repeated work the brute force does and what would remove it: a hash map for lookups, sorting plus two pointers, a prefix sum, a heap, a monotonic stack. State the invariant your main loop keeps in one sentence.
items.done: You can name the structure or invariant that takes the solution from the brute-force complexity to the target.

items.text: Implement, then write edge-case tests.
items.how: Implement the fast version, then write pytest cases for empty input, one element, duplicates, negative numbers and the maximum size. Add a randomised test that compares it with the brute force on small inputs.
items.done: The fast and brute-force versions agree on hundreds of random small inputs, and the edge-case tests pass.

items.text: Explain the solution out loud or in your notes.
items.how: Write three to five sentences: the key idea, why it is correct, its complexity, and what you missed at first. Or explain it aloud without looking at the code, and write down any step you could not justify.
items.done: A week later you can explain the solution from your notes alone, without rereading the code.

items.text: Re-solve any problem you needed help on, 48 hours later, from scratch.
items.how: Log every problem you needed a hint or solution for, with the date. Two days later, solve it again in a blank file without looking at the old code, then compare the two versions.
items.done: You re-solve each logged problem from scratch, with no hints, within your original time budget.

sections.title: Challenge ladder
sections.guide: Optional. Climb one level at a time within a topic: a direct problem, then the harder variant, then mixed problems with no category given, then a messy real-world one. Move up when you solve two in a row at a level without hints.

items.text: Level 1 — direct implementation of a known technique.
items.how: Pick easy problems labelled with the technique you studied last, for example an easy binary search problem on NeetCode or a matching Exercism exercise, and apply the standard technique directly.
items.done: You solve an easy problem in the named category within 20 minutes without hints.

items.text: Level 2 — same problem, optimize the complexity.
items.how: Take a problem you solved slowly and improve its complexity, for example O(n^2) to O(n log n) or O(n). Time both versions with timeit on the largest allowed input.
items.done: The faster version passes the full limits, and your timings show the gap against the first version.

items.text: Level 3 — solve without being told the category.
items.how: Solve problems whose category is hidden: Codewars katas at your rank or Advent of Code puzzles from past years. Before coding, write down which technique you chose and why.
items.done: You pick a working technique before coding for most unlabelled problems, and your notes record the reasoning.

items.text: Level 4 — real-world problem with messy input and hard constraints.
items.how: Solve a full Advent of Code day, including parsing the raw input file, or process a real dataset under a memory or time limit. Handle malformed lines explicitly and test the parser on a small sample first.
items.done: The solution gives the accepted answer on the full input within the limits, and bad lines are reported, not silently skipped.

gate.note: On a problem you've never seen, in one sitting:

items.text: Identify the likely data structure before writing code.
State a target complexity and justify it.
Implement a correct solution.
Write tests that cover the edge cases you predicted.
Explain why it's correct, not just that it passes.

phases.name: Linux & systems
phases.aim: Learn the operating system your Python runs on. Many production bugs come from the environment.

resources.name: MIT — The Missing Semester
resources.why: Shell, tooling, scripting: the class no one teaches

resources.name: Linux Journey
resources.why: Command line, permissions, processes, filesystem

resources.name: OverTheWire — Bandit
resources.why: Terminal fluency through puzzles

resources.name: subprocess
resources.why: Launching and controlling processes from Python

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The command-line and OS basics the rest of the course assumes. Work top to bottom on a real Linux shell (WSL or a VM is fine), spending about two thirds of the time typing commands and one third reading. Play OverTheWire Bandit alongside items 3 to 5.

items.text: Filesystem layout, paths, permissions, ownership.
items.how: Run ls -l, stat and id on files in /etc, /tmp and your home directory. Create a file, set chmod 640, then try to read it as another user and explain the error. Read man hier to learn what lives in /usr, /var and /proc.
items.done: You can read a mode string such as drwxr-x--- and say who can list, enter and write that directory.

items.text: Environment variables, PATH, and shell startup files.
items.how: Set a variable with and without export and check which one bash -c 'echo $X' sees. Add a directory to PATH in ~/.bashrc, open a login and a non-login shell, and note which startup files ran. Read the same value from Python with os.environ.
items.done: You can explain why a variable set in ~/.bashrc is missing inside a cron job or a systemd service.

items.text: Processes, PIDs, signals, exit codes.
items.how: Start sleep 300 &, find its PID with ps, then send SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGKILL with kill and read $? after wait. In Python, register a handler with signal.signal and confirm it runs for SIGTERM but not for SIGKILL.
items.done: You can say why SIGKILL cannot be caught and why a shell reports exit status 143 after SIGTERM.

items.text: stdin, stdout, stderr — and redirecting each independently.
items.how: Write a script that prints one line to sys.stdout and one to sys.stderr. Run it with > out.txt, 2> err.txt, > all.txt 2>&1 and 2>&1 > all.txt, and work out why the last two give different results.
items.done: You can send stdout and stderr to separate files, or merge them, without checking notes.

items.text: Pipes, and composing small tools into a pipeline.
items.how: Answer a question about a log file with a pipeline: cut a field, sort, uniq -c, sort -rn, head. Then write a Python filter that reads sys.stdin line by line and put it mid-pipeline. Add set -o pipefail and see how a failing stage changes $?.
items.done: You can build a one-line pipeline that answers a log question, such as the ten most frequent IP addresses.

items.text: grep · find · sed · awk · xargs at working level.
items.how: Play OverTheWire Bandit levels 0 to 15, which mostly need find, grep and pipes. Then on a source tree run find . -name '*.py' -print0 | xargs -0 grep -l TODO, rename a word with sed -i, and total a column with awk.
items.done: You can find files by name, size or age and edit text in place across many files without opening an editor.

items.text: SSH, key auth, and port forwarding.
items.how: Generate a key with ssh-keygen -t ed25519, install it on a VM or WSL host running sshd with ssh-copy-id, and log in without a password. Add a Host block to ~/.ssh/config, then forward a remote port with ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 and open it locally.
items.done: You can log in with a key only and say which end listens in an -L forward and which in an -R forward.

items.text: Services, journald/syslog, and reading logs under pressure.
items.how: Write a small systemd unit that runs a Python script, start it with systemctl start, and follow it with journalctl -u name -f. Make the script crash, then find the traceback with systemctl status and journalctl -u name --since '10 min ago'.
items.done: You can find why a service stopped, with its timestamp and error line, in under two minutes.

items.text: cron and scheduled work.
items.how: Add a crontab -e entry that runs a Python script every five minutes and appends to a log. Use absolute paths, redirect stderr too, and confirm it ran. Then make it rely on your PATH, watch it fail, and read the failure in the log.
items.done: You can write a cron line for a given schedule and name the usual reasons a job works in a terminal but fails under cron.

items.text: Shell scripting: variables, conditionals, loops, set -euo pipefail.
items.how: Write a backup script that takes a directory argument, checks it exists, loops over its files and exits non-zero on failure. Start it with set -euo pipefail, quote every variable, and run it through ShellCheck until it reports nothing.
items.done: Your script passes ShellCheck and stops at the first failing command, including one inside a pipeline.

sections.title: Build — process manager CLI
sections.guide: A Python CLI that applies what you learned about processes, signals and streams. Build the items in order, since stopping and logging depend on starting. Spend most of the time on items 1, 2 and 5; the listing and report steps are short.

items.text: List processes with CPU and memory usage.
items.how: Use psutil.process_iter to read pid, name, CPU and memory. Call cpu_percent once, sleep briefly, then read it again, since the first call returns 0.0. Catch psutil.NoSuchProcess and psutil.AccessDenied for processes that exit or are protected.
items.done: Your list matches top or Task Manager within a few percent and never crashes when a process exits mid-scan.

items.text: Start a command and capture its output correctly.
items.how: Run commands with subprocess.run using a list of arguments rather than shell=True, with capture_output=True, text=True and a timeout. Return stdout, stderr and the return code separately, and test with a failing command and a missing one.
items.done: A failing command, a missing command and a timeout each produce a distinct, clear result instead of a traceback.

items.text: Stop a process cleanly, then forcibly, and handle both.
items.how: Start the child with subprocess.Popen, call terminate(), then wait(timeout=5), and on TimeoutExpired call kill(). Test with a child that ignores SIGTERM. On Linux pass start_new_session=True and signal the group so grandchildren stop too.
items.done: A child that ignores SIGTERM is killed after the grace period, and your tool reports which path it took.

items.text: Record activity to a rotating log.
items.how: Configure logging.handlers.RotatingFileHandler with maxBytes and backupCount, and log each start, stop and exit code with a timestamp. Set maxBytes to a few kilobytes and run a loop to watch the files rotate.
items.done: The log directory never holds more than backupCount + 1 files and the newest entries are in the unsuffixed file.

items.text: Export a report as JSON and as a formatted table.
items.how: Collect results as a list of dicts, write them with json.dumps(indent=2), and render the same data as an aligned text table using format specs such as {:>8}. Add a --format option with argparse that picks json or table.
items.done: The JSON output loads back with json.loads and the table columns line up for names of any length.

items.text: Handle a process that writes gigabytes to stdout without exploding.
items.how: Run a script that prints without end under capture_output=True and a timeout, and watch memory climb. Replace it with Popen(stdout=PIPE) read in fixed-size chunks, keeping only a tail in a collections.deque, or send stdout straight to a file.
items.done: Your tool's memory stays flat, measured with psutil, while the child writes several gigabytes.

gate.note: Work only on your own machine. The goal is understanding the system.

items.text: Diagnose why a script works in your shell but fails under cron.
Find which process is holding a port, and explain how you found it.
Write a shell script that's safe under spaces-in-filenames and failure.
Explain what a zombie process is and how one is created.
Clear at least level 15 of OverTheWire Bandit.

phases.name: Networking
phases.aim: Learn every step between a client and a server, so you can find where a failed API call broke.

resources.name: MDN — HTTP
resources.why: Methods, headers, status codes, caching, CORS

resources.name: Python socket
resources.why: TCP and UDP at the level below the framework

resources.name: HTTPX
resources.why: Modern HTTP client, sync and async

sections.title: Learn in this order
sections.guide: How bytes get from a client to a server and back, lowest layer first. Keep the order, since each item assumes the ones above. Pair every item with a command you run, such as ss, dig, curl -v or openssl s_client; aim for about half reading and half probing.

items.text: IP addresses, ports, and what 'listening' means.
items.how: Run ss -tlnp (or netstat -ano on Windows) and match each listening port to a program. Start python -m http.server 8000, then restart it with --bind 127.0.0.1, and try to reach each from another machine on your network.
items.done: You can explain the difference between binding to 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0 and find which process owns a port.

items.text: TCP vs UDP: ordering, delivery, handshake, cost.
items.how: Capture a curl request with Wireshark or tcpdump -i any port 80 and find the SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK. Then send UDP datagrams with sendto on a SOCK_DGRAM socket to a port nobody listens on and note that no error comes back.
items.done: You can say what TCP guarantees that UDP does not, and what the handshake costs in round trips.

items.text: DNS resolution and where it's cached.
items.how: Resolve a name with dig or nslookup, then with socket.getaddrinfo, and compare the answers and TTL. Read /etc/resolv.conf and /etc/nsswitch.conf, add an entry to /etc/hosts, and check which of the two lookups it changes.
items.done: You can list where a lookup can be answered: hosts file, local cache, recursive resolver, authoritative server.

items.text: The HTTP request/response cycle, byte by byte.
items.how: Run curl -v http://example.com and read every request and response line. Then open a TCP connection with nc example.com 80, type a GET request with a Host header and a blank line, and label the status line, headers and body in the reply.
items.done: You can write a valid HTTP/1.1 request from memory and explain how the client knows where the body ends.

items.text: Headers, cookies, sessions, and where auth state lives.
items.how: Log in to a site with browser developer tools open and follow the Set-Cookie header and the Cookie header on later requests. Compare with an API that sends Authorization: Bearer. Note what the HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite attributes each block.
items.done: For a given app you can say whether auth state lives in a server session, a signed cookie or a token, and how it travels.

items.text: TLS conceptually: certificates, chains, and what verification proves.
items.how: Run openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com and read the certificate chain. Then connect with ssl.create_default_context() to wrong.host.badssl.com and expired.badssl.com and read each verification error.
items.done: You can say what verification proves (a trusted CA vouches that this key belongs to this name) and what it does not.

items.text: REST semantics, idempotency, and correct status codes.
items.how: Read the method and status references, then design endpoints for one resource and assign each a method and the codes it can return. Mark which methods are idempotent and explain why a retried POST can create duplicates while a retried PUT cannot.
items.done: You can choose between 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 and 422 for a given case and justify the choice.

items.text: WebSockets and when to use them over polling.
items.how: Read the opening handshake in RFC 6455 section 1.3 and watch the Upgrade request in developer tools on a site that uses WebSockets. Then compare the cost of polling and a WebSocket for a feed updated once a minute and one updated ten times a second.
items.done: You can explain how a connection upgrades from HTTP and give one case where polling or server-sent events fit better.

items.text: Timeouts, retries with jitter, and rate limiting — where each belongs.
items.how: Read the AWS article on timeouts, retries and jitter. Write a retry helper that retries only connection errors, 429 and 5xx, with exponential backoff and full jitter, and honours Retry-After. Note that timeouts and retries belong in the client, rate limits in the server or gateway.

where.name: AWS: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter

items.done: You can explain why retries without jitter cause a thundering herd and why a POST must not be retried blindly.

sections.title: Build, in this order
sections.guide: Five programs that turn the theory into code. Do them in order and use only the standard library for the first three. The raw HTTP client and server take the longest; budget about half the section's time for those two.

items.text: TCP chat: server accepts multiple clients, broadcasts messages.
items.how: Start with a socket server that accepts one client and echoes lines. Add a thread per client or a selectors loop, keep the set of connected sockets, and send each line to all the others. Drop clients on disconnect and test with three nc sessions.
items.done: Three clients chat at once, and killing one client does not crash the server or block the others.

items.text: HTTP client using raw sockets — parse the response yourself.
items.how: Connect with socket.create_connection, send a GET with Host and Connection: close headers, and read until the server closes. Split the headers at the first blank line, parse the status line and headers, then handle Content-Length and chunked transfer encoding.
items.done: Your client fetches a page and returns the same status, headers and body bytes as curl -i.

items.text: Minimal HTTP server: routing, headers, status codes, static files.
items.how: Accept connections with socket, parse the request line and headers yourself, and dispatch on method and path through a routing dict. Serve files from one directory with a Content-Type from mimetypes, and reject paths that escape it, such as ../../etc/passwd.
items.done: curl -i shows correct 200, 404 and 405 responses, and a path traversal attempt gets 403 or 404.

items.text: WebSocket chat with reconnection handling.
items.how: Build the server and client with the websockets library on asyncio and broadcast each message to every connection. Then make the client reconnect with backoff when the server restarts, and show a clear status while it is disconnected.
items.done: Restarting the server mid-chat makes clients reconnect on their own within a few seconds and carry on chatting.

items.text: Concurrent downloader with a timeout budget and retry policy.
items.how: Use httpx.AsyncClient with an asyncio.Semaphore to cap concurrency. Set per-request limits with httpx.Timeout, wrap the whole run in asyncio.timeout for an overall budget, and retry 5xx and connection errors with jittered backoff.
items.done: With one URL that hangs, the run still ends within the budget and reports which downloads failed and why.

gate.note: Take one real API call and describe every step.

items.text: Name resolution → connection → TLS → request → response → parse → error handling.
Say where a timeout belongs at each layer, and what happens if it's missing.
Explain why retrying a POST can be dangerous and how idempotency keys fix it.
Debug a failing request using only headers and status codes.
Explain what your minimal HTTP server does wrong that a real one handles.

phases.name: SQL & PostgreSQL
phases.aim: Learn how the database behaves on its own, not only through an ORM.

resources.name: PostgreSQL Tutorial
resources.why: Tables, queries, joins, constraints, transactions

resources.name: PostgreSQL Documentation
resources.why: Indexes, locking, planning, internals

resources.name: SQLAlchemy
resources.why: Only after you can write the SQL yourself

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: How PostgreSQL behaves, from single-table queries to plans and pooling. Work in psql against a real database and type every query. Items 0 to 5 are core and fairly quick; items 6, 8 and 9 need the most time. Keep a scratch file of the queries you write.

items.text: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and the WHERE clause.
items.how: Create a table in psql, insert rows, and practise SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT. Run each UPDATE and DELETE inside BEGIN and check the reported row count before COMMIT. Add RETURNING to see the rows a write touched.

where.name: PostgreSQL: Returning Data from Modified Rows

items.done: You can write filtered reads and safe writes without notes, and you check the row count before committing.

items.text: Joins: inner, left, and thinking relationally rather than procedurally.
items.how: Make two related tables, such as authors and books, and ask the same question with an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN. Find authors with no books using LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL. Then rewrite a Python loop that queries per row as one joined query.
items.done: You can predict the row count of an inner join and a left join before running either.

items.text: GROUP BY, HAVING, and aggregate functions.
items.how: Count and sum per group with GROUP BY, then filter rows with WHERE and groups with HAVING in the same query. Select a column that is not grouped to see the error, and compare count(*) with count(column) on a column that holds NULLs.
items.done: You can explain the difference between WHERE and HAVING and why count(column) skips NULLs.

items.text: Subqueries and CTEs; when a CTE hurts performance.
items.how: Write one question three ways: a subquery in WHERE, a correlated subquery, and a WITH clause, and compare them with EXPLAIN. Since PostgreSQL 12 a CTE used once is inlined; add MATERIALIZED and see how it can stop the planner pushing a filter down.
items.done: You can say when PostgreSQL 12+ materialises a CTE and show a plan where forcing it makes the query slower.

items.text: Constraints: primary keys, foreign keys, unique, check, not null.
items.how: Add each constraint type to a table, then write an INSERT that breaks each one and read the error. Create one foreign key with ON DELETE RESTRICT and one with ON DELETE CASCADE, and a CHECK such as due_date > loan_date.
items.done: You can name the constraint that stops each kind of bad row and say which rules only the database can enforce reliably.

items.text: Transactions, ACID, and explicit rollback.
items.how: Open two psql sessions. In one, BEGIN and update a row, and check the other still sees the old value until COMMIT. Then run a transfer between two accounts, cause an error halfway, ROLLBACK, and confirm both balances are unchanged.
items.done: You can explain each letter of ACID with an example from your own sessions.

items.text: Indexes: B-tree, composite ordering, and why an index can be ignored.
items.how: Load 100,000 rows, time a query on an unindexed column, add a B-tree index and time it again. Build an index on (a, b) and test filters on a, on b, and on both. Then find cases where the planner skips an index, such as a function on the column or a filter matching most rows.
items.done: You can predict whether a query will use a given composite index and confirm it with EXPLAIN.

items.text: Normalization to 3NF, and when you'd deliberately denormalize.
items.how: Take a flat sheet of loans that repeats member and book details on every row and split it step by step into 1NF, 2NF and 3NF tables. Then pick one derived value, such as a loan count on users, that you would store on purpose, and say how you would keep it correct.
items.done: You can point to a transitive dependency in a table and show the split that removes it.

items.text: Isolation levels, locking, and deadlocks.
items.how: In two sessions, read the same row twice under READ COMMITTED and then REPEATABLE READ while the other session commits a change, and compare. Then have each session update two rows in opposite order to cause a deadlock, and read the error PostgreSQL returns.
items.done: You can reproduce a deadlock on demand and state the usual fix: take row locks in a consistent order.

items.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE — read a query plan and act on it.
items.how: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a slow query and read it from the innermost node outwards. Compare estimated and actual rows, find the node with the most time, and note Seq Scan versus Index Scan. Change one thing, such as an index or running ANALYZE, and rerun.
items.done: You can name the most expensive node in a plan and say whether a bad row estimate caused it.

items.text: Connection pooling and why it matters under load.
items.how: Check SHOW max_connections, then open connections in a Python loop until the server refuses one. Repeat through a SQLAlchemy engine with pool_size and max_overflow and watch pg_stat_activity. Read how PgBouncer puts few server connections behind many clients.
items.done: You can explain why each PostgreSQL connection is costly and what an app does when its pool is exhausted.

sections.title: Build — LibraryOS
sections.guide: LibraryOS: a lending database built by hand before any ORM touches it. Follow the order exactly: schema on paper, DDL, data, reports, tuning, then SQLAlchemy. Seeding and the EXPLAIN work take the longest, so leave about half the time for them.

items.text: Design the schema on paper first: users, authors, books, loans, returns.
items.how: Write down each entity, its columns and every relationship with its cardinality, for example one user has many loans and each loan covers one book. Decide whether a return is its own table or a returned_at column on loans. List the business rules the schema must enforce.
items.done: You have a diagram with keys and cardinalities, and a written list of rules to turn into constraints.

items.text: Write the DDL by hand with every constraint you can justify.
items.how: Write schema.sql with CREATE TABLE statements, primary keys, foreign keys with a chosen ON DELETE action, and UNIQUE, NOT NULL and CHECK constraints. Put a comment above each constraint naming the rule it enforces, and apply it with psql -f schema.sql to a fresh database.
items.done: schema.sql applies cleanly to an empty database, and a bad INSERT for each rule is rejected.

items.text: Seed realistic data — tens of thousands of rows, not five.
items.how: Generate rows with generate_series and random() in SQL, or with Faker in Python loaded through COPY. Aim for about 10,000 users, 50,000 books and 200,000 loans with a realistic spread of dates and some overdue. Run ANALYZE afterwards.
items.done: Row counts reach the target, every constraint still holds, and a full reload takes seconds rather than minutes.

items.text: Write the reporting queries: overdue loans, top borrowers, stats by month.
items.how: Write each report as a named .sql file: overdue loans with days late, the top 10 borrowers in the last year, and loans and returns per month using date_trunc. Check each against a small hand-made data set where you already know the answer.
items.done: Each query returns the known answer on your hand-made data and completes on the full data set.

items.text: Find one slow query, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, add an index, measure the gain.
items.how: Time your reports with \timing in psql and pick the slowest. Save its EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output, add one index aimed at its filter or join, rerun, and save the new plan. Record both timings next to the plans.
items.done: You have before and after plans with a measured speed-up, and can say which plan node changed.

items.text: Only now, wrap it in SQLAlchemy and confirm the generated SQL matches your intent.
items.how: Map the tables with SQLAlchemy 2.0 declarative models and rewrite two reports with select(). Set echo=True on the engine, compare the logged SQL with your hand-written queries, and fix any N+1 pattern with selectinload or a join.
items.done: The ORM version returns the same rows as your SQL and issues a fixed number of queries, not one per row.

items.text: Design a normalized schema for a new domain from a plain-English description.
Write a five-table join with aggregation, from memory.
Show a query that got measurably faster because of an index you chose.
Explain what happens when two transactions update the same row.
Explain one thing your ORM does that you'd never have written by hand.

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The parts of a web service, taught through FastAPI. Items 0 to 2 set up the framework, 3 to 5 cover security, and 6 to 11 cover running and testing a service. Build one small practice app and extend it with each item; spend about two thirds of the time coding.

items.text: Routing, path and query params, and correct HTTP semantics.
items.how: Work through the FastAPI pages on path and query parameters. Build a small items API with typed path parameters, optional query parameters with defaults, and the fitting method for each action. Return 201 from creates and 404 when an item does not exist.
items.done: Wrong parameter types get a 422 without extra code, and each route uses the method and status code that fits.

items.text: Pydantic models for request validation and response shaping.
items.how: Define separate models for input and output, such as UserCreate with a password and UserOut without. Set response_model on the route, add a field_validator, and send bad payloads to read the 422 error body.
items.done: The password never appears in a response, and you can read a 422 body and say which field failed and why.

items.text: Dependency injection and why it makes testing trivial.
items.how: Write a get_db dependency and a get_current_user dependency and use both with Depends. In a test, replace each through app.dependency_overrides and call the route with TestClient.
items.done: A test calls a protected route with a fake user and no real database, only by overriding dependencies.

items.text: Authentication vs authorization.
items.how: Read the OWASP authentication and authorization cheat sheets. For your practice API, list which routes need a logged-in user (401 if not) and which need a role or ownership (403 if not). Implement one of each.
items.done: You can say when to return 401 and when 403, with an example of each from your own routes.

items.text: Sessions vs JWT: tradeoffs, revocation, refresh.
items.how: Implement login twice: once with a server-side session ID in a cookie, once with a short-lived JWT access token and a refresh token. For each, work out how to log a user out on every device and what that costs.
items.done: You can explain why a JWT cannot be revoked before expiry without server-side state, and how refresh tokens limit the damage.

items.text: Role and permission checks at the boundary, not scattered in handlers.
items.how: Write a dependency factory such as require_role('admin') that raises 403, and attach it with dependencies=[Depends(...)] on a route or a whole router. Remove every inline role check from handler bodies and add a test for each protected route.

where.name: FastAPI: Dependencies in path operation decorators

items.done: A search for role checks finds them only in dependencies, and each protected route has a test that expects 403.

items.text: Middleware: logging, request IDs, error handling.
items.how: Write an @app.middleware('http') function that assigns a request ID, stores it in a contextvars.ContextVar, adds it to the response headers and logs method, path, status and duration. Add an exception handler that returns JSON with the request ID instead of a traceback.
items.done: Every response carries an X-Request-ID header, and an unhandled error returns JSON with that ID and is logged once.

items.text: Background tasks, and when you need a real queue instead.
items.how: Run a slow task, such as sending an email, with FastAPI BackgroundTasks and note that it runs in the same process after the response. List what is lost if the process restarts mid-task, then compare a queue such as Celery or RQ that stores jobs and retries them.
items.done: You can say when BackgroundTasks is enough and name two needs, such as retries or surviving restarts, that call for a queue.

items.text: Pagination, filtering, and sorting that survives a million rows.
items.how: Load a million rows and compare OFFSET 900000 LIMIT 20 with a keyset query that filters on the last seen (created_at, id), using EXPLAIN ANALYZE on both. Allow filters and sorting only on an allow-list of indexed columns.

where.name: Use The Index, Luke: No Offset

items.done: A deep page loads as fast as page one, and an unknown sort field returns 422 instead of running a slow query.

items.text: Migrations with Alembic.
items.how: Run alembic init, point env.py at your models' metadata, and create a migration with alembic revision --autogenerate. Read and correct the generated file before alembic upgrade head, then test alembic downgrade -1.
items.done: A fresh database reaches the current schema with upgrade head, and the latest migration downgrades cleanly.

items.text: Configuration and secrets from the environment, never in Git.
items.how: Move every setting into a pydantic-settings BaseSettings class read from environment variables, with a .env file for local use listed in .gitignore. Commit a .env.example with dummy values, and search the history with git log -p for any secret already committed.
items.done: The app starts from environment variables alone, and no real secret appears anywhere in the repository history.

items.text: Testing an API: client fixtures, a test database, isolation between tests.
items.how: Write pytest fixtures for a test database, a TestClient and a logged-in user. Wrap each test in a transaction that rolls back, or recreate tables per test, and run the suite in shuffled order with pytest-randomly to prove tests do not depend on each other.
items.done: Every test passes alone and in any order, and no test leaves rows behind.

sections.title: Build — Nexus API
sections.guide: Nexus API: a service with users, roles, files and search. Build in the listed order, since permissions need users and search needs persistence. Write tests for each feature as you add it, so item 7 fills gaps rather than starting from nothing.

items.text: Registration, login, password hashing done correctly.
items.how: Add a users table, a register route that hashes passwords with Argon2 through argon2-cffi or pwdlib, and a login route that verifies and issues a token. Enforce a unique email in the database and return the same error for a wrong email or a wrong password.
items.done: Stored hashes start with $argon2id$, and a wrong email and a wrong password give identical responses.

items.text: Roles and permissions enforced by a dependency.
items.how: Store roles and permissions in tables, load them with the current user, and write require_permission('items:write') as a dependency. Apply it on routers, then test each protected route as an anonymous user, a normal user and an admin.
items.done: Permission tests pass with 401 for anonymous users, 403 for a missing permission and 2xx when allowed.

items.text: PostgreSQL persistence with migrations.
items.how: Use SQLAlchemy 2.0 with a PostgreSQL driver such as psycopg, one session per request from a dependency, and Alembic for every schema change. Run PostgreSQL in Docker for development and tests, and keep create_all out of application code.
items.done: Dropping the database and running alembic upgrade head recreates the full schema, and the app works against it.

items.text: File uploads with size and type validation.
items.how: Accept an UploadFile, read it in chunks and stop once the size limit is passed, and check the type from the file's first bytes, not the filename or Content-Type header. Store it under a generated name outside any served directory.
items.done: Tests show an oversized file gets 413, a renamed executable gets 415, and a valid file is saved under a new name.

items.text: Search, filtering, and cursor pagination.
items.how: Add query parameters for search text, filters and a sort field from an allow-list. Return one page plus an opaque next_cursor that encodes the last row's sort key and id, and back the common filter and sort with a composite index.

where.name: Use The Index, Luke: No Offset

items.done: Paging through all results with cursors returns each row once, with no gaps, and page 1,000 is as fast as page 1.

items.text: Background work for anything slow.
items.how: List every slow operation, such as thumbnails or emails. Move each to BackgroundTasks or a queue worker, return 202 with a job ID, and add a route that reports job status. Make each job idempotent so a retry does no harm.
items.done: The triggering request returns quickly with 202, and the status route shows the job finish or fail.

items.text: Structured JSON logging with a request ID on every line.
items.how: Configure logging or structlog to write one JSON object per line with timestamp, level, message and the request ID from your middleware's ContextVar. Log from handlers and helper functions without passing the ID by hand.
items.done: Every log line from one request, including from helper functions, parses as JSON and carries the same request_id.

items.text: Test suite covering auth, permissions, and validation failures.
items.how: Write parametrised pytest cases for each protected route across anonymous, normal and admin users, and for each model's invalid inputs expecting 422. Add login failure cases, run with pytest --cov, and cover any branch in auth code that is still missed.
items.done: The suite passes on a fresh database, and coverage of the auth and permission modules is close to 100%.

items.text: OpenAPI docs that a stranger could build a client from.
items.how: Give every route a summary, tags, a response model and example payloads, and declare error responses with responses=. Check /docs, then generate a client from /openapi.json with a tool such as openapi-generator and call two endpoints with it.
items.done: A client generated from /openapi.json can register, log in and call a protected route without reading your code.

items.text: Ship the API with tests passing and docs generated.
Show that an unauthorized user cannot reach a protected route — by test, not by clicking.
Show a request ID flowing from request to log line to error response.
Explain your auth choice and what an attacker would have to do to break it.
Add a new endpoint end-to-end — model, route, tests, docs — in under an hour.
