sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The patterns every automation job depends on: talking to APIs, reading pages, driving browsers, and surviving failure. Work in order, since retries, idempotency and scheduling build on the API items. Spend about a day per item, each ending with a small script against a public API or a local test server.

items.text: API authentication patterns: keys, OAuth, token refresh.
items.how: Write three small clients with httpx: one sending an API key in a header, one using httpx.BasicAuth, and one that holds an OAuth access token and refreshes it on a 401 before retrying once. Read the key from an environment variable, never from the source file.
items.done: You can explain access token versus refresh token, and your client recovers from an expired token without crashing.

items.text: Pagination: cursor, offset, and link headers.
items.how: Page through a real paginated API (the GitHub REST API works without a key) until the last page by following the Link header via response.links. Then write a generator that hides the paging so callers only see items, and note when cursor paging beats offset paging.
items.done: Your generator yields every item exactly once, and you can say why offset paging skips or repeats rows when data changes mid-scan.

items.text: HTML parsing and writing selectors that don't break weekly.
items.how: Save a page to disk and parse it with BeautifulSoup. Write each selector twice: once by position (div:nth-child(3)) and once by a stable attribute, id or visible label. Edit the saved HTML to move elements around and see which selectors still work.
items.done: Your attribute-based selectors survive the edited HTML, and your tests parse a saved file instead of the live site.

items.text: Browser automation: waits, selectors, and headless quirks.
items.how: Script a login-and-search flow on a demo site with Playwright's sync API. Use page.get_by_role and page.get_by_label locators, rely on auto-waiting, and remove every time.sleep. Run it headed, then headless, and compare what differs.
items.done: The script passes ten headless runs in a row with no fixed sleeps, and you can say what Playwright waits for before a click.

items.text: Filesystem and process automation.
items.how: Write a script that sorts a downloads folder into subfolders by file type with pathlib and shutil.move, supports a --dry-run flag, and then archives the result by calling an external tool through subprocess.run with check=True and a list of arguments.
items.done: The dry run prints the same moves the real run makes, and a failing subprocess raises CalledProcessError that you catch and log.

items.text: Webhooks: receiving, verifying signatures, responding fast.
items.how: Build a small FastAPI endpoint that receives a webhook, checks an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the raw body with hmac.compare_digest, queues the work, and returns 2xx at once. Send it signed and unsigned requests from a local script.
items.done: Tampered or unsigned requests get a 401, valid ones a fast 2xx, and you can say why the signature is checked over the raw body.

items.text: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter.
items.how: Write a retry decorator with exponential backoff, full jitter and a cap on attempts. Test it against a local server that fails the first three calls with 503, and log each delay. Then compare it with the tenacity library.
items.done: Your log shows growing, randomised delays, and you can explain why many clients retrying without jitter overload a recovering server.

items.text: Idempotency so a rerun doesn't duplicate work.
items.how: Take a script that appends rows to a SQLite table and make it idempotent: give each record a natural key, use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, and send an idempotency key header on any POST it makes. Run it twice on the same input.
items.done: Running the script twice leaves the same row count as running it once.

items.text: Scheduling, and making a job safe to run twice.
items.how: Schedule one of your scripts with cron or Windows Task Scheduler every five minutes. Add a lock file so a second copy exits if the first is still running, and record the last successful run time so a missed slot catches up.
items.done: Two copies started together produce one run and one clean exit, and a killed run is picked up correctly next time.

items.text: Rate limits and crawling respectfully.
items.how: Before fetching a site, check its rules with urllib.robotparser. Add a fixed delay per host, a descriptive User-Agent with contact details, and honour 429 responses and the Retry-After header. Read how Scrapy's AutoThrottle adjusts delay.
items.done: Your fetcher skips disallowed paths, waits between requests to one host, and backs off when it receives a 429.

sections.title: Build — automation engine
sections.guide: One engine that runs declared tasks through pluggable actions and records what happened. Build in order: format, dispatcher, adapters, result shape, persistence, notifications, then resume. Keep each step working end to end with two sample tasks before adding the next; resumability usually takes the most time.

items.text: Task definition format — declarative, not hardcoded.
items.how: Define tasks in TOML files with a name, action type, parameters and retry policy. Load them with tomllib into a pydantic model that validates fields, and write three sample task files, one of them deliberately invalid.
items.done: Adding a new task needs only a new file, and the invalid file fails at load time with a message that names the bad field.

items.text: Dispatcher that routes a task to the right action type.
items.how: Write a registry that maps an action type string to a handler, filled by a @register("http") decorator. The dispatcher looks up the handler, calls it with the task parameters, and raises a clear error for an unknown type.
items.done: A unit test registers a fake action, dispatches a task to it, and asserts an unknown type raises your error without running anything.

items.text: Action adapters: HTTP, browser, filesystem, subprocess.
items.how: Implement four adapters behind one interface: HTTP with httpx, browser with Playwright, filesystem with pathlib and shutil, subprocess with subprocess.run. Give each a timeout and write one test per adapter against a local target.
items.done: All four adapter tests pass offline, and each adapter stops at its timeout instead of hanging.

items.text: Normalize every result into one shape.
items.how: Define a Result dataclass with task id, status, start and end times, output, and error details. Make every adapter return one, and convert any exception into a failed Result at the dispatcher boundary.
items.done: Every task, successful or not, produces a Result you can serialise to JSON with the same keys.

items.text: Persist results and logs so failures are reconstructable.
items.how: Store each run and its Results in SQLite, and write logs with logging to a rotating file that includes the run id and task id on every line. After a forced failure, reconstruct what happened using only the database and the log.
items.done: Given a run id, one query and one log search show every task, its inputs, its outcome and its error.

items.text: Notification on completion and on failure.
items.how: Add a notifier interface with two backends, such as email via smtplib and a push service like ntfy. Send one summary per run, not one per task, and make a notifier failure log a warning without failing the run.
items.done: A run with one failed task sends one message listing that failure, and a broken notifier does not stop the engine.

items.text: Make the whole thing resumable after a crash mid-run.
items.how: Record each task's status in the database before and after it runs. On start, skip tasks already marked done for the current run and retry those left running. Kill the process mid-run with Task Manager or kill -9 and restart it.
items.done: After a hard kill and restart, every task has run to completion once and no finished task repeats.

items.text: Run the engine against a real workflow you actually needed done.
Kill it mid-run and restart — it resumes without duplicating work.
Show it surviving a 429 and a 500 without losing tasks.
Explain where each retry and timeout lives and why.
Hand the config to someone else and have them add a task without touching your code.

phases.name: Async, concurrency & performance
phases.aim: Choose between async, threads and processes, and back the choice with measurements.

resources.name: asyncio
resources.why: Coroutines, tasks, synchronization, networking

resources.name: concurrent.futures
resources.why: Thread and process pools

resources.name: cProfile and profile — the Python profilers
resources.why: Find the bottleneck before optimizing it

resources.name: Locust
resources.why: Load-test your own service

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The concepts behind every concurrency choice. Do items 0 to 4 as one asyncio block, then 5 and 6 on threads and processes, then races, timeouts and profiling. Write a short script for every item and keep them; the benchmark exercise reuses most of them.

items.text: Concurrency vs parallelism.
items.how: Read the Real Python concurrency article, then write two functions: one that sleeps 1 second (I/O-like) and one that sums squares to 10 million (CPU-bound). Run four of each with threads and with processes and time every run.

where.name: Real Python: Speed up your program with concurrency

items.done: You can explain, using your own timings, why threads speed up the sleeps but not the sums on the default build.

items.text: The event loop, coroutines, and what await yields.
items.how: Write three coroutines that print, await asyncio.sleep, and print again, and run them with asyncio.run. Then replace one sleep with time.sleep and observe that it blocks all three. Turn on debug mode to see the slow-callback warning.
items.done: You can say what the event loop does at each await, and why a blocking call stalls every coroutine.

items.text: Tasks, gather, TaskGroup, and structured concurrency.
items.how: Fetch ten URLs from a local server three ways: asyncio.create_task plus awaits, asyncio.gather, and asyncio.TaskGroup. Make one fetch raise and compare what happens to the others in each version.
items.done: You can say what happens to sibling tasks when one fails under gather and under TaskGroup.

items.text: Cancellation and cleanup that doesn't leak.
items.how: Write a task that holds a resource (an open file or a client) and cancel it with task.cancel(). Release the resource in try/finally or async with, and confirm CancelledError is re-raised, not swallowed.
items.done: Cancelling the task always closes the resource, and a test shows the task ends in the cancelled state.

items.text: Semaphores and queues for bounded concurrency.
items.how: Limit 100 fetches to 10 at once with asyncio.Semaphore, then rebuild the same thing as a producer, an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=20), and 10 workers. Print the number in flight each second to confirm the cap.
items.done: The in-flight count never exceeds 10, and you can say when a queue fits better than a semaphore.

items.text: Threads for I/O-bound work; the GIL on the default build, what it does and doesn't block, and what the free-threaded build changes.
items.how: Run 50 blocking HTTP requests through a ThreadPoolExecutor and time it against a plain loop. Then run a pure-Python CPU loop on four threads. Read the free-threading HOWTO and, if you can install a 3.13t or later build, repeat the CPU run on it.
items.done: You can say which operations release the GIL, and show that threads speed up I/O but not pure-Python CPU work on the default build.

items.text: CPU-bound work on the default build: processes and the cost of pickling across them, subinterpreters, or native code that releases the GIL.
items.how: Run a CPU-bound function over 8 inputs with ProcessPoolExecutor. Then pass a large list as an argument and time the pickling overhead. Compare with a NumPy version, which releases the GIL inside its native code.
items.done: You have timings showing the process speed-up and the point where pickling cost cancels it out.

items.text: Race conditions, locks, deadlocks — reproduce each one deliberately.
items.how: Write a counter incremented by 8 threads with no lock and show a wrong total (add a time.sleep(0) between read and write if needed). Fix it with threading.Lock. Then create a deadlock with two locks taken in opposite orders, and fix it with a fixed lock order.
items.done: You can reproduce the race and the deadlock on demand and explain the fix for each.

items.text: Timeouts at every layer.
items.how: Set explicit timeouts on every layer of one request path: httpx.Timeout for connect and read, asyncio.timeout around the whole operation, and a timeout on any queue get. Point it at a local server that never responds.
items.done: Against a server that hangs, your program fails with a timeout error within the limit you set.

items.text: Profiling with cProfile and a memory profiler; fair benchmarks.
items.how: Profile one of your scripts with python -m cProfile -s cumtime, and track memory with tracemalloc snapshots. Benchmark a function with timeit, repeating runs and reporting the median, after a warm-up, with other programs closed.
items.done: You can name the top three functions by cumulative time and the line that allocates the most memory.

sections.title: Build — Crawler-X
sections.guide: A crawler that exercises everything from the Learn section. Start with the queue and worker pool against a local test server, then add rate limiting, retries, normalisation, caching and persistence in order. Leave logs, metrics and shutdown for last, and test each feature before moving on.

items.text: Bounded concurrent URL queue with a worker pool.
items.how: Start with an asyncio.Queue of seed URLs, N worker tasks sharing one httpx.AsyncClient, and a local test site of a few hundred linked pages. Workers parse links and enqueue new ones; stop when the queue is empty and all workers are idle.
items.done: The crawler visits every page of the test site and exits by itself with no hanging tasks.

items.text: Per-host rate limiting.
items.how: Keep a dictionary of per-host limiters (a semaphore plus a minimum delay, or a token bucket) keyed by urlparse(url).netloc. Have each worker acquire the host's limiter before fetching.
items.done: Request timestamps in your log show no host receives more than your configured rate.

items.text: Timeouts, retries, and a dead-letter path for permanent failures.
items.how: Classify failures: timeouts, connection errors and 5xx are retried with backoff up to a limit; 4xx and exhausted retries go to a dead-letter table with the URL, status and last error. Test with a local server that returns each case.
items.done: Every URL ends either fetched or in the dead-letter table, and a 404 is never retried.

items.text: URL normalization and deduplication.
items.how: Write a normalise(url) function: lower-case scheme and host, drop default ports and fragments, resolve relative links with urljoin, and sort query parameters. Store seen URLs in a set and unit-test ten tricky cases.
items.done: Your tests show URLs that differ only in case, fragment or parameter order map to one key, and no page is fetched twice.

items.text: Response caching.
items.how: Cache responses on disk or in SQLite keyed by normalised URL, storing body, ETag and Last-Modified. On a repeat crawl send If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since and treat a 304 as a cache hit.
items.done: A second crawl of the unchanged test site makes mostly 304 or no requests, and your metrics show the hit rate.

items.text: Database persistence with batched writes.
items.how: Have workers put results on a queue, and let one writer task collect them into batches of 100 or every 2 seconds and insert them with executemany in one transaction. Compare total time against one insert per page.
items.done: Batched writes are measurably faster than single inserts, and no result is lost when the crawl ends mid-batch.

items.text: Structured logs and live metrics.
items.how: Log one JSON object per event with URL, status, duration and worker id. Keep counters for pages fetched, errors, queue size and in-flight requests, and print them every few seconds or expose them with prometheus_client.
items.done: While the crawl runs you can read pages per second and error count live, and filter the log by URL.

items.text: Graceful shutdown on SIGINT that finishes in-flight work.
items.how: Catch Ctrl+C: asyncio.run turns SIGINT into cancellation of the main task (use loop.add_signal_handler on Unix if you want your own handler). Stop taking new URLs, let in-flight fetches finish with a time limit, flush the final batch, then exit.
items.done: Pressing Ctrl+C mid-crawl exits within your time limit, and every page reported fetched is in the database.

sections.title: Benchmark exercise — the real deliverable
sections.guide: The measured comparison that justifies your concurrency choice. Build one harness first, run the I/O-bound workload three ways, then the CPU-bound one, and write up the numbers. Plan about a third of the time for the harness, a third for runs, a third for the write-up.

items.text: Run the same workload sequentially, with threads, and with asyncio.
items.how: Write one harness that takes a workload function and a runner (loop, ThreadPoolExecutor, asyncio.gather with a semaphore). Use the same URL list against a local server with fixed latency so network noise does not dominate.
items.done: All three runners complete the same workload and produce the same set of results.

items.text: Record throughput, p50/p95 latency, CPU, memory, and failure behaviour.
items.how: Record per-request durations with time.perf_counter and compute p50 and p95 with statistics.quantiles. Sample CPU and memory with psutil. Inject failures at a set rate on the server and record how each runner copes.
items.done: You have a table with throughput, p50, p95, peak CPU, peak memory and error handling for each runner, averaged over at least three runs.

items.text: Repeat with a CPU-bound workload and multiprocessing.
items.how: Swap in a CPU-bound workload such as hashing or prime counting and run it sequentially, with threads, and with ProcessPoolExecutor. Vary worker count from 1 to your core count and record the speed-up.
items.done: Your numbers show processes scaling with cores while threads stay near sequential speed on the default build.

items.text: Write a one-page conclusion with a table and a recommendation.
items.how: Write one page: the workloads, the machine and Python version, the method, a results table, and a recommendation for which model to use for each workload type. State the limits of your test.

where.name: Real Python: Speed up your program with concurrency

items.done: Someone else could rerun your benchmark from the page and reach the same recommendation.

items.text: Show the benchmark table and defend which model wins for which workload.
Explain the GIL accurately, including what it does not prevent and what the free-threaded build changes.
Demonstrate a deadlock you created, then fix it.
Cancel a running task and prove the cleanup ran.
Profile a slow function and show the before/after numbers.

phases.name: Docker, CI/CD & deployment
phases.aim: Make your software run the same way on any machine.

resources.name: Docker — Python guide
resources.why: Containerize, compose, develop

resources.name: GitHub Actions
resources.why: Automated tests, checks, and releases

resources.name: Packaging guides
resources.why: Building and publishing distributions

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The container and CI basics you need before shipping the stack. Work through items 0 to 8 with one small FastAPI app, rebuilding and running it after each change, then set up CI and releases on the same repository. Most items take an evening; Compose and CI take longer.

items.text: Images vs containers vs volumes.
items.how: Pull python:3.12-slim, start two containers from it, write a file in one, and confirm the other cannot see it. Then create a named volume, mount it in both, and repeat. Use docker ps -a, docker images and docker volume ls as you go.
items.done: You can explain in one sentence each what an image, a container and a volume are, and which one survives docker rm.

items.text: Writing a Dockerfile: layer order, caching, and why order matters.
items.how: Write a Dockerfile for a small FastAPI app that copies the whole project, then build it twice after editing one source file. Reorder it to copy and install requirements.txt before the source, add a .dockerignore, and rebuild after the same edit.
items.done: After a source-only edit the rebuild shows the dependency layer as CACHED and finishes in seconds.

items.text: Multi-stage builds and small final images.
items.how: Split the Dockerfile into a builder stage that installs dependencies into a virtual environment and a final python:3.12-slim stage that copies only that environment and your code. Compare sizes with docker images.
items.done: The final image is noticeably smaller than the single-stage one and contains no compilers or build tools.

items.text: Non-root users in containers.
items.how: Add a user with useradd in the Dockerfile, chown the app directory, and switch with USER. Run whoami through docker exec and try to write to a root-owned path to see it refused.
items.done: whoami inside the container prints your app user, not root, and the app still starts.

items.text: Volumes for data, bind mounts for development.
items.how: Run PostgreSQL with a named volume for its data directory, remove and recreate the container, and confirm the data is still there. Then run your app with a bind mount of the source folder and uvicorn --reload, and edit a file on the host.
items.done: Database data survives container removal, and host edits reload the app without a rebuild.

items.text: Networks and service discovery between containers.
items.how: Create a user-defined network with docker network create, start PostgreSQL and your app on it, and connect from the app using the container name as host. Then try the same on the default bridge network and note the difference.
items.done: Your app reaches the database by name, and you can explain why localhost inside a container does not mean the host.

items.text: Docker Compose for a multi-service stack.
items.how: Write a compose.yaml for your app and PostgreSQL with a named volume, then run docker compose up, logs, ps and down. Add depends_on with condition: service_healthy.
items.done: docker compose up starts both services with the app waiting for a healthy database, and down removes them cleanly.

items.text: Environment variables and secret handling — what never goes in an image.
items.how: Move all settings to environment variables read by your app, and supply them from a .env file listed in .gitignore and .dockerignore. Run docker history on your image to confirm no secret appears in any layer.
items.done: The image contains no keys or passwords, and you can say why ENV or ARG with a secret leaks it.

items.text: Health checks and restart policies.
items.how: Add a /health endpoint and a healthcheck in Compose that calls it, plus restart: unless-stopped. Make the endpoint fail on purpose and watch docker compose ps report the service as unhealthy.
items.done: You can make the service show healthy and unhealthy on demand, and it restarts after you kill its process.

items.text: CI: run tests, lint, and type checks on every push.
items.how: Add .github/workflows/ci.yml that runs on push and pull request: set up Python, install dependencies, then run pytest, ruff check and mypy. Push a commit that breaks a test to see the run fail.
items.done: Every push shows a green or red check on GitHub, and the broken commit turns it red.

items.text: Tagged releases and a repeatable deploy step.
items.how: Add a workflow triggered by pushing a tag such as v0.1.0 that builds the image, tags it with the version, and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry. Write down the deploy step as a single command that pulls a given tag.
items.done: Pushing a new tag produces an image with that tag in the registry, and deploying an older tag rolls back.

sections.title: Build — deploy the stack
sections.guide: Your API, database, cache and worker running from one command, tested in CI, and reachable online. Build in order: Compose file, slim Dockerfile, health checks, migrations, CI, the one command, then the deploy. Check each step from a clean state with docker compose down -v before moving on.

items.text: Compose file: FastAPI service, PostgreSQL, Redis, a worker.
items.how: Write compose.yaml with four services: api (FastAPI), db (postgres with a named volume), redis, and worker built from the same image with a different command. Wire them with environment variables and bring it up.
items.done: docker compose ps shows all four running, and a request to the API that queues a job gets processed by the worker.

items.text: Dockerfile under 200MB final image, running as non-root.
items.how: Use a multi-stage build on python:3.12-slim, install only runtime dependencies in the final stage, add a .dockerignore, and set a non-root USER. Check size with docker images and remove what you do not need until it fits.
items.done: docker images reports under 200MB and docker compose exec api whoami prints a non-root user.

items.text: Health checks on every service.
items.how: Add a healthcheck to each service: pg_isready for PostgreSQL, redis-cli ping for Redis, an HTTP call to /health for the API, and a heartbeat check for the worker. Use condition: service_healthy in depends_on.
items.done: docker compose ps shows every service as healthy, and stopping the database turns the API unhealthy.

items.text: Migrations that run safely on startup.
items.how: Manage schema with Alembic and run alembic upgrade head in a one-off migrate service that the API waits for with service_completed_successfully. Keep migrations backward-compatible so an old API still works against the new schema.
items.done: Starting the stack twice in a row runs migrations once and succeeds both times, and scaling the API to two replicas does not run them twice.

items.text: CI pipeline: tests, lint, types, and a build of the image.
items.how: Extend the CI workflow: run ruff, mypy and pytest with a PostgreSQL service container, then build the image with docker/build-push-action. Make the build job depend on the test job with needs.
items.done: A push runs lint, types, tests and the image build, and a failing test stops the build job.

items.text: One documented command that brings the whole stack up from clean.
items.how: Write a README section and a script or Makefile target that copies .env.example if needed and runs docker compose up --build -d. Test it from a fresh clone after docker compose down -v and docker system prune.
items.done: On a fresh clone the one command brings the stack to all-healthy with no manual steps.

items.text: Deploy it somewhere real and hit it from the internet.
items.how: Rent a small VPS or use a container host such as Fly.io or Render. Pull your tagged image, set secrets through the host's secret store, put HTTPS in front, and expose only the API port. Keep the database off the public internet.
items.done: curl https://your-domain/health from another network returns 200, and the database port is not reachable from outside.

items.text: A machine that has never seen the project runs it from your README alone.
CI catches a deliberately broken test before it can merge.
Explain what would happen if the database container restarted mid-request.
Show your image size and explain what you did to reduce it.
Roll back to the previous release and show it working.

phases.name: Application security
phases.aim: Find and fix security flaws in what you have built.

resources.name: OWASP Top 10
resources.why: The major web application risks

resources.name: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide
resources.why: A structured testing methodology

resources.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series
resources.why: Concrete guidance per topic

resources.name: Python secrets
resources.why: Cryptographically strong tokens

sections.title: Study
sections.guide: The main classes of web application flaw, taken from the OWASP Top 10. For each item read the OWASP page and the matching cheat sheet, then find one place in your own code where it could apply. About an evening per item; keep notes, since the lab and review use them.

items.text: Broken access control — the most common real-world failure.
items.how: Read the OWASP entry and the Authorization cheat sheet. In one of your APIs, list every endpoint that takes an object id and check the handler confirms the current user owns or may access that object, not only that they are logged in.
items.done: You can explain IDOR and show where in your code the ownership check happens for each object endpoint.

items.text: Cryptographic failures: at rest, in transit, and in your password hashing.
items.how: Read the Password Storage cheat sheet. Hash a password with argon2-cffi, verify it, and compare with an unsalted SHA-256 hash. Generate tokens with secrets.token_urlsafe and check which of your services use TLS end to end.
items.done: You can say why a fast hash is wrong for passwords and why random is wrong for tokens.

items.text: Injection: SQL, command, and template.
items.how: Read the SQL and OS command injection cheat sheets. In a local script, build a query by string formatting, pass it a quote character to break it, then rewrite it with placeholders. Do the same with subprocess using shell=True against a list of arguments.

where.name: OS Command Injection Defense cheat sheet

items.done: You can explain why parameterised queries and argument lists prevent injection where escaping and filtering do not.

items.text: Insecure design: flaws no library fixes.
items.how: Read the OWASP Insecure Design entry and the Threat Modeling cheat sheet. Draw a data-flow diagram of one of your apps, mark trust boundaries, and list what a user could abuse in the business logic, such as unlimited retries or negative quantities.
items.done: You have a diagram with trust boundaries and at least three design-level risks, each with a planned control.

items.text: Security misconfiguration and default credentials.
items.how: Read the OWASP entry, then audit one of your deployments: debug mode off, default passwords changed, unused ports closed, directory listing off, security headers set. Run your container config against the Docker Security cheat sheet.
items.done: You have a checklist for your stack with every line marked pass or fixed.

items.text: Vulnerable and outdated components; dependency scanning.
items.how: Run pip-audit on one of your projects and read each advisory it reports. Pin dependencies in a lock file and turn on Dependabot alerts for the repository.
items.done: You can read a CVE advisory, say whether your code reaches the affected function, and name the fixed version.

items.text: Authentication failures: session fixation, credential stuffing, weak resets.
items.how: Read the Session Management, Credential Stuffing and Forgot Password cheat sheets. Check that your app issues a new session id at login, rate-limits login attempts, and uses single-use, expiring reset tokens.
items.done: You can explain session fixation and credential stuffing and name the control in your code that stops each.

items.text: Software and data integrity failures; supply chain risk.
items.how: Read the OWASP entry. Install dependencies with pip install --require-hashes from a hashed lock file, pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs, and never unpickle data from an untrusted source.

where.name: OWASP A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures

items.done: Your CI installs only hash-checked packages, and you can explain why pickle.loads on untrusted input runs code.

items.text: Logging and alerting failures — what you'd need to detect a breach.
items.how: Read the Logging cheat sheet. Add log lines for logins, failed logins, permission denials and admin actions with user id, IP and time, never passwords or tokens. Then write down which alert would tell you about a brute-force attempt.

where.name: OWASP A09 Logging and Monitoring Failures

items.done: From your logs alone you can list every failed login in the last hour and who performed each admin action.

items.text: SSRF and why your server fetching a user-supplied URL is dangerous.
items.how: Read the SSRF cheat sheet. In a local app with a fetch-this-URL feature, confirm it will request http://localhost services and the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254. Fix it with an allow-list of hosts, resolving the name and rejecting private addresses via ipaddress.
items.done: Your fetch feature refuses localhost, private and link-local addresses, including via redirects, and you can explain why that matters in the cloud.

sections.title: Local lab — your machine only
sections.guide: A lab on your own machine where you add a flaw to a toy app you wrote, confirm it, fix it and lock the fix with a test. Do one full cycle of items 0 to 3 first, then repeat for the other flaw types, and finish with the dependency audit. Never point any of this at systems you do not own.

items.text: Build a deliberately vulnerable toy app with one flaw at a time.
items.how: Build a small FastAPI or Flask app with SQLite that runs only on 127.0.0.1. Add exactly one flaw, such as a login query built with an f-string, and keep it in its own Git branch so you can switch between vulnerable and fixed.
items.done: The app runs only on localhost, and git diff between branches shows the single flaw.

items.text: Exploit it yourself and record exactly what you did.
items.how: Against your own local app only, trigger the flaw with curl or httpx and write down the exact request, the response, and what data or action it exposed. Save the request as a script you can rerun.
items.done: Rerunning your saved script against the vulnerable branch reproduces the issue every time.

items.text: Patch it properly, not with input filtering alone.
items.how: Fix the cause, not the symptom: parameterised queries instead of stripping quotes, a server-side ownership check instead of hiding a button, a proper session reset instead of blocking one input. Rerun your reproduction script.
items.done: The reproduction script fails against the fixed branch, and you can explain why the fix holds for inputs you did not test.

items.text: Add a regression test that fails against the vulnerable version.
items.how: Turn the reproduction into a pytest test using FastAPI's TestClient that asserts the safe behaviour. Check out the vulnerable branch and confirm the test fails, then switch back and confirm it passes.
items.done: The test fails on the vulnerable branch and passes on the fixed one.

items.text: Repeat for injection, broken access control, and an auth flaw.
items.how: Run the full cycle of flaw, reproduction, fix and test three times: SQL injection in a search endpoint, a missing ownership check on GET /items/{id}, and a login that keeps the old session id or has no attempt limit.
items.done: You have three branches or commits, each with a reproduction script and a regression test that fails before the fix and passes after.

items.text: Run a dependency audit against your own real projects and fix what it finds.
items.how: Run pip-audit and bandit -r on each of your real projects. Upgrade the affected packages, rerun your tests, and record anything you cannot fix with the reason.
items.done: pip-audit reports no known vulnerabilities, or each remaining one has a written reason, and your tests still pass.

sections.title: Review pass on Nexus API
sections.guide: A structured security review of your own Nexus API. Go through the five questions in order, one pass each across the whole codebase, and record each finding with the file, the risk and the fix. Fix the findings after the review, not during, so the list stays complete.

items.text: For every endpoint: who can call it, and is that enforced server-side?
items.how: List every route from the FastAPI app, for example by iterating app.routes. For each, write who may call it and point to the dependency or check that enforces it on the server. Write a test for each role calling each protected route.
items.done: You have a table of every route with its allowed callers, and tests prove a wrong role gets 401 or 403.

items.text: For every input: what happens on malformed, oversized, or hostile input?
items.how: For every request model, add types and limits with Pydantic Field constraints (lengths, ranges, patterns) and cap request body size. Send empty, oversized, wrong-type and unexpected-field payloads from tests and check each response.
items.done: Every hostile payload gets a 4xx with a clean message, and none causes a 500.

items.text: For every secret: where does it come from, and is it in Git history?
items.how: List every secret the API uses and where it is loaded from. Scan the full history with gitleaks detect. Rotate any secret that was ever committed, since removing it from history does not make it safe again.
items.done: Every secret comes from the environment or a secret store, the history scan is clean, and any leaked secret has been rotated.

items.text: For every error: does it leak stack traces or internal details?
items.how: Add exception handlers that return a generic message and an error id to the client, and log the full traceback server-side with that id. Force a failure in each layer (database, validation, unhandled) and inspect what the client receives.
items.done: No response body contains a traceback, SQL, file path or library version, and each error id matches a full log entry.

items.text: For every action: is there a log line you could investigate later?
items.how: For every state-changing endpoint, add a structured log line with user id, action, target id, result and request id. Then pick a made-up incident, such as a deleted record, and try to answer who, what and when from the logs alone.
items.done: For any create, update or delete you can find from the logs who did it and when.

items.text: Find and fix a real vulnerability in your own code.
Show the regression test that would catch it coming back.
Explain why input validation alone is not a fix for injection.
Explain your password storage choice at the level of the algorithm and its parameters.
Produce a short threat model for one of your services.

phases.name: AI engineering
phases.aim: Build models from scratch to understand them, then build reliable systems around models you did not train.

resources.name: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero — Karpathy
resources.why: Backprop, then a GPT, built from nothing — the from-scratch path

resources.name: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero — course page
resources.why: Course page with notebooks and repos

resources.name: PyTorch — Learn the Basics
resources.why: Tensors, autograd, datasets, training loops

resources.name: scikit-learn
resources.why: Classical ML, and the evaluation discipline

resources.name: NumPy
resources.why: Vectorized thinking underneath everything

resources.name: pandas
resources.why: Tabular data manipulation

resources.name: Practical Deep Learning — fast.ai
resources.why: Top-down counterpart to Karpathy's bottom-up

sections.title: Layer 1 — numerical foundations
sections.guide: The numerical groundwork for everything after it. Work top to bottom: NumPy, pandas, then splits, metrics and a full scikit-learn pipeline. Give it about a quarter of the phase and move on once you can build a leak-free, cross-validated pipeline without looking things up.

items.text: NumPy arrays, broadcasting, and vectorizing a loop you wrote.
items.how: Write a pairwise Euclidean distance function for two arrays of points with nested Python loops, then rewrite it with broadcasting (a[:, None, :] - b[None, :, :]). Time both with timeit on 500 x 500 points and confirm the results agree with np.allclose.

where.name: NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners

items.done: You can predict a broadcast's output shape from the input shapes, and your vectorised version is at least 50 times faster than the loop.

items.text: pandas: load, clean, join, group, reshape.
items.how: Take a messy public CSV, load it with read_csv using explicit dtype and parse_dates, fix missing values, merge it with a second table, then answer three questions with groupby and pivot_table. Check the row count after every join.

where.name: pandas: Merge, join, concatenate and compare

items.done: You can explain why a merge changed the row count, and you produce each summary table without a Python loop.

items.text: Train/validation/test splits, and every way leakage sneaks in.
items.how: Read scikit-learn's common pitfalls page. Then leak on purpose: fit a StandardScaler on the full data before splitting, and put duplicate rows in both train and test. Compare the scores with a leak-free version. For time-ordered data, split by date, not at random.

where.name: scikit-learn: Common pitfalls and recommended practices

items.done: You can list four leakage sources (preprocessing, duplicates, time order, target-derived features) and show one inflating a score.

items.text: Metrics: accuracy is usually the wrong one — know when.
items.how: Make a dataset with 1 per cent positives, train a DummyClassifier and a real model, and compare accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC AUC and average precision. Plot the precision-recall curve and pick a threshold for a stated cost of false positives versus false negatives.
items.done: You can pick the right metric for a given problem and explain how 99 per cent accuracy can come from a useless model.

items.text: Classical ML with scikit-learn: a full pipeline, cross-validated.
items.how: Build a Pipeline with a ColumnTransformer (scale numeric columns, one-hot encode categorical ones) and a model. Tune it with GridSearchCV, score it with cross_val_score, and keep a final test set untouched until the very end.
items.done: One Pipeline object goes from raw DataFrame to predictions, and its cross-validated score is close to the held-out test score.

sections.title: Layer 2 — build the model from scratch
sections.guide: The core of the phase: build a neural network stack from a blank file so nothing later is a black box. Follow Karpathy's Zero to Hero in order, writing each piece yourself before you watch the solution. Expect this to take the largest share, about 40 per cent of the phase.

items.text: Implement a scalar autograd engine (micrograd) from a blank file.
items.how: Watch the micrograd lecture once, then close it and write a Value class with +, *, tanh and backward() using a topological sort. Check every gradient against a central difference, (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h.
items.done: Your gradients match finite differences to about 1e-6 on an expression of ten or more nodes that uses one variable twice.

items.text: Implement a neuron, layer, and MLP on top of it, and train it.
items.how: Add Neuron, Layer and MLP classes on your Value engine, each with a parameters() method. Train on sklearn.datasets.make_moons with a hand-written loop: forward pass, zero the gradients, backward(), update.
items.done: Loss falls steadily, accuracy on the moons data passes 95 per cent, and you can show what goes wrong when you skip zeroing the gradients.

items.text: Derive and hand-implement backprop for one layer; verify against autograd.
items.how: On paper, derive the gradients of a linear layer followed by softmax cross-entropy with respect to the weights, bias and input. Implement them with tensor operations and no autograd, in float64, then compare with the result of loss.backward() using torch.allclose.
items.done: torch.allclose passes for every parameter, and you can derive the logits gradient (softmax minus one-hot) on paper.

items.text: Rebuild the same thing in PyTorch and compare.
items.how: Rewrite your MLP with nn.Module, nn.Linear and torch.optim.SGD. Train it on the same data with the same seed and learning rate, plot both loss curves on one chart, and time one epoch of each.
items.done: Both versions reach a similar loss, and you can map each micrograd piece to its PyTorch equivalent.

items.text: Build a character-level language model and train it.
items.how: Follow makemore: a bigram count table on the names dataset, then a neural bigram, then an MLP with a context window of three characters. Record train and validation loss for each and sample 20 names from the best model.
items.done: Validation loss drops at each stage (the bigram sits near 2.45 nats) and the sampled names look plausible.

items.text: Implement self-attention from scratch.
items.how: Implement single-head causal self-attention: project to Q, K and V, compute softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) with a lower-triangular mask, then multiply by V. Extend it to multiple heads and compare against F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True).
items.done: Your output matches scaled_dot_product_attention under torch.allclose, and you can say why the scaling and the mask are there.

items.text: Build a small transformer end to end and generate text with it.
items.how: Follow the 'Let's build GPT' lecture: add position embeddings, feed-forward blocks, residual connections and LayerNorm around your attention. Train on tiny Shakespeare on CPU or a free GPU, then generate 500 characters.
items.done: Validation loss is clearly below your MLP language model's, and the generated text has real words and play-script line structure.

items.text: Explain, in your own words, what the gradients are doing at each step.
items.how: Take one training step of your MLP or transformer and write a one-page explanation: what each gradient's sign and size mean, why gradients add where a value is used twice, and what the optimiser does with them. Then give the explanation aloud without notes.
items.done: Without notes, you can explain gradient accumulation at a reused node and what vanishing gradients look like in the numbers.

sections.title: Layer 3 — AI systems engineering
sections.guide: Concepts for building reliable systems on models you did not train. Items 0 to 3 build on each other, so take them in order; 4 to 8 can go in any order. For each one write a small script that demonstrates it and keep it, since the build section reuses them. About 15 per cent of the phase.

items.text: Embeddings and vector similarity — what the numbers mean.
items.how: Embed 20 sentences with a sentence-transformers model and print the cosine similarity matrix. Include paraphrases, negations and off-topic sentences, then look at each sentence's nearest neighbours to see where similarity fails.
items.done: You can explain cosine similarity and normalisation, and show a sentence and its negation scoring as highly similar.

items.text: Chunking strategies and why they dominate retrieval quality.
items.how: Split one document set three ways: fixed 500-token windows, the same with 20 per cent overlap, and by headings or paragraphs. Run the same 20 questions against each and record how often the correct chunk lands in the top 5.
items.done: You have a recall@5 table per chunking strategy and can explain why the winner won.

items.text: Vector stores, hybrid search, and reranking.
items.how: Store your chunks in a vector index (pgvector or a NumPy array), add BM25 keyword search, merge the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion, then rerank the top 20 with a cross-encoder. Measure recall@5 after each stage.
items.done: You can show a query keyword search gets right and vector search misses, the reverse, and the recall gain from reranking.

items.text: RAG architecture end to end.
items.how: Read the RAG paper's introduction and Anthropic's contextual retrieval post, then draw the pipeline: ingest, chunk, embed, retrieve, rerank, build the prompt, generate, cite. Mark where each failure enters: missed retrieval, wrong chunk, ignored context, invented answer.
items.done: You can draw the pipeline from memory and say which stage to inspect first for a given wrong answer.

items.text: Structured outputs and schema-constrained generation.
items.how: Define a Pydantic model for the answer (answer text, cited sources, confidence), send its model_json_schema() to a model that supports structured output or tool use, and parse every reply with model_validate_json. On failure, retry once with the validation error in the prompt.
items.done: Malformed output raises ValidationError in your code instead of reaching the user, and you can show the retry fixing one case.

items.text: Tool calling and agent loops with real failure handling.
items.how: Write an agent loop by hand: send the tool definitions, run the tool the model asks for, return the result or the error, repeat until a final answer. Add a step limit, a per-tool timeout, and handling for unknown tools and bad arguments, then trigger each failure on purpose.
items.done: Each injected failure (bad arguments, tool exception, runaway loop) ends the loop cleanly with a logged reason.

items.text: Prompt injection and untrusted content boundaries.
items.how: Read OWASP's LLM01 entry. Plant an instruction inside a document your pipeline retrieves and see whether the model follows it. Then add defences: mark retrieved text as untrusted data, give tools the least permission they need, and require confirmation for side effects.
items.done: You can explain why prompt injection has no complete fix and show a permission boundary that limits what a successful one can do.

items.text: Evaluation sets, offline evals, and regression tracking.
items.how: Write 30 question and expected-answer pairs for a small RAG system. Write a script that scores retrieval hit rate and answer correctness (exact match, or an LLM grader you spot-check by hand) and appends each run's scores with the git commit to a CSV or SQLite table.

where.name: Hamel Husain: Your AI product needs evals
Claude docs: Create strong empirical evaluations

items.done: One command runs the evals and prints the change against the previous run, and a deliberate regression shows as a lower score.

items.text: Cost, latency, and caching in production.
items.how: Log input tokens, output tokens and latency for every model call and compute cost per request from the provider's price list. Add an exact-match response cache keyed on a hashlib hash of the prompt, try provider prompt caching on a long shared prefix, and compare p50 and p95 latency.
items.done: You can state the cost and p95 latency of one request and show a cache hit reducing both.

sections.title: Build — AI engine
sections.guide: Build one retrieval-augmented engine over a document set you know well, in the order listed. Write the evaluation set (item 4) as soon as retrieval works and rerun it after every change. Budget about 20 per cent of the phase.

items.text: Document ingestion: parse, chunk, embed, store.
items.how: Write an ingest command that converts PDF, Markdown or HTML to text, chunks it with the strategy that won in s2.1, embeds in batches, and stores each chunk with its source path, position and a content hash. Make reruns skip unchanged files.
items.done: Ingesting the same folder twice adds zero rows, and every chunk traces back to its file and position.

items.text: Retrieval with reranking and a relevance threshold.
items.how: Implement retrieve(query): hybrid search for the top 20, cross-encoder rerank, then drop results below a score threshold chosen from your eval data. When nothing passes, return an explicit empty result so the generator can say it does not know.
items.done: Off-topic questions return no context and get an 'I don't know' answer, while recall@5 on the eval set holds at its measured level.

items.text: Generation with a strict output schema.
items.how: Generate answers into a Pydantic schema with fields for the answer, the cited chunk IDs and a refusal flag. Add a validator that rejects any citation ID not present in the retrieved context for that request.
items.done: Every response validates against the schema, and a test that injects a made-up citation ID fails validation.

items.text: Tools the model can call, with permission boundaries.
items.how: Add two or three tools, such as corpus search, fetch document and save note. Tag each as read-only or side-effecting, run side-effecting tools only after explicit user confirmation, and log every call with its arguments and result.
items.done: A planted instruction that asks for a side-effecting tool is held for confirmation, and the log records the attempt.

items.text: An evaluation set of at least 50 labelled cases.
items.how: Write at least 50 cases covering answerable, unanswerable, multi-chunk and adversarial questions. Label each with the expected answer and the chunk IDs that should be retrieved. Run the set after every change and keep the score history.

where.name: Hamel Husain: Your AI product needs evals
Claude docs: Create strong empirical evaluations

items.done: One command runs all 50 or more cases and reports retrieval and answer scores separately.

items.text: A failure inspector: every bad answer traceable to its retrieved context.
items.how: Store a trace for each request: query, retrieved chunk IDs with scores, the final prompt, the raw model output and the parsed answer. Build a small CLI or page that lists failed eval cases and shows each trace next to the expected chunks.

where.name: Hamel Husain: Your AI product needs evals

items.done: For any failed case you can tell within a minute whether retrieval, reranking or generation caused it.

items.text: API + minimal UI, with logging on every request.
items.how: Wrap the engine in a FastAPI app with a POST /ask endpoint and a single HTML page with a form. Write one JSON log line per request with a request ID, latency, token counts, cost and the trace ID from s3.5.
items.done: A question asked through the page produces one log line that joins to its full trace by request ID.

gate.note: Measure quality with an evaluation set, not by whether answers look plausible.

items.text: Train a working neural net you wrote yourself, with no framework.
Explain backpropagation without hand-waving.
Show your evaluation set and a score that moved because of a change you made.
Show a failure case, trace it to its cause, and describe the fix.
Explain where prompt injection could enter your system and what stops it.

phases.name: Architecture & orchestration
phases.aim: Design systems that handle growth, failures and concurrent workers.

resources.name: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
resources.why: The standard book on distributed data systems; read it slowly

resources.name: Redis
resources.why: Caching, queues, streams, coordination

resources.name: Celery
resources.why: Distributed task processing in Python

resources.name: Temporal

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The distributed-systems ideas the build depends on. Read in order: items 2 to 6 form one chain about delivery and failure, and 9 to 11 prepare the build. For each item write a short script or diagram that shows the behaviour, and read the matching part of Designing Data-Intensive Applications alongside. About 40 per cent of the phase.

items.text: Layered vs modular architecture, and dependency inversion at the boundary.
items.how: Read the Repository pattern chapter of Cosmic Python. Refactor one earlier project so its business logic depends on a typing.Protocol for storage, write a SQL implementation and an in-memory fake, and run the same tests against both.
items.done: Your core module imports nothing from the database or web framework, and the test suite passes against the fake.

items.text: Caching strategies: cache-aside, write-through, and invalidation.
items.how: Read the AWS caching best practices page. Put cache-aside in front of a slow function with Redis GET and SET key value EX 60, then write a write-through version. Write a test that shows a stale read after an update when you skip invalidation.
items.done: You can say when each strategy serves stale data, and your test shows the stale read and then its fix.

items.text: Queues and workers: at-least-once delivery and its consequences.
items.how: Run a Celery worker with RabbitMQ as the broker and acks_late=True on a slow task. Kill the worker with kill -9 mid-task, restart it, and watch the task run again. Note which side effects now happened twice.
items.done: You can show the same task ID executed twice in the logs and explain why at-least-once delivery forces idempotent handlers.

items.text: Retries, exponential backoff, jitter, and retry storms.
items.how: Read the AWS article on exponential backoff and jitter. Write a retry decorator with a maximum attempts cap, exponential backoff and full jitter. Simulate 100 clients retrying against a failing server and plot requests per second with and without jitter.

where.name: AWS Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter

items.done: Your plot shows synchronised spikes without jitter and a spread-out load with it, and you can explain how a retry storm starts.

items.text: Idempotency keys and exactly-once as an illusion.
items.how: Read Stripe's post on idempotency. Add an Idempotency-Key header to a POST endpoint, store the key and response in a table with a unique constraint, and return the stored response on repeats. Fire the same request twice concurrently.

where.name: Stripe: Designing robust APIs with idempotency

items.done: Two concurrent identical requests cause one side effect and return the same response, and you can explain why delivery itself cannot be exactly-once.

items.text: Dead-letter queues and what you do with them.
items.how: Configure a queue so messages that fail N times move to a dead-letter queue, using a RabbitMQ dead-letter exchange or an SQS redrive policy. Send a poison message, confirm it lands there, and write down what you would alert on and how you would replay it.
items.done: The poison message stops blocking the main queue after N attempts, and you can list the steps to inspect, fix and replay it.

items.text: Distributed locks and why they're harder than they look.
items.how: Read Kleppmann's post on distributed locking. Build a Redis lock with SET key token NX PX 30000 and a release that checks the token. Pause the holder past the expiry with time.sleep to get two holders at once, then add a fencing token that the storage side checks.

where.name: Martin Kleppmann: How to do distributed locking

items.done: You can reproduce the double-holder bug with a paused process and explain how a fencing token rejects the stale write.

items.text: Horizontal scaling and statelessness.
items.how: Read the twelve-factor page on processes. Take a small web app that keeps sessions or uploads in memory or on local disk, move that state to Redis or object storage, and run three copies behind nginx with docker compose up --scale web=3.
items.done: Any request can hit any copy with the same result, and stopping one copy loses no user state.

items.text: Consistency models and partial failure.
items.how: Read the replication and consistency chapters of Designing Data-Intensive Applications and the Jepsen consistency map. For a primary with one asynchronous replica, write out what a client sees if it writes then reads from the replica, and if the primary dies before replicating.
items.done: You can give an example of read-your-writes, eventual consistency and linearisability, and say which one your system provides.

items.text: Observability: structured logs, metrics, traces, and correlation IDs.
items.how: Add JSON structured logs to a service with a request ID on every line, carried with contextvars. Expose a request counter and a latency histogram, and create a span per request with the OpenTelemetry Python SDK exporting to the console.
items.done: Given one request ID you can find its log lines, its trace and its effect on the metrics.

items.text: Capacity reasoning: find the bottleneck before adding machines.
items.how: Read Brendan Gregg's USE method. Under load, measure utilisation, saturation and errors for CPU, memory, disk, network and the database connection pool of one service. Use Little's law (concurrency = throughput x latency) to predict the throughput limit.
items.done: You can name the saturated resource from measurements and predict the throughput ceiling to within about 20 per cent.

items.text: Workflow orchestration: durable state, checkpoints, and resuming mid-flight.
items.how: Read Temporal's page on workflow execution. Run a three-step workflow with the Temporal Python SDK where step 2 is slow, kill the worker during step 2, restart it, and confirm step 1 is not run again.
items.done: The killed workflow completes, and you can explain event-history replay and why workflow code must be deterministic.

sections.title: Build — orchestrated system
sections.guide: Build one small system in the listed order and keep it runnable after every step. Get one worker correct before scaling to three, then add workflows, dead letters, tracing and metrics. Run the load test last, when there is something real to measure. About half the phase.

items.text: API → queue → worker pool → database → cache, all containerized.
items.how: Write a compose.yaml with a FastAPI service, a broker, a Celery worker, Postgres and a Redis cache, each with a health check. Start with one endpoint that enqueues a job and one that reads the result through the cache.
items.done: docker compose up on a clean clone brings every service to healthy, and a submitted job's result comes back through the API.

items.text: Workers that are safe to run in triplicate on the same queue.
items.how: Make each task idempotent: a unique job ID, an upsert or unique constraint on the result, and no external side effect before the commit. Run docker compose up --scale worker=3, submit 1,000 jobs including deliberate duplicates, and kill a worker mid-run.
items.done: A SQL count afterwards shows exactly one result per job ID and no missing jobs.

items.text: A workflow with checkpoints that survives a worker crash.
items.how: Model a multi-step job (fetch, process, store) as a Temporal workflow, or as a state table updated after each step that a worker resumes from. Kill the worker during the middle step, restart it, and check the step log.
items.done: The job finishes after the restart, earlier steps are not repeated, and the log shows where it resumed.

items.text: Dead-letter handling with a replay path.
items.how: Send tasks that fail after their final retry to a dead-letter queue or a failed_jobs table holding the payload and the error. Write a replay command that re-enqueues selected entries once the cause is fixed.
items.done: A forced failure lands in the dead-letter store, and after the fix the replay command completes it exactly once.

items.text: Distributed tracing across API, queue, and worker.
items.how: Add the OpenTelemetry instrumentation packages for FastAPI and Celery, check that the trace context travels in the task headers, and export spans over OTLP to a Jaeger container in the compose file.
items.done: In Jaeger, one trace shows the API request, the enqueue and the worker execution as connected spans.

items.text: A dashboard or metrics endpoint showing queue depth and worker health.
items.how: Expose /metrics with prometheus_client: queue depth, jobs processed and failed, a task duration histogram and a per-worker heartbeat timestamp. Scrape it with Prometheus or poll it with curl during a run.
items.done: Stopping all workers makes queue depth rise and the health metric go stale within one scrape interval.

items.text: Load-test it and find the actual bottleneck.
items.how: Write a Locust file that submits jobs at stepped rates. At each step record throughput, p95 latency and queue depth, and watch CPU, database connections and worker utilisation. Change one thing at a time and rerun.
items.done: You can name the resource that saturates first, with a measurement, and show the throughput gain after fixing it.

sections.title: Architecture decision record
sections.guide: Write one architecture decision record, about two pages, for the system you built. Fill each item from measurements and tests you ran, not from intentions. Allow a day.

items.text: State the expected load and the bottleneck you predict.
items.how: Write the expected requests per second, job size and peak factor. Predict the first bottleneck with Little's law and your notes from s0.10, then put the load-test result from s1.6 next to the prediction.
items.done: The record gives a number for expected load and compares the predicted bottleneck with the measured one.

items.text: List the failure modes and what happens in each.
items.how: For each component (API, broker, worker, database, cache), write what happens when it is down, slow or returning errors: what the user sees, what is retried, and what can be lost or duplicated. Confirm at least two rows by stopping that container.
items.done: Every component has a failure row, and at least two rows are backed by a test you ran.

items.text: Justify the storage, queue, and cache choices.
items.how: For the database, broker and cache, write the requirement each meets (durability, ordering, latency, operational cost), the alternative you considered, and the measurement or constraint that decided it.
items.done: Each choice cites a requirement and a trade-off rather than a preference.

items.text: Describe the retry and idempotency strategy.
items.how: Write the retry policy for each task (attempts, backoff, jitter, which errors retry), the idempotency key for each side effect, and what happens after the final retry. Link each rule to the code that implements it.

where.name: AWS Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter
Stripe: Designing robust APIs with idempotency

items.done: A reader can predict from the record alone what happens to a duplicated job and to a permanently failing one.

items.text: Say what you did NOT choose, and why.
items.how: For each major choice, name the rejected alternative (for example Kafka instead of RabbitMQ, Temporal instead of a state table, several services instead of one) and the specific reason, including the load or requirement at which you would revisit it.
items.done: The record has a rejected-options section with at least three entries, each with the condition that would reverse it.

API
