items.text: Kill a worker mid-job and show the job completes anyway.
Show a trace spanning API, queue, and worker for one request.
Prove a job running twice causes no duplicate side effects.
Show the load test and name the bottleneck it revealed.
Defend your ADR against a changed requirement someone else invents.

phases.name: Systems programming & internals
phases.aim: Learn what happens below Python. Do this after the core phases.

resources.name: Extending and Embedding Python
resources.why: The CPython boundary

resources.name: CS50 — C and memory (week 4)
resources.why: Pointers, allocation, and what leaks

resources.name: CPython source
resources.why: The interpreter's source, for when you are ready

resources.name: dis — bytecode disassembler
resources.why: See the bytecode your Python compiles to

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The layers under Python. Items 0 to 4 cover C and the machine: write, compile and run a small C program for each, on Linux or WSL. Items 5 to 9 cover how CPython runs your code: test each idea in the REPL. Spend about 60 per cent of the phase here.

items.text: C syntax at reading level.
items.how: Work through CS50 week 1 or the first chapters of Beej's Guide to C, typing and compiling each example. Then open a short CPython file such as Objects/boolobject.c and annotate every declaration, type, loop and function call.
items.done: You can read a 100-line C function and describe what it does, including its types, control flow and return values.

items.text: Pointers, arrays, and pointer arithmetic.
items.how: Write C programs that swap two ints through pointers, walk an array with pointer arithmetic, and print element addresses with %p. Compile with gcc -Wall -g -fsanitize=address, add an out-of-bounds write, and read the sanitiser report.
items.done: You can explain why a[i] is *(a + i) and predict the address step between elements of an int and a double array.

items.text: Stack vs heap; manual allocation and freeing.
items.how: Write a function that returns a pointer to a local array and observe the bug, then fix it with malloc and free. Add a leak and a double free on purpose, and run each version under Valgrind or AddressSanitizer.
items.done: You can say which values live on the stack and which on the heap in a given function, and your fixed program runs clean under Valgrind.

items.text: System calls and what the kernel does for you.
items.how: On Linux or WSL, run strace -f python3 -c "open('x.txt', 'w').write('hi')" and find the openat, write and close calls. Run it again with strace -c for a summary, then repeat using os.open and os.write.
items.done: You can name the system calls behind a Python file write and explain what the kernel does that user code cannot.

items.text: Compilation, linking, and what a binary contains.
items.how: Compile a two-file C program in stages: gcc -E, gcc -S, gcc -c, then link. Inspect the object files with nm and objdump -d, remove one function definition, and read the undefined-reference error from the linker.

where.name: GCC: Options controlling the kind of output

items.done: You can explain preprocessing, compiling, assembling and linking, and fix an undefined-reference error without searching.

items.text: Python bytecode — disassemble your own functions.
items.how: Run dis.dis on five of your own functions: a loop, a list comprehension, a closure, a try/except and an f-string. Look up each unfamiliar opcode in the dis documentation and note what it does to the value stack.

where.name: Python: dis, disassembler for Python bytecode

items.done: You can read a short disassembly aloud and explain what LOAD_FAST, BINARY_OP and CALL do to the stack.

items.text: The CPython object model: everything is a PyObject.
items.how: Read the PyObject and PyVarObject sections of the C API object structures page, then Include/object.h in the CPython source. In the REPL, compare sys.getsizeof for an int, an empty list, a list of ten items and a class instance, and explain each size.

where.name: Python C API: Common object structures

items.done: You can name the two header fields of every PyObject in the default build (reference count and type pointer) and how type(x) is found.

items.text: Reference counting, cycles, and the generational GC.
items.how: Watch sys.getrefcount change as you bind and delete names for a list. Then build a two-object cycle, delete the names, and use a weakref.finalize callback to show it is freed only by gc.collect(). Read the gc docs for your exact 3.14 point release.
items.done: You can explain why reference counting alone cannot free a cycle and how the generations decide what the collector scans.

items.text: The C extension boundary and why libraries like NumPy are fast.
items.how: Read NumPy's 'What is NumPy?' page and the first section of Extending Python with C. Time a Python loop that sums a million floats against built-in sum on a list and np.sum on an array, and account for the gap.

where.name: Python: Extending Python with C or C++

items.done: Using your timings, you can explain the gap in terms of boxed objects, per-element interpreter dispatch and contiguous memory.

items.text: Where the free-threaded build (officially supported since 3.14, PEP 779) changes the picture, and what it costs.
items.how: Read the free-threading HOWTO and PEP 779. Install the free-threaded 3.14 build (python3.14t), check sys._is_gil_enabled(), and run a CPU-bound function on 1 and 4 threads on both builds. Record wall time for each.

where.name: Python: Python support for free threading

items.done: You can state your measured thread speed-up and single-thread slowdown, and why an extension not marked safe re-enables the GIL.

sections.title: Build
sections.guide: Five hands-on exercises that apply the Learn section. Do them in order, since items 1 and 2 use the same hot function. Record every prediction and measurement in one notes file so you can compare them later.

items.text: Disassemble three functions and predict the bytecode before you look.
items.how: Write three functions, for example a nested loop, a with block and a generator. Write down the opcodes you expect for each, then run dis.dis and mark every difference with its reason.

where.name: Python: dis, disassembler for Python bytecode

items.done: At least one prediction matches the real opcode sequence in full, and every miss has a written reason.

items.text: Write a C extension or a Cython module for one hot function.
items.how: Profile one of your projects with cProfile and pick a hot, numeric, pure-Python function. Rewrite it as a Cython module with typed variables, or as a C extension using PyArg_ParseTuple, build it, and keep the Python version beside it.

where.name: Python: Extending Python with C or C++

items.done: The compiled module imports, and a test shows it returns identical results to the Python version on the same inputs.

items.text: Benchmark it honestly against the pure-Python version.
items.how: Benchmark both versions with pyperf, or timeit with several repeats, on the same inputs at three or more sizes including a tiny one. Report the median and spread, and note the machine, Python version and build flags.
items.done: A table shows median and spread per input size, and you can say where call overhead cancels the speed-up.

items.text: Trace the refcount of a heap object you created (a list or a class instance, never a small int, None or a bool — those are immortal since 3.12 and report a fixed sentinel count).
items.how: Create a list and print sys.getrefcount after binding it to a second name, storing it in a dict, appending it to another list, and deleting each of those references in turn. Write your predicted count before each line runs.
items.done: Your predicted change matches every step, and you can explain the extra reference held by the getrefcount argument.

items.text: Find and fix a reference cycle keeping memory alive.
items.how: Build parent-child trees where each child holds a strong reference to its parent. With gc.disable(), create and drop many trees while taking tracemalloc snapshots. Confirm the cycle with gc.get_referrers, then store the parent as a weakref.ref.
items.done: Before the fix memory grows with each batch; after it, tracemalloc shows memory flat across 100,000 trees with the collector disabled.

items.text: Explain what happens in memory when you append to a list until it resizes.
Predict the bytecode of a small function and be right.
Show a measured speedup from a native extension, with the benchmark.
Explain why the GIL exists, and what the free-threaded build pays to remove it.

phases.name: Data engineering
phases.aim: Move data reliably at volume. Much paid Python work is data engineering.

resources.name: Data Engineering Zoomcamp
resources.why: Free cohort-based course: pipelines, warehouse, dbt, Spark, Kafka

resources.name: Apache Airflow
resources.why: Scheduled DAG orchestration, the industry default

resources.name: Prefect
resources.why: Lighter-weight Python-native orchestration

resources.name: dbt
resources.why: Transformations as version-controlled, tested SQL

resources.name: Polars
resources.why: DataFrames that don't fall over at scale

resources.name: DuckDB
resources.why: Analytical SQL on local files

resources.name: PySpark
resources.why: Distributed processing when one machine isn't enough

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Concepts for moving data reliably. Read items 0 to 5 first, since they set the vocabulary, then take 6 to 11 alongside the build. Run a small example for each item in DuckDB or Python rather than only reading. About 40 per cent of the phase.

items.text: Batch vs streaming, and how to tell which one a problem actually needs.
items.how: Read the Kafka introduction and the batch and stream processing chapters of Designing Data-Intensive Applications. For five cases (daily sales report, fraud check at checkout, hourly dashboard, search index update, monthly billing), write the latency needed and choose batch, micro-batch or streaming.
items.done: You can justify each choice from the required latency and explain why streaming costs more to run and debug.

items.text: ETL vs ELT and why the industry moved to ELT.
items.how: Read dbt's article on ETL versus ELT. Do the same transform twice: once in Python before loading into DuckDB, and once by loading the raw data and transforming it with SQL inside DuckDB. Note what you can rebuild later in each case.
items.done: You can explain how cheap warehouse compute and keeping raw data made ELT the default, and when ETL is still required.

items.text: Idempotent pipelines: rerunning yesterday must not double-count.
items.how: Read Airflow's best practices on idempotent tasks. Write a daily load that deletes and rewrites the rows for its run date inside one transaction, or upserts on a key with INSERT OR REPLACE. Run it three times for the same date and compare counts and totals.
items.done: Three runs for the same date leave identical row counts and totals, checked by a query.

items.text: Backfills and late-arriving data.
items.how: Read Airflow's DAG run page on catchup and backfill. Load a day, then add records for that day with an older event time, and write a rule for reprocessing by event date with a lookback window of N days. Apply the rule and check the late rows arrive.
items.done: You can explain event time versus processing time, and your pipeline picks up late records that fall inside its lookback window.

items.text: Partitioning strategies and file formats — Parquet over CSV, always.
items.how: Write the same 10-million-row table to CSV and to Parquet partitioned by date with DuckDB COPY tbl TO 'out' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (dt)). Compare total size and the run time of a one-day filtered query on each.
items.done: You have measured size and query-time figures for both formats and can explain column pruning and partition pruning.

items.text: Data warehouse vs lake vs lakehouse, in plain terms.
items.how: Read the introduction of the CIDR 2021 Lakehouse paper. Write one paragraph each on a warehouse, a lake and a lakehouse covering where the data sits, who enforces the schema, and how updates are made atomic. Note the role of table formats such as Delta Lake and Iceberg.

where.name: Databricks: What is a data lakehouse?

items.done: You can explain the three in two minutes and say which one DuckDB over a folder of Parquet files resembles.

items.text: Schema evolution and contracts between producers and consumers.
items.how: Read dbt's page on model contracts. In a source table, add a column, rename a column and change a type, and see which downstream queries break or silently change. Then add a contract to one model so a breaking change fails the build.
items.done: You can say which changes are backward compatible, and a renamed column now fails your build instead of producing nulls.

items.text: Data quality tests: nulls, ranges, uniqueness, referential integrity.
items.how: Write not_null, unique, accepted_values and relationships tests in dbt, or the same checks with pandera or plain SQL, plus a value-range check. Insert one bad row per check on purpose and run the tests.
items.done: Each of the five checks fails on its planted row and passes on clean data.

items.text: Incremental models and change data capture.
items.how: Build a dbt incremental model using is_incremental() and a unique_key, or the same logic in SQL with a high-water mark on an updated-at column. Then read the Debezium overview to see how change data capture reads the database log instead of polling.
items.done: A rerun processes only new or changed rows, shown by row counts, and you can explain why log-based CDC sees deletes and polling does not.

items.text: Orchestration: DAGs, dependencies, retries, SLAs, alerting.
items.how: Read Airflow's pages on DAGs and tasks. Write a DAG with three dependent tasks, set retries and retry_delay, add an on_failure_callback that posts to a webhook or writes a file, and add a check that alerts if the run has not finished by a set time. Make one task fail.
items.done: The failing task retries the configured number of times and then fires the alert, visible in the UI or the log.

items.text: Streaming basics: topics, partitions, consumer groups, offsets.
items.how: Run Kafka locally from the quickstart, create a topic with 3 partitions, and produce keyed messages. Start two consumers in one group, stop one to watch the partitions rebalance, and read committed offsets with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe.
items.done: You can explain why order holds only within a partition and what is lost if offsets are committed before processing.

items.text: Cost awareness — scanning terabytes is a bill, not just a wait.
items.how: Read BigQuery's cost-control best practices. In DuckDB, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a query over partitioned Parquet with and without a partition filter, and with SELECT * versus two columns. Compare rows scanned and run time.
items.done: You can estimate how much data a query will scan before running it and show a filter cutting that by an order of magnitude.

sections.title: Build — a pipeline that runs unattended
sections.guide: Build one pipeline from a public API into DuckDB that runs on a schedule without you. Work in order: raw landing, transform, load, tests, orchestration, then backfill, lineage and the Polars swap. Leave it running for a week before you call it done.

items.text: Ingest from an API on a schedule, landing raw data untouched.
items.how: Choose a public API with daily data, such as weather or transport. Write a script that fetches one day with httpx, handles paging and rate limits, and writes the untouched JSON to raw/source=name/date=YYYY-MM-DD/ with a fetch timestamp.
items.done: Each run writes one raw file per date, and rerunning a date replaces its file rather than adding a second one.

items.text: Transform into a clean, tested model layer.
items.how: Set up dbt with the dbt-duckdb adapter. Write staging models that parse and type the raw JSON, then mart models for the questions you want answered, and add tests to every staging model.
items.done: dbt build runs every model and test from raw to marts with no failures.

items.text: Load into a warehouse or DuckDB file with partitioning.
items.how: Write the mart tables to a DuckDB file and export the main fact table as Parquet partitioned by date. Make each load replace only the partitions for the dates in that run.
items.done: Loading one date changes only that date's partition, confirmed by per-date row counts before and after.

items.text: Add data quality tests that fail the run, not just warn.
items.how: Keep test severity at error, the dbt default, and make the orchestrator task fail on a non-zero exit from dbt build. Add source freshness and row-count checks, plant a duplicate key, and confirm the run stops before the marts are built.
items.done: A planted bad row turns the scheduled run red and no downstream task runs.

items.text: Orchestrate it with Airflow or Prefect, with retries and alerting.
items.how: Wrap ingest, transform, test and load as tasks in an Airflow DAG or a Prefect flow on a daily schedule. Give the ingest task retries with a delay, send an alert on failure, and run it under the scheduler, not by hand.
items.done: The pipeline runs daily for a week without you, and a forced API failure retries and then alerts.

items.text: Write a backfill command and run it for a past month.
items.how: Add a backfill --start --end command that loops over dates and runs the same idempotent per-date task, or use your orchestrator's backfill feature. Run it for a past month, run it again, and compare per-day totals.
items.done: A month backfills with one command, and the second run leaves every per-day row count unchanged.

items.text: Add lineage docs so someone else knows what feeds what.
items.how: Add descriptions for every model and column in the dbt YAML files, run dbt docs generate and dbt docs serve, and check the lineage graph. Add a README section naming the source API, schedule, owner and each mart.
items.done: Someone new can find, from the docs alone, which source feeds a given mart column and when it refreshes.

items.text: Replace pandas with Polars somewhere and measure the difference.
items.how: Take the heaviest pandas step in the pipeline and rewrite it with the Polars lazy API: scan_parquet, filter, group_by, collect. Run both on the same data, measure time and peak memory, and compare outputs.
items.done: The outputs are equal row for row, and you have measured time and memory figures for both versions.

gate.note: The deliverable is a pipeline that runs without supervision.

items.text: Run the pipeline twice on the same window and prove the output is identical.
Backfill a past period and show correct results.
Break an upstream schema and show the pipeline fails loudly, not silently.
Explain your partitioning choice and what query it optimizes.
Show a data quality test catching a real defect.

resources.why: Short exercises in the browser

resources.name: Matplotlib user guide
resources.why: Figures, axes and the object-oriented API

resources.name: seaborn tutorial
resources.why: Statistical plots on top of Matplotlib

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Core pandas and plotting skills in the order you will use them on a real dataset: arrays, frames, loading, cleaning, reshaping, time series, statistics, charts. Spend about half the time on items 1 to 4, since most analysis time goes on loading and cleaning. Work every item in a notebook against one real CSV rather than toy data.

items.text: NumPy arrays, dtypes, broadcasting and vectorized operations.
items.how: Create arrays with np.arange and np.zeros, check .dtype and .shape, then add a (3, 1) array to a (4,) array and predict the result shape before running it. Rewrite one Python loop over a list as a single vectorised expression and time both with %timeit.
items.done: You can predict the shape of a broadcast result, or say why it raises, before running it.

items.text: pandas Series and DataFrame: indexing with loc and iloc, and why chained assignment fails.
items.how: Select rows and columns with loc (labels) and iloc (positions), including a boolean mask. Then write df[mask]["b"] = 1, observe that df is unchanged, and rewrite it as one call: df.loc[mask, "b"] = 1.
items.done: You can explain why chained assignment writes to a temporary copy and fix it with one loc call.

items.text: Reading CSV, Excel, JSON and SQL; setting dtypes and parsing dates on load.
items.how: Load the same small dataset from CSV, JSON and an SQLite table with read_csv, read_json and read_sql. Pass dtype= and parse_dates= on load, then confirm with df.dtypes that no column is left as object by mistake.
items.done: Every column loads with the intended dtype, and dates arrive as datetime64 without a separate conversion step.

items.text: Cleaning: missing values, duplicates, inconsistent categories, outliers.
items.how: On a messy CSV, count missing values with isna().sum(), remove duplicates with drop_duplicates, normalise category spellings with str.strip().str.lower() and a mapping, and flag outliers with an IQR rule. Record each decision and the row count before and after.
items.done: You can state, for each cleaning step, how many rows it changed and why that choice was acceptable.

items.text: groupby, aggregation, pivot tables, melt and merge.
items.how: Answer three questions on one dataset: a groupby with named aggregations in agg, a pivot_table across two categories, and a merge with a lookup table. Turn the pivot back into long form with melt, and check the row count after each merge to catch duplicated keys.
items.done: You can pick between groupby, pivot_table and merge for a new question without looking it up.

items.text: Time series: resampling, rolling windows, time zones.
items.how: Load a timestamped dataset, set a DatetimeIndex, resample it to daily and monthly totals with resample, and add a 7-day rolling mean. Attach a zone with tz_localize, convert with tz_convert, then inspect the rows around a daylight-saving change.
items.done: You can produce a monthly series with a rolling mean and explain what happens to the data at a DST change.

items.text: Descriptive statistics, distributions, correlation vs causation.
items.how: Run describe, plot a histogram of each numeric column, and compute corr for two pairs. For one strong correlation, name a variable that could cause both, then check whether the correlation still holds within groups of that variable.
items.done: You can describe a distribution's centre, spread and skew, and say why a given correlation may not be causal.

items.text: Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals with SciPy, and when they apply.
items.how: Compare two groups with scipy.stats.ttest_ind and with scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu, then compute a confidence interval for the difference in means with scipy.stats.bootstrap. Write each test's assumptions next to the call and check them on your data.
items.done: You can say in plain words what a p-value and a 95% interval mean, and when a t-test does not apply.

items.text: Charts with Matplotlib and seaborn: choosing the chart for the question.
items.how: Using the fig, ax = plt.subplots() style, make one chart per question type: line for change over time, bar for comparison, histogram for distribution, scatter for relationship. Redo two of them in seaborn and label every axis with units.
items.done: Given a question, you can name the chart type that answers it and build it with labelled axes.

items.text: Notebooks for exploration, scripts for anything you run twice.
items.how: Take a working notebook, move its loading and cleaning code into functions in a .py module with an if __name__ == "__main__": block, and import that module back into the notebook. Run the script from a terminal to confirm it works on its own.
items.done: The same cleaning code runs from the command line and from the notebook, with no copy of it in either.

sections.title: Build — an analysis report
sections.guide: One end-to-end analysis, from a written question to a published report. Write the question first, then the cleaning script, then the charts, then the limitations, then the report generator. Expect the cleaning script to take the largest share of the time.

items.text: Pick a public dataset and write down the question before opening it.
items.how: Browse a public data portal, pick a dataset under about 1 GB, and write the question in a README.md before downloading. State what result would answer it and which columns you expect to need.
items.done: The README states one answerable question and the expected columns, written before any analysis code.

items.text: Clean it in a script that runs end to end from the raw file.
items.how: Write clean.py that reads the untouched raw file, applies each cleaning step as a named function chained with DataFrame.pipe, and writes the cleaned file to a separate folder. Delete the output and rerun to check it rebuilds.
items.done: Running python clean.py on a fresh clone recreates the cleaned data with no manual steps.

items.text: Answer the question with at least three charts, each with a one-line takeaway.
items.how: Draft each chart in the notebook, then move it into a function that saves it with fig.savefig. Write the takeaway sentence first and adjust the chart until it shows that point without further explanation.
items.done: Three or more saved charts exist, each with a title, labelled axes and a takeaway the chart supports.

items.text: State the limitations: sample, bias, missing data.
items.how: Write a limitations section covering who is in the sample and who is missing, how the data was collected, the share of missing values in each key column, and what the cleaning removed. Give numbers where you have them.
items.done: The report lists at least three concrete limitations with numbers, and says which conclusions each one weakens.

items.text: Publish the report as a static page or PDF generated by the script.
items.how: Write report.py that runs the cleaning, builds the charts and writes an HTML page using DataFrame.to_html for tables, or a PDF with PdfPages. Run it from a clean checkout, then publish the output.
items.done: One command regenerates the whole report from the raw file, and the published copy matches its output.

gate.note: Use a dataset you have not seen before.

items.text: Clean a messy dataset without looping over rows.
Explain the difference between a merge that multiplies rows and one that does not.
Pick the right chart for a comparison, a trend and a distribution, and justify each.
Explain why a correlation in your data does not prove causation.

phases.name: Desktop & mobile apps
phases.aim: Build graphical applications in Python and ship them as installable programs.

resources.name: Qt for Python (PySide6)
resources.why: Official docs and tutorials for PySide6

resources.name: tkinter
resources.why: The GUI toolkit in the standard library

resources.name: BeeWare tutorial
resources.why: Native desktop and mobile apps from one codebase

resources.name: Kivy
resources.why: Touch-first UI framework for desktop and mobile

resources.name: PyInstaller
resources.why: Bundle an app and its interpreter into one folder or file

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The Qt concepts a working desktop app depends on, followed by packaging and a look at mobile. Work items 1 to 5 in order in one small PySide6 practice window, since each builds on the last. Items 6 to 9 can be read in any order; spend most time on threading and model/view.

items.text: Event loops: why a GUI freezes when you block the main thread.
items.how: Build a window with a button whose slot calls time.sleep(5), click it, and try to move or resize the window. Then replace the sleep with a QTimer.singleShot callback and compare. Write two sentences on what app.exec() is doing while the window is idle.
items.done: You can explain why a blocking call in a slot stops repainting and input, and name two ways to avoid it.

items.text: Widgets, layouts and size policies in Qt.
items.how: Build a form with QVBoxLayout, QHBoxLayout and QFormLayout, with no fixed sizes. Resize the window and note which widgets grow; then change one widget's QSizePolicy and a layout stretch factor and observe the difference.
items.done: Your form resizes cleanly at any window size with no call to setFixedSize or setGeometry.

items.text: Signals and slots, and keeping logic out of widget classes.
items.how: Write a plain Python class holding the app's logic, give a QObject wrapper a custom Signal, and connect it to a slot in the window. Keep all calculation in the plain class and unit-test it without importing Qt widgets.

where.name: Qt for Python: signals and slots

items.done: The window class contains only wiring and display code, and the logic class has tests that pass without a display.

items.text: Running long work in a worker thread or process and reporting progress safely.
items.how: Move a slow task into a QRunnable run on QThreadPool, or a QObject moved to a QThread. Report progress through a signal to a QProgressBar, and never touch a widget from the worker thread.
items.done: The window stays responsive during the task and the progress bar updates only through signals.

items.text: Model/view: displaying large tables without creating a widget per row.
items.how: Subclass QAbstractTableModel with rowCount, columnCount and data over a list of 100,000 rows and show it in a QTableView. Compare start-up time and memory with a QTableWidget filled with the same rows.
items.done: The model-backed table opens 100,000 rows at once and scrolls smoothly, and you can say why.

items.text: Styling, high-DPI scaling, dark mode and accessibility basics.
items.how: Style the practice window with a Qt style sheet, then run it at 150% display scaling and under the system dark theme. Give every input a label with setBuddy or an accessible name, and move through it with the keyboard alone.
items.done: The window is readable at 100% and 150% scaling, in light and dark themes, and is usable without a mouse.

items.text: Storing settings and user data in the platform's standard locations.
items.how: Save window geometry and one preference with QSettings, and write a user data file to the folder returned by QStandardPaths.writableLocation(AppDataLocation). Print that path on Windows and read where it maps on macOS and Linux.
items.done: You can name where settings and user data live on each of the three platforms, and none of it is written next to the code.

items.text: Packaging with PyInstaller or Briefcase, and code signing on Windows and macOS.
items.how: Package the practice app with pyinstaller --windowed, run the result, and fix missing data files through the spec file. Read the Briefcase tutorial steps for the same app, and note what code signing needs on Windows and macOS.
items.done: Your packaged app starts from its own folder, and you can explain why an unsigned build triggers an OS warning.

items.text: Mobile with BeeWare or Kivy: what differs from desktop.
items.how: Work through the first steps of the BeeWare tutorial to build a Toga app and run it in the Android emulator or on a phone. List three differences from desktop: screen size, touch input, app lifecycle, file access or permissions.
items.done: A sample app runs on a phone or emulator, and you can name three things you would change to port a desktop tool.

sections.title: Build — a desktop tool
sections.guide: One small desktop tool that a real person uses, built and shipped. Write the logic layer and its tests first, then the window, then threading and cancel, then settings and keyboard access, and package last. Leave a day for packaging problems on a clean machine.

items.text: A single-purpose tool someone else uses, such as a file renamer or a log viewer.
items.how: Ask one person what repetitive file or log task they do, and write the tool's single job and its inputs in a README. Build the logic as functions that take paths and return results, then add the window on top.
items.done: The named user has completed their task with the tool at least once without your help.

items.text: Long operations run off the main thread with a working cancel button.
items.how: Run the long operation in a QRunnable that checks a cancel flag between units of work, and emit progress and finished signals. Wire a Cancel button to set the flag, and disable the Start button while a job runs.
items.done: Cancel stops a running job within about a second, leaves no half-written output, and the window never freezes.

items.text: Settings persist between runs in the correct per-user folder.
items.how: Store preferences and window geometry with QSettings using your organisation and app names, and load them before the window is shown. Delete the settings, start the app, and confirm it falls back to defaults.
items.done: A changed setting survives a restart, and removing the stored settings gives clean defaults instead of an error.

items.text: Keyboard shortcuts and a usable tab order.
items.how: Add QShortcut or QAction shortcuts with standard QKeySequence values for the main actions, and set the focus order with QWidget.setTabOrder. Unplug the mouse and complete the main task.
items.done: The main task can be completed with the keyboard alone, and Tab moves through fields in reading order.

items.text: An installer or bundle that runs on a machine without Python.
items.how: Build with PyInstaller or Briefcase, load bundled files through a path helper that handles sys._MEIPASS, then copy the output to a machine or VM with no Python installed and run it there.
items.done: The bundle starts and completes the main task on a clean machine with no Python installation.

items.text: Tests for the logic layer that run without a display.
items.how: Write pytest tests for the logic module covering normal input, empty input and one error case. Run them with Qt not installed in a separate venv, or on CI without a display, to prove the logic does not import widgets.
items.done: pytest passes in an environment where no display is available.

gate.note: Test the build on a machine that has never had Python installed.

items.text: Explain why the window freezes when a button handler sleeps, and fix it.
Show your logic tested without starting the GUI.
Install and run your app from its bundle on a clean machine.
Explain where your app stores user data on Windows, macOS and Linux.

phases.name: Command-line tools
phases.aim: Write command-line programs other people install and script against.

resources.name: Typer
resources.why: CLI apps from type hints, with a step-by-step tutorial

resources.name: argparse tutorial
resources.why: The standard library parser

resources.name: Click
resources.why: Composable commands, the base Typer is built on

resources.name: Rich
resources.why: Tables, progress bars and formatted terminal output

resources.name: pipx
resources.why: Install Python CLIs in isolated environments

resources.name: MkDocs
resources.why: Project documentation from Markdown

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: How a command-line tool behaves so that people and scripts can rely on it. Work items 1 to 4 in order on one small tool, rewriting it as you go; they cover most of what users notice. Items 5 to 9 are about configuration, output, installation and documentation, and each takes about an hour.

items.text: Arguments, options, subcommands and help text with argparse.
items.how: Write a wordcount.py with argparse: one positional file argument, a --lines flag, and two subcommands via add_subparsers. Give every argument a help= string and read the output of -h for each subcommand.
items.done: Running the tool with -h and with each subcommand's -h prints accurate, complete help.

items.text: The same interface with Typer or Click, and when a framework is worth it.
items.how: Rewrite the same tool with Typer using type hints, then with Click using decorators, and compare line counts and help output with the argparse version. Note what each framework adds: type conversion, testing helpers, completion.
items.done: You have the same interface in three versions and can say when a framework is worth the extra dependency.

items.text: Exit codes, stdout vs stderr, and output meant for other programs.
items.how: Make the tool return 0 on success, 1 on a failed check and 2 on bad usage via sys.exit. Send errors and progress to sys.stderr and results only to stdout, then run tool args 2>/dev/null and check that stdout still holds only results.
items.done: Redirecting stderr leaves only machine-usable output, and echo $? shows the documented code in each case.

items.text: Reading from stdin and writing to pipes so the tool composes with others.
items.how: Accept - as a file name meaning stdin, and read with sys.stdin or fileinput when no file is given. Test it in a pipeline such as cat log.txt | tool count | sort, and handle a closed pipe by catching BrokenPipeError.
items.done: The tool works as a middle stage of a pipe and exits quietly when piped into head.

items.text: Configuration precedence: flags, environment variables, config files, defaults.
items.how: Load settings in this order, each overriding the last: built-in defaults, a TOML file read with tomllib, environment variables from os.environ, then command-line flags. Write a test that sets all four and checks the flag wins.
items.done: A test shows flags beat environment variables, which beat the file, which beats defaults; --help states the order.

items.text: Progress bars and tables with Rich, and turning them off when output is not a terminal.
items.how: Add a Rich Progress bar to a slow loop and print results as a Rich Table. Check Console.is_terminal, or sys.stdout.isatty(), and print plain lines when output is redirected to a file or pipe.
items.done: tool args > out.txt produces a file with no colour codes or progress-bar characters.

items.text: Entry points in pyproject.toml, and installing with pipx.
items.how: Add a [project.scripts] table to pyproject.toml pointing a command name at your main function, build with python -m build, and install the wheel with pipx install dist/*.whl. Run the command from a new terminal.
items.done: The command runs from any directory in a new shell, and pipx uninstall removes it cleanly.

items.text: Shell completion and man-page-style help.
items.how: Install completion for your Typer or Click tool with its --install-completion option or the documented shell snippet, and check that subcommands and options complete. Add a long description and usage examples to the top-level help.
items.done: Pressing Tab after the command name lists your subcommands in at least one shell.

items.text: Documentation with MkDocs or Sphinx, published from CI.
items.how: Create a docs folder with mkdocs new, write a usage page for each subcommand, preview with mkdocs serve, then add a CI job that runs mkdocs gh-deploy or uploads the built site on each push to the main branch.
items.done: A push to the main branch updates the public docs site without any manual step.

sections.title: Build — a tool on PyPI
sections.guide: A real CLI published to TestPyPI or PyPI. Write the subcommands and their tests first, add the --json output and exit-code tests, then package and install with pipx, and build the docs site last. Test the install on a clean machine or venv before calling it done.

items.text: A CLI with at least two subcommands that solves a real task.
items.how: Pick a task you currently do by hand in a terminal, list the subcommands it needs, and write the core functions with tests before adding the CLI layer. Keep argument parsing in one module and the work in another.
items.done: You use the tool yourself for the task, and each subcommand has at least one passing test.

items.text: Machine-readable output with a --json flag.
items.how: Add a --json flag that builds a list or dict and prints it with json.dumps, with no other text on stdout. Pipe the output into python -m json.tool or jq to confirm it parses.
items.done: Every subcommand's --json output parses as valid JSON, checked by a test that calls json.loads on it.

items.text: Correct exit codes, tested.
items.how: Write a table of cases (success, failed check, bad arguments, missing file) with the expected exit code, and test each with Typer's or Click's CliRunner, or with subprocess.run and returncode.
items.done: Every documented exit code has a test that asserts it, and the suite passes.

items.text: Installable with pipx from PyPI or TestPyPI.
items.how: Build an sdist and wheel with python -m build, upload to TestPyPI with twine upload --repository testpypi dist/*, then install with pipx on a clean machine or venv using the TestPyPI index.
items.done: A pipx install from the package index on a clean environment gives a working command.

items.text: A documentation site built from the repository.
items.how: Write mkdocs.yml and a docs folder in the repository with install, quick start and one page per subcommand. Build it in CI and deploy it with mkdocs gh-deploy or your host's build step.
items.done: The docs site is live, is rebuilt from the repository by CI, and every subcommand has a page.

gate.note: Another person installs and uses the tool from its documentation alone.

items.text: Pipe your tool's output into another command and back.
Show that errors go to stderr with a non-zero exit code.
Explain how your tool resolves a setting given as a flag, an environment variable and a config file.
Publish a release to TestPyPI or PyPI.

phases.name: Games, graphics & media
phases.aim: Build games and interactive graphics, and process images, audio and video in Python.

resources.name: PyGame primer — Real Python
resources.why: A complete small game, step by step

resources.name: pygame
resources.why: Surfaces, sprites, events, sound

resources.name: Python Arcade
resources.why: Modern 2D game library with many examples

resources.name: Game Programming Patterns
resources.why: Game loop, update method, component patterns; free online

resources.name: Pillow
resources.why: Image processing

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The structure every real-time game shares, then media processing. Work items 1 to 5 in order in one small pygame sketch that you keep extending. Add items 6 to 8 to the same sketch once it has enough objects to be worth measuring. Do item 9, Pillow and ffmpeg, as a separate script.

items.text: The game loop: input, update, render, and a fixed or variable timestep.
items.how: Write a pygame window whose while loop has three clearly separated functions: handle events from pygame.event.get, update positions, then draw and call pygame.display.flip. Read the fixed versus variable timestep sections of the game loop chapter.
items.done: You can draw the loop from memory and say what goes wrong when drawing and updating are mixed together.

items.text: Delta time, so movement speed does not depend on frame rate.
items.how: Get dt = clock.tick(fps) / 1000 from pygame.time.Clock and move a sprite by speed * dt. Run it at 30 and 144 FPS and time how long the sprite takes to cross the screen in each case.
items.done: The crossing time is the same, within a frame, at 30 and 144 FPS.

items.text: Sprites, sprite sheets and animation frames.
items.how: Load a sprite sheet once with pygame.image.load(...).convert_alpha(), cut frames with Surface.subsurface, and advance the frame index on a timer in a pygame.sprite.Sprite subclass. Draw a group of them with Group.draw.
items.done: An animated character plays at a set frame rate that does not change when the game FPS changes.

items.text: Collision detection: rectangles, circles, and spatial partitioning when there are many objects.
items.how: Detect hits with Rect.colliderect, then with a circle distance check, and use pygame.sprite.spritecollide for groups. Spawn 2,000 objects, time the all-pairs check, then add a uniform grid and time it again.
items.done: You have before and after timings showing the grid cuts collision time with 2,000 objects.

items.text: Game state machines: menus, playing, paused, game over.
items.how: Define the states MENU, PLAYING, PAUSED and GAME_OVER with enum.Enum, give each its own handle, update and draw functions, and switch between them in one place. Add pause on Escape and check the game does not advance while paused.
items.done: The main loop has no if chains about state beyond one dispatch, and pausing freezes all movement.

items.text: Entity-component structure, and when plain classes are enough.
items.how: Read the Component chapter, then write the same enemy two ways: one class with position, health and render code, and an entity holding separate component objects. Note how many lines each needs for a second enemy type.
items.done: You can say for your own game whether plain classes are enough, with a reason based on how many entity types it has.

items.text: Sound effects and music, and loading assets once.
items.how: Load every pygame.mixer.Sound and image once at start-up into a dict keyed by name, and play background music with pygame.mixer.music. Add a print in the loader to confirm no file is loaded twice during play.
items.done: Sounds play without a stall on first use, and the loader runs once per asset.

items.text: Profiling a frame and keeping it under 16 ms.
items.how: Run the game under python -m cProfile -s cumtime for 30 seconds and find the top three functions. Also time update and draw each frame with time.perf_counter, print the worst frame, and fix the largest cost.
items.done: You have a measured worst-case frame time below 16 ms under normal play, with before and after numbers.

items.text: Image processing with Pillow; audio and video with ffmpeg from Python.
items.how: With Pillow, open an image, resize it, crop it and save it as a thumbnail. Then call ffmpeg through subprocess.run with an argument list to extract audio from a video file, and check the return code.
items.done: One script creates thumbnails for a folder of images and another extracts an audio track, both raising on failure.

sections.title: Build — a finished game
sections.guide: One small, complete game rather than a large unfinished one. Build the playable core with delta-time movement first, then the start, pause and game-over states, then levels and difficulty, then settings, and package last. Stop adding features once the core loop is fun.

items.text: A complete 2D game with a start screen, scoring and a game-over state.
items.how: Choose a small genre such as a shooter, a platformer or a puzzle game, write its rules on one page, and build the core loop first. Add the start screen, score display and game-over screen using the state machine from the Learn section.
items.done: Someone else can start the game, play, lose, see their score and start again without help.

items.text: Movement driven by delta time.
items.how: Pass dt in seconds from Clock.tick into every update function, and express all speeds and timers in units per second. Cap dt at a maximum so a stall does not move objects through walls.
items.done: The game plays the same with the frame rate capped at 30 and at 120 FPS.

items.text: At least one level or difficulty curve.
items.how: Store level layouts or difficulty parameters (spawn rate, enemy speed) in data such as a JSON file, not in code. Increase difficulty with score or time, then play from the start and record the point where you lose.
items.done: Difficulty changes during play, and adding a new level means editing data rather than code.

items.text: Settings for volume and controls.
items.how: Add a settings screen that changes music and effect volume with set_volume and rebinds the movement keys. Save the choices to a JSON file and load it on start-up.
items.done: Changed volume and key bindings take effect immediately and are still set after a restart.

items.text: A packaged build that runs without Python installed.
items.how: Load all assets through a path helper that handles sys._MEIPASS, build with PyInstaller including the assets folder, then run the result on a machine or VM that has no Python installed.
items.done: The packaged game starts with sound and images on a clean machine without Python.

gate.note: Someone else plays the game to the end without help.

items.text: Explain what breaks if movement ignores delta time, and show the fix.
Show your game's state machine.
Measure your frame time and name what dominates it.
Batch-process a folder of images or clips with a script.

phases.name: Scientific computing & optimization
phases.aim: Use Python for numerical work, simulation, optimization and domain science.

resources.name: Scientific Python Lectures
resources.why: NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and more, from the community

resources.name: NumPy user guide
resources.why: Arrays, broadcasting, linear algebra

resources.name: SciPy user guide
resources.why: Optimization, integration, statistics, signal processing

resources.name: SymPy tutorial
resources.why: Symbolic mathematics

resources.name: OR-Tools
resources.why: Linear programming, routing and scheduling solvers

resources.name: GeoPandas
resources.why: Geospatial data in DataFrames

resources.name: Biopython tutorial
resources.why: Sequences, file formats and databases for biology

resources.name: Numba
resources.why: Compile numerical Python functions to machine code

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Numerical methods and the tools that implement them. Start with item 1 on floating point, since every later check depends on choosing tolerances. Items 2 to 5 are the core SciPy toolkit and deserve most of the time; items 6 to 9 are specialist areas to sample by interest, and item 10 applies to all of them.

items.text: Floating-point error, cancellation, and choosing tolerances.
items.how: Evaluate 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, then compute (1 - cos(x)) / x**2 for x from 1e-1 down to 1e-9 and watch it lose accuracy; rewrite the numerator as 2*sin(x/2)**2 and compare. Replace exact float comparisons with math.isclose or numpy.isclose with stated tolerances.
items.done: You can explain catastrophic cancellation with an example and choose rtol and atol values for a given check.

items.text: Vectorizing with NumPy, and when Numba or Cython is the next step.
items.how: Write a pairwise-distance function with Python loops, then with NumPy broadcasting, then decorate the loop version with numba.njit. Time all three with timeit at two input sizes, excluding Numba's first compile call.
items.done: You have a timing table for three versions and can say when a loop cannot be vectorised and Numba is the better choice.

items.text: Linear algebra: solving systems, least squares, eigenvalues.
items.how: Solve a small system with numpy.linalg.solve and check the residual, fit a line to noisy points with numpy.linalg.lstsq, and find eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix with numpy.linalg.eigh. Check numpy.linalg.cond for an ill-conditioned case.
items.done: You can say why solve is preferred over computing an inverse, and what a large condition number means for your answer.

items.text: Root finding, minimization and curve fitting with scipy.optimize.
items.how: Find a root of a nonlinear equation with scipy.optimize.root_scalar using a bracket, minimise the Rosenbrock function with minimize from two starting points, and fit a model to noisy data with curve_fit. Read the parameter uncertainties from the returned covariance.
items.done: You recover known parameters from synthetic noisy data within their reported uncertainties.

items.text: Numerical integration and ODE solving with scipy.integrate.
items.how: Integrate a function with a known antiderivative using scipy.integrate.quad and compare with the exact value. Solve exponential decay and a damped oscillator with solve_ivp, tightening rtol and atol until the result stops changing.
items.done: Your ODE solution matches the analytic solution to the tolerance you requested.

items.text: Symbolic math with SymPy: derive, simplify, then generate numeric code.
items.how: Define symbols with sympy.symbols, differentiate and simplify an expression with diff and simplify, then turn the result into a NumPy function with lambdify. Check it against a finite-difference estimate at several points.
items.done: A symbolically derived gradient, run through lambdify, agrees with finite differences to about 1e-6.

items.text: Linear and integer programming, and routing or scheduling with OR-Tools.
items.how: Solve a small production-planning problem with scipy.optimize.linprog, then the integer version with OR-Tools. Work through the OR-Tools vehicle routing example and change the number of vehicles to see the effect on total distance.
items.done: You can write the objective and constraints for a small problem as code and say whether it needs integer variables.

items.text: Monte Carlo simulation and reproducible random seeds.
items.how: Estimate pi by random sampling using numpy.random.default_rng(seed), run it at sample sizes from 1e3 to 1e7, and plot the error against n on log axes. Rerun with the same seed and confirm identical output.
items.done: The same seed reproduces the same result, and your error plot shows roughly a 1/sqrt(n) slope.

items.text: Geospatial data with GeoPandas and Shapely.
items.how: Load a public boundaries file with geopandas.read_file, check its crs, reproject with to_crs to a metric projection, and compute areas. Build a Shapely point and polygon and test contains and buffer.
items.done: You can compute areas in square metres and say why doing it in latitude and longitude gives wrong numbers.

items.text: Reproducible research: pinned environments, scripts over notebooks, versioned data.
items.how: Create a project with a venv, pin versions with pip freeze into a requirements file, move notebook code into scripts with a single entry command, and record the source and checksum of each data file.
items.done: A fresh clone plus the pinned requirements reproduces your results with one command.

sections.title: Build — a simulation or solver
sections.guide: One simulation or solver with evidence that its numbers are right. Build the model, check it against an analytic case, then run a convergence study, then optimise the hot loop, and write the generated report last. Do not optimise before the validation passes.

items.text: Model a real system: a physical process, an epidemic, a queue, or a schedule.
items.how: Choose a system with a simple analytic special case, such as an SIR epidemic, an M/M/1 queue or a projectile with drag. Write its equations or rules down first, then implement them as a function taking parameters and returning results.
items.done: The model runs from one function call with parameters, and the equations are written in the repository.

items.text: Validate the numerical method against a known analytic case.
items.how: Pick parameters where the exact answer is known, such as no drag, a mean number in an M/M/1 system of rho/(1-rho), or pure exponential growth. Write a pytest test that compares the simulation to that answer with numpy.isclose and a stated tolerance.
items.done: A test checks the analytic case and passes, and it fails if you introduce a deliberate bug in the model.

items.text: Measure how the error changes with step size or sample count.
items.how: Run the analytic case at five or more step sizes or sample counts, compute the error against the exact answer each time, and plot error against step on log-log axes. Fit the slope with numpy.polyfit on the logs.
items.done: The measured convergence order matches the method's theoretical order, or you can explain the difference.

items.text: Speed up the hot loop and report the before and after times.
items.how: Profile a full run with cProfile to find the hot loop, then vectorise it with NumPy or compile it with numba.njit. Time before and after with timeit on the same inputs and rerun the validation test.
items.done: The report gives before and after timings with the speed-up factor, and the validation test still passes.

items.text: A report generated from the code, with every figure reproducible.
items.how: Write one script that runs the model, the validation and the convergence study, saves every figure with savefig from fixed seeds, and writes the report. Delete all outputs and regenerate them to check.
items.done: Deleting the outputs and running one command reproduces every figure and number in the report.

gate.note: Every number in your results must be reproducible from the repository.

items.text: Explain why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 and how you compare floats in your code.
Solve a small optimization problem and verify the answer is optimal.
Show a solver's error shrinking as you refine the step or sample count.
Rerun your whole analysis from a clean environment and get the same figures.

phases.name: Quantitative finance
phases.aim: Analyse market data, build backtests without bias, and measure risk correctly.

resources.name: QuantEcon lectures
resources.why: Quantitative economics and finance in Python

resources.name: pandas time series
resources.why: Date ranges, resampling, rolling statistics

resources.name: decimal
resources.why: Exact decimal arithmetic for money

resources.name: PyPortfolioOpt
resources.why: Mean-variance and other portfolio optimization

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Work in order: returns and money handling first (s0.0 to s0.2), then bias, risk and portfolio maths (s0.3 to s0.6), then data storage and code discipline (s0.7, s0.8). Spend about two thirds of the time running small pandas experiments on real daily prices and one third reading. This is education only, not investment advice.

items.text: Prices vs returns: simple and log returns, and adjusting for splits and dividends.
items.how: Load daily prices for one stock and compute simple returns with pct_change() and log returns with np.log(p).diff(). Check that log returns sum to the total log return and simple returns compound with (1 + r).prod(). Compare close and adjusted close across a known split date.
items.done: You can say which return type adds across time and which across assets, and your split day shows no fake -50% return.

items.text: Money with Decimal, and where float is acceptable.
items.how: Check sum([0.1] * 10) == 1.0 with floats, then with Decimal('0.1'). Write a fee function that takes Decimal amounts and rounds with quantize(Decimal('0.01'), rounding=ROUND_HALF_EVEN). Note where float is fine: returns, volatility and other statistics.
items.done: You can explain why Decimal(0.1) differs from Decimal('0.1') and when a float result is acceptable.

items.text: Resampling and aligning time series across markets and time zones.
items.how: Load two markets with different closing times, set each index's zone with tz_localize, convert both to UTC with tz_convert, then resample('W').last() and join. Use merge_asof to attach the latest known value of one series to the other without looking ahead.
items.done: Your joined frame has no row where one market's value comes from a later timestamp than the row's own time.

items.text: Backtesting: lookahead bias, survivorship bias, fees and slippage.
items.how: Reproduce each bias on purpose: shift a signal the wrong way to create lookahead, backtest only today's index members to see survivorship, and rerun with 10 basis points of fees and slippage per trade. Write down how much each one changes the result.
items.done: You can name the bias behind a too-good backtest and show the one-line fix for lookahead.

items.text: Risk metrics: volatility, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, value at risk.
items.how: From daily returns compute annualised volatility with std() * sqrt(252), the Sharpe ratio as mean excess return over its standard deviation (annualised), maximum drawdown from cummax() of the equity curve, and 95% historical VaR with quantile(0.05).
items.done: Your four functions match hand-calculated values on a 10-day example to 6 decimal places.

items.text: Portfolio construction: diversification and mean-variance optimization.
items.how: Take 5 to 10 assets, estimate expected returns and a covariance matrix, and use PyPortfolioOpt's EfficientFrontier to get minimum-volatility and maximum-Sharpe weights. Compare them with equal weights, then nudge one expected return and watch how far the weights move.
items.done: You can explain why optimised weights swing when expected returns change slightly, and why equal weights are a fair baseline.

items.text: Train/test splits over time, walk-forward testing, and why random splits leak.
items.how: Build features from past prices and score a model with TimeSeriesSplit, then with KFold(shuffle=True). Then write a walk-forward loop by hand: fit on a window, test on the next block, move both forward.
items.done: You can show that the shuffled split scores higher and explain which future information leaked into it.

items.text: Market data APIs, rate limits and storing data for reproducible research.
items.how: Pick one free data API and read its rate limits. Write a downloader that sets timeouts, retries with backoff, caches raw responses and saves cleaned data with to_parquet. Store the source, download date and price adjustments in a metadata file next to the data.
items.done: Your research script reads only local files and gives the same numbers with the network switched off.

items.text: The difference between research code and execution code.
items.how: List what research code can skip and execution code cannot: input validation, logging, error handling, safe restarts and reconciliation of records. Take one of your notebooks and mark every place that would fail silently if it ran unattended.
items.done: You can list five differences between research and execution code and point to an example of each in your own code.

sections.title: Build — an honest backtester
sections.guide: Build in the listed order: the simulation with costs, the lookahead test, the metrics, the benchmark, then walk-forward. Keep each part in its own module with tests. Treat the whole build as a data-analysis exercise, not a trading system.

items.text: Simulate a simple strategy on daily data with fees and slippage.
items.how: Load daily prices, compute a moving-average crossover with rolling(), turn it into positions and earn the next day's return. Charge fees and slippage in basis points on every change in position, and keep the cost settings in one config object.
items.done: With costs set to zero you get the gross result, and raising costs lowers returns by trades times cost per trade.

items.text: Make lookahead impossible by construction, and test that it is.
items.how: Route every strategy through one function that shifts signals by one bar before they meet returns. Write a pytest test that changes prices after day t and asserts that positions up to day t stay the same.
items.done: The test fails when you remove the shift and passes when it is in place.

items.text: Report returns, volatility, Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown.
items.how: Write one report() function that takes a daily return series and returns total and annualised return, annualised volatility, Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown. Reuse the risk functions you already checked by hand instead of writing new ones.
items.done: report() reproduces your hand-checked example and runs unchanged on any daily return series.

items.text: Compare against a buy-and-hold benchmark.
items.how: Run buy-and-hold on the same asset, dates and cost settings. Plot both equity curves from (1 + r).cumprod() and put both reports side by side, adding the strategy's time in the market so a drawdown saved by sitting in cash is visible.
items.done: Strategy and benchmark cover identical dates, and you can say whether the strategy beat buy-and-hold after costs.

items.text: Run a walk-forward test and report out-of-sample results separately.
items.how: Split the history into consecutive train and test windows, choose parameters on each train window only, and record results on the test window that follows. Join the test windows into one out-of-sample equity curve and report it apart from in-sample figures.
items.done: The report has separate in-sample and out-of-sample tables, and no test date falls inside its own training window.

gate.note: Paper trading only. Nothing in this phase uses real money.

items.text: Show a test that fails if your strategy reads a future price.
Explain how fees and slippage change your strategy's result.
Compute maximum drawdown by hand for a short series and match your code.
Explain why a strategy that works in-sample can fail out-of-sample.

phases.name: Computer vision
phases.aim: Process images and video, and train and evaluate vision models.

resources.name: CS231n course notes
resources.why: Stanford's convolutional networks course

resources.name: OpenCV-Python tutorials
resources.why: Image processing, features, video

resources.name: PyTorch transfer learning tutorial
resources.why: Fine-tune a pretrained network

resources.name: torchvision
resources.why: Datasets, transforms and pretrained models

resources.name: Ultralytics YOLO docs
resources.why: Object detection and segmentation models

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Work from pixels up: arrays and classical OpenCV operations first (s0.0 to s0.2), then CNNs, transfer learning and augmentation (s0.3 to s0.5), then detection metrics, evaluation and video (s0.6 to s0.8). Spend at least half the time running code on your own images rather than reading.

items.text: Images as arrays: channels, color spaces, dtypes.
items.how: Load an image with cv2.imread and print its shape and dtype. Convert BGR to RGB and HSV with cv2.cvtColor, split the channels, and compare adding two uint8 images with + against cv2.add.
items.done: You can explain why OpenCV loads BGR, why 200 + 100 gives 44 in uint8, and how to convert an image to float in [0, 1].

items.text: Filtering, thresholding, edges and morphology with OpenCV.
items.how: On one noisy photo apply GaussianBlur, then threshold with Otsu, then Canny, then morphologyEx with opening and closing. Change one parameter at a time and save each output side by side.
items.done: You can clean speckle noise and small holes from a binary mask and explain what each kernel size changed.

items.text: Feature detection and matching, and homographies.
items.how: Detect ORB keypoints in two photos of the same flat object, match them with BFMatcher, estimate a homography with cv2.findHomography using RANSAC, and warp one image onto the other with warpPerspective.
items.done: The warped image lines up with the target, and you can explain which matches the RANSAC inlier mask removed.

items.text: Convolutional networks: convolution, pooling, receptive fields.
items.how: Read the CS231n notes on convolutional networks, then work out by hand the output size of a Conv2d layer for a given kernel, stride and padding. Build a small network, print each layer's output shape, and calculate the receptive field of the last layer.
items.done: You predict every layer's output shape before running the model, and the printed shapes match.

items.text: Transfer learning: fine-tuning a pretrained model on a small dataset.
items.how: Follow the PyTorch transfer learning tutorial on its ants and bees data. Run it twice: backbone frozen with only the new head trained, then the whole network fine-tuned at a lower learning rate. Record validation accuracy and training time for both.
items.done: You have accuracy and time for both runs and can say when freezing the backbone is the better choice.

items.text: Data augmentation, and augmentations that change the label.
items.how: Apply torchvision.transforms.v2 augmentations to a batch and view the results. Find one that changes the label, such as a horizontal flip on left and right arrows or a crop that cuts out the object. For detection, check that the boxes move with the image.
items.done: You can list the augmentations that are safe for your task and one that would corrupt its labels.

items.text: Object detection and segmentation, and their metrics: IoU and mAP.
items.how: Write an iou(box_a, box_b) function and check it against torchvision.ops.box_iou. Read how mAP averages precision over recall and IoU thresholds, then run validation on a pretrained detector and read its mAP50 and mAP50-95.
items.done: Your IoU matches box_iou on random boxes, and you can explain the difference between mAP50 and mAP50-95.

items.text: Evaluating on a held-out set that matches deployment conditions.
items.how: Test a trained classifier on images from a different source than its training data: another camera, lighting or background. Compare the accuracy with the original test split, and check that no near-duplicate images sit in both train and test.
items.done: You can report the accuracy drop between the original and the shifted test set and name its likely cause.

items.text: Running models on video in real time: batching and frame skipping.
items.how: Read frames with cv2.VideoCapture, run a model on each one and measure frames per second. Then process every second or third frame, and batch several frames per forward pass under torch.no_grad(). Compare throughput and latency for each setting.
items.done: You have FPS and per-frame latency for each setting and can say which one meets a stated real-time target.

sections.title: Build — a vision model in use
sections.guide: Fix the task and dataset first, since every later step depends on them. Train a baseline before fine-tuning, keep the test split untouched until the metrics step, and build the inference command last.

items.text: Collect or choose a dataset for a specific task.
items.how: Write a short task definition: classes, input images and where the model will run. Collect images or choose a public dataset, split it into train, validation and test folders by source or date so near-duplicates stay in one split, and count images per class.
items.done: You have a written task definition, three split folders, and a per-class count table.

items.text: Fine-tune a pretrained model and beat a simple baseline.
items.how: Train a baseline first: a majority-class predictor and a frozen pretrained backbone with a linear head. Then fine-tune a pretrained torchvision model with augmentation, pick the checkpoint by validation score, and evaluate both on the same test split.
items.done: The fine-tuned model beats the baseline on the test split, and you report the margin.

items.text: Report per-class metrics and a confusion matrix.
items.how: Collect test-set predictions and run classification_report for per-class precision, recall and F1, then plot ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions. For a detector, use the per-class mAP table from the validation run instead.
items.done: You can name the two classes the model confuses most, with the count from the confusion matrix.

items.text: Review the worst errors and write down their causes.
items.how: Sort test errors by loss or by confidence on the wrong answer, and save the 20 worst to a folder with true and predicted labels in the file names. Tag each with a cause, such as wrong label, blur, occlusion, rare viewpoint or overlapping classes, and count the tags.
items.done: You have a table of error causes with counts and one planned fix for the largest group.

items.text: Run inference on a webcam, video file or folder with a command.
items.how: Write a command with argparse that takes --source as a webcam index, a video file or a folder of images, loads the saved model once, and writes annotated output or a CSV of predictions. Print the average FPS at the end.
items.done: One command runs on all three source types and produces output without any code edits.

gate.note: Evaluate on data the model never saw during training or tuning.

items.text: Explain what a convolution layer learns and why it suits images.
Compute IoU for two boxes by hand and match your code.
Show an augmentation that would corrupt your labels, and why.
Show the failure cases of your model and a plan to reduce them.

phases.name: Natural language processing
phases.aim: Process text at scale: classification, extraction, search and language models.

resources.name: Advanced NLP with spaCy
resources.why: Free interactive course from the spaCy authors

resources.name: Hugging Face LLM course
resources.why: Transformers, tokenizers and fine-tuning

resources.name: scikit-learn text tutorial
resources.why: Bag of words, TF-IDF and linear classifiers

resources.name: Sentence Transformers
resources.why: Text embeddings for search and clustering

resources.name: NLTK book
resources.why: Classic introduction to language processing; free online

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Start with text handling (s0.0 to s0.2), then the TF-IDF baseline and spaCy (s0.3, s0.4), then embeddings and transformers (s0.5, s0.6), and finish with evaluation and search (s0.7, s0.8). Give evaluation as much time as the models; most wrong conclusions in NLP come from bad metrics.

items.text: Unicode, normalization and cleaning text without losing meaning.
items.how: Write 'café' once with a precomposed é and once with e plus a combining accent, and compare len, == and unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s). Then write a cleaner that normalises, fixes whitespace and applies casefold(), and list what it must keep, such as accents in names.
items.done: Your cleaner makes both forms of 'café' equal, and you can say when NFKC normalisation loses meaning.

items.text: Tokenization: words, subwords, and why models use subwords.
items.how: Tokenise the same sentences with str.split, spaCy and a Hugging Face AutoTokenizer. Pass a rare word and a misspelling through the subword tokenizer and look at the pieces. Read how BPE builds its vocabulary by merging frequent pairs.

where.name: Hugging Face LLM course: BPE tokenization

items.done: You can explain how a subword tokenizer handles a word it has never seen, and why that avoids an unknown-word token.

items.text: Regular expressions for extraction, and where they break.
items.how: Write patterns with re.findall and named groups that extract dates, prices and email addresses from 50 real lines of text. Keep the lines where they fail, such as mixed formats, nested structure or text that looks like a match but is not.
items.done: Your patterns pass a test file of positive and negative examples, and you can name a task where regex is the wrong tool.

items.text: Bag of words and TF-IDF with a linear classifier as a strong baseline.
items.how: Build a Pipeline of TfidfVectorizer and LogisticRegression on a labelled set such as 20 Newsgroups. Try word and character n-grams and different min_df values, then print the highest-weighted terms for each class.
items.done: You have a baseline macro F1 and can explain the top features for two classes.

items.text: spaCy pipelines: tagging, parsing and named entity recognition.
items.how: Work through chapter 1 of the spaCy course, then run spacy.load('en_core_web_sm') on a news article. Print each token's pos_, dep_ and head, list doc.ents, and view the parse with displacy.
items.done: You can pull every organisation and date out of an article in a few lines and point to one entity the model got wrong.

items.text: Embeddings and semantic similarity.
items.how: Encode 20 sentences with a Sentence Transformers model and compute the cosine similarity matrix. Include paraphrases, a negated sentence, and pairs that share words but not meaning, then check which pairs score highest.
items.done: You can show a pair with high word overlap but low similarity, and a paraphrase pair that scores high.

items.text: Transformers: fine-tuning a pretrained model for classification.
items.how: Follow the Hugging Face text classification guide: tokenise a dataset, load AutoModelForSequenceClassification, and train a small model with Trainer for one or two epochs. Evaluate on the held-out split with the same metric as your TF-IDF baseline.

where.name: Hugging Face LLM course: fine-tuning with Trainer

items.done: You have a fine-tuned model saved to disk and a test score next to the baseline's.

items.text: Evaluation: precision, recall, F1, and class imbalance.
items.how: Build a test set that is 95% one class and show that always predicting the majority scores 95% accuracy and zero minority recall. Compute per-class precision, recall and F1 with classification_report, then try class_weight='balanced' and a different decision threshold.
items.done: You can explain macro versus weighted F1 and choose a threshold from a precision-recall curve for a stated goal.

items.text: Search: keyword, semantic and hybrid ranking.
items.how: Index a few thousand documents three ways: BM25 with rank_bm25, embeddings with Sentence Transformers, and a hybrid that merges both rankings with reciprocal rank fusion. Write 20 queries with known relevant documents and compare recall at 10.
items.done: You have recall@10 for each method on your 20 queries and can say which query types each one handles best.

sections.title: Build — a text classifier or search engine
sections.guide: Write the labelling guide and label the data before training anything. Build the TF-IDF baseline, then the transformer, on one frozen test set. Do the error analysis before the command or API, and write the limits note last, from what the error analysis showed.

items.text: A labelled dataset with a written labelling guide.
items.how: Write a labelling guide with a definition and two examples per label, plus rules for edge cases. Label at least 500 examples, have a second person or a second pass relabel 100 of them, and measure agreement with cohen_kappa_score.
items.done: You have the guide, the labelled file and a kappa score, and you revised the guide where the labellers disagreed.

items.text: A TF-IDF baseline, then a transformer, compared on the same test set.
items.how: Freeze one test split first. Train the TF-IDF and LogisticRegression baseline, then fine-tune a small transformer, and score both with the same evaluation script. Record training time and inference time per 1,000 texts as well.
items.done: One table shows both models' macro F1, training time and inference speed on the same test set.

items.text: Error analysis grouped by error type.
items.how: Export every test error with text, true label, predicted label and confidence. Read them and tag each with a type, such as label noise, negation, sarcasm, very short text, domain terms or an unclear class boundary, then count the tags for each model.
items.done: You have error counts by type for both models and can say which types the transformer fixed and which it did not.

items.text: A command or API that takes text and returns predictions with confidence.
items.how: Wrap the better model in a command that reads text from an argument or stdin, or a FastAPI endpoint that takes JSON. Return the label and its probability, load the model once at start-up, and write a test that calls it.
items.done: A call on sample text returns a label and a probability between 0 and 1, and the test passes.

items.text: A note on the languages and domains where it should not be used.
items.how: Using the error analysis and the training data, write a short note in model card format: training languages and sources, text types it was not tested on, known failure types, and the shortest text length it handles well.
