items.done: The note names specific languages, domains and text types to avoid, each backed by data or an error example.

gate.note: Report results on a test set you did not tune against.

items.text: Explain why accuracy is misleading for imbalanced classes, with your own numbers.
Show your baseline and explain why it matters.
Explain how subword tokenization handles a word the model never saw.
Show ten errors from your model and what they have in common.

phases.name: Testing & quality engineering
phases.aim: Design test suites that catch real defects quickly, from unit tests to end-to-end.

resources.name: Obey the Testing Goat
resources.why: Test-driven development with Python; free online

resources.name: pytest documentation
resources.why: Fixtures, parametrize, markers, plugins

resources.name: Hypothesis
resources.why: Property-based testing

resources.name: Playwright for Python
resources.why: Browser end-to-end tests

resources.name: Locust
resources.why: Load testing in Python

resources.name: mutmut
resources.why: Mutation testing for Python

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Read the test-pyramid material first so each later tool has a place in it. Then pytest and test doubles (s0.1, s0.2), Hypothesis and mutation testing (s0.3, s0.4), the slower levels (s0.5 to s0.8), and finally flaky tests and CI speed. Write a working test for every item rather than only reading.

items.text: The test pyramid, and what each level catches that the others miss.
items.how: Read Martin Fowler's practical test pyramid article. For one of your projects, list three bugs you have had and say which level (unit, integration or end-to-end) would have caught each first, and how long that test would take to run.
items.done: You can give one bug that only an integration test would catch and one that only an end-to-end test would catch.

items.text: pytest fixtures, scopes, parametrize, markers and conftest.py.
items.how: Write a fixture that uses yield for set-up and tear-down, give it scope='module' and move it into conftest.py. Add @pytest.mark.parametrize with five cases, register a slow marker in your config, and run pytest -m 'not slow'.

where.name: pytest how to mark test functions

items.done: You can explain fixture scopes and how pytest finds conftest.py, and pytest -m 'not slow' skips the marked tests.

items.text: Test doubles: stubs, fakes and mocks, and mocking only at boundaries.
items.how: Write a function that calls an HTTP API and stores the results. Test it with a stub that returns fixed data, a fake in-memory repository, and unittest.mock.patch with assert_called_once_with. Then pass the HTTP client in as a parameter and drop the patch.
items.done: Your doubles replace only the network and storage, and renaming an internal helper breaks no test.

items.text: Property-based testing with Hypothesis.
items.how: Write a @given test for an encode and decode pair: for any input, decode(encode(x)) == x. Add a sort or dedupe function and test properties such as idempotence and preserved contents. Let Hypothesis shrink a failing case, then fix the code.
items.done: You can name three kinds of property (round-trip, idempotence, invariant), and your tests pass the default 100 examples.

items.text: Coverage vs mutation testing: what each measures.
items.how: Run coverage run --branch -m pytest on a small module and read coverage report -m. Then run mutmut run on the same module, find a surviving mutant on a line coverage marks as covered, and add the assertion that kills it.
items.done: You can explain why 100% line coverage can still leave surviving mutants, with an example from your own code.

items.text: Testing against a real database in containers.
items.how: Start PostgreSQL with PostgresContainer from testcontainers in a session-scoped fixture, run your migrations, and roll back a transaction after each test. Write one test that would pass on SQLite but checks PostgreSQL behaviour, such as a JSONB query or a constraint.
items.done: Your integration tests run against a real PostgreSQL container and leave no data behind between tests.

items.text: Browser tests with Playwright, and avoiding flaky waits.
items.how: Install pytest-playwright, write a test that logs in and checks a page, and find elements with get_by_role locators. Replace every time.sleep and fixed timeout with expect(...) assertions, which retry until the condition holds.
items.done: Your browser tests contain no sleeps and pass 20 runs in a row in a shell loop.

items.text: Contract tests between services.
items.how: Read how Pact works, then write a consumer test with pact-python that records the requests a client makes to a provider. Verify the provider against the recorded contract, rename a field in the provider, and watch verification fail.
items.done: Verification fails on a breaking provider change, and you can say what a contract test checks that a mocked unit test does not.

items.text: Load testing with Locust and reading the results.
items.how: Write a locustfile.py with an HttpUser and two weighted tasks against a local app. Run it headless with --users, --spawn-rate and --run-time, read the median, 95th percentile and failure rate, and find the user count where latency climbs.

where.name: Locust running without the web UI

items.done: You can state the request rate and p95 latency your app sustains and the load at which errors start.

items.text: Finding and fixing flaky tests; test speed in CI.
items.how: Run the suite in random order with pytest-randomly to expose tests that depend on each other, and fix the shared state. Find the slowest tests with pytest --durations=10, then run in parallel with pytest -n auto from pytest-xdist.
items.done: Your suite passes in random order, and you have wall-clock timings before and after the speed changes.

sections.title: Build — a test strategy for a real project
sections.guide: Choose a project with real users or real data, not one written for this phase. Write the risk list first; every test you add afterwards should point to a risk on it. Set up CI last, once you know which tests are fast and which are slow.

items.text: Take an existing project and write down its risks.
items.how: Read the project's code, issue tracker and commit history, and list its risks: what breaks most often, what costs most when it breaks, and what is hardest to check by hand. Rate each by likelihood and impact and sort the list.
items.done: You have a ranked list of at least 8 risks, each tied to a file, feature or past bug.

items.text: Unit, integration and end-to-end tests matched to those risks.
items.how: For each high-ranked risk pick the cheapest level that catches it: unit for logic, integration for the database and external services, end-to-end for the main user flows. Write them in that order and note the risk each test covers.
items.done: Every high-ranked risk has at least one test, and a table shows which test covers which risk.

items.text: At least one property-based test that finds a real bug.
items.how: Pick a function with a clear invariant, such as parsing, serialisation, date handling or money arithmetic. Write the property, raise the example count with @settings(max_examples=1000), and after fixing the bug keep the shrunk failing input as a plain regression test.
items.done: You have a commit that fixes a bug the property test found, with the shrunk example saved as its own test.

items.text: A mutation-testing run and the tests it made you add.
items.how: Run mutmut on the highest-risk modules rather than the whole project. Go through the surviving mutants, write tests for the ones that matter, note the equivalent ones, and record the mutation score before and after.
items.done: You have before and after mutation scores and a list of the tests the survivors made you write.

items.text: CI that runs fast tests on every push and slow ones on a schedule.
items.how: Write a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the fast tests on push, and a second job triggered by schedule with a cron line for integration, browser and mutation tests. Use your pytest markers to split them and cache dependencies.

where.name: GitHub Actions: building and testing Python
GitHub Actions: events that trigger workflows

items.done: The push job finishes in under five minutes, and the scheduled job has run at least once with results you can open.

gate.note: Use a codebase that is not yours if you can.

items.text: Show a bug your tests caught before it merged.
Explain when a mock makes a test worse.
Show a test with 100% coverage that still misses a bug, and the mutation that reveals it.
Make a flaky test deterministic and explain the cause.

phases.name: Network automation
phases.aim: Configure, validate and audit network devices with Python, safely and repeatably.

resources.name: Cisco DevNet learning labs
resources.why: Free labs and sandboxes for network programmability

resources.name: Netmiko
resources.why: SSH to network devices across vendors

resources.name: NAPALM
resources.why: One API over many network operating systems

resources.name: Nornir
resources.why: Inventory and concurrent tasks in plain Python

resources.name: ncclient
resources.why: NETCONF client

resources.name: TextFSM
resources.why: Parse command output into structured data

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Set up a lab device or a Cisco DevNet sandbox before reading, so every item ends with a command run against a real device. Work in order: connect and parse (s0.0 to s0.2), generate and deploy (s0.3 to s0.5), then the safety items (s0.6 to s0.8), which deserve the most time.

items.text: Connecting over SSH with Netmiko, and handling prompts and timeouts.
items.how: Connect to a lab device with ConnectHandler inside a with block and run send_command('show version'). Trigger a timeout with a slow command and fix it with read_timeout, then answer a confirmation prompt using expect_string or send_command_timing.
items.done: Your script runs three show commands and exits cleanly, and prints a clear error when the host is unreachable.

items.text: Parsing show-command output with TextFSM or TTP.
items.how: Run show ip interface brief with use_textfsm=True to get a list of dicts from ntc-templates. Then write your own TextFSM template for a command that has none, and test it on saved output from two devices.
items.done: Your template turns saved output into structured rows, and a test compares them with expected values.

items.text: Inventories in YAML, and running tasks concurrently with Nornir.
items.how: Write hosts.yaml, groups.yaml and defaults.yaml, load them with InitNornir, and run a Netmiko task on every host with nr.run. Narrow the run with nr.filter, and time it with one worker against the default thread pool.
items.done: One command runs a task on every lab device in parallel, and you can read per-host results and failures from the result object.

items.text: Rendering configuration from Jinja2 templates and data.
items.how: Write a Jinja2 template for interfaces and a YAML data file, and render with Environment(undefined=StrictUndefined) using a loop, a conditional and a filter. Delete a required variable from the data and check that rendering fails instead of producing blank config.
items.done: The rendered text matches a saved expected config file, and a missing variable raises an error.

items.text: NAPALM: getters, config diff, commit and rollback.
items.how: Open a device with get_network_driver and call get_facts and get_interfaces. Load a small change with load_merge_candidate, print compare_config() and call discard_config(). Repeat with commit_config(), then undo it with rollback().
items.done: You can show the diff before a commit and return the device to its previous config with rollback().

items.text: NETCONF and RESTCONF with YANG models.
items.how: On a device with NETCONF and RESTCONF enabled, such as an IOS XE sandbox, call get_config in ncclient with a subtree filter for interfaces. Fetch the same data over RESTCONF with requests and the application/yang-data+json header, and find the YANG model used.
items.done: You can read and change one interface description over both NETCONF and RESTCONF and name the YANG model involved.

items.text: Dry runs, change windows and automatic rollback.
items.how: Add a --dry-run mode, on by default, that prints diffs and discards them. Refuse to commit outside a configured change window, and where the driver supports it use commit-confirm, such as NAPALM's commit_config(revert_in=300), so an unconfirmed change reverts.
items.done: A default run changes nothing, and in the lab a commit you do not confirm reverts on its own.

items.text: Validating state before and after a change.
items.how: Before a change, save interface states, route counts and routing neighbour states; after it, collect the same and compare. Use NAPALM's compliance_report with a validation YAML file, or your own getters and a dict comparison.
items.done: Your check prints pass or fail per device and names each value that changed.

items.text: Credentials from a vault or environment, never in code.
items.how: Read credentials from environment variables with os.environ, prompt with getpass for interactive runs, or fetch them from HashiCorp Vault with hvac. Add a secret scanner as a pre-commit hook and search the git history for your lab password.

where.name: hvac, the Python client for Vault

items.done: Your scripts run with no password in any file, and a search of the repo history for the lab password finds nothing.

sections.title: Build — a change pipeline
sections.guide: Build the lab first, then the source-of-truth file and templates, then the dry run. Add pre- and post-change checks with rollback before you ever apply to every device, and write the compliance report last. Run all of it against the lab only.

items.text: A lab with at least three virtual devices.
items.how: Install containerlab and write a topology file with at least three devices, such as Arista cEOS or Nokia SR Linux, linked together. Deploy it, reach each device over SSH, and commit the topology file to the repo.
items.done: containerlab deploy brings the lab up from the file, and your Nornir inventory reaches every device.

items.text: Configuration generated from templates and a source-of-truth file.
items.how: Keep device data such as hostnames, interfaces, addresses and VLANs in one YAML file and validate it when loading. Render each device's config with Jinja2 into a build/ folder, one file per device.
items.done: Two builds in a row produce identical files, and changing one value in the YAML changes only the expected lines.

items.text: A dry run that shows the diff before anything is applied.
items.how: Through Nornir with nornir_napalm, load each rendered config as a candidate, write compare_config() output to a per-device diff report, and discard the candidate. Make this the default mode; applying needs an explicit flag.
items.done: The dry run prints a diff per device and leaves every running config unchanged.

items.text: Pre- and post-change checks that trigger a rollback on failure.
items.how: Run the checks and save the results, apply the change, then run the checks again. If a check fails or a device stops responding, call rollback() on every changed device and exit with a non-zero code.
items.done: A deliberately bad change in the lab triggers the rollback and leaves the devices as they were before.

items.text: A compliance report across the whole inventory.
items.how: Write rules in a validation file, such as the NTP servers, the login banner, SSH version 2 and no unused interfaces left enabled. Run them across the inventory with Nornir and write a CSV or HTML report with one row per device and rule.
items.done: The report shows pass or fail per device and rule, and fixing one device's config turns its failing row to pass.

gate.note: Only on lab devices or equipment you are authorized to change.

items.text: Push a change to many devices concurrently and roll it back.
Show the diff your tool produces before a change.
Explain why structured data beats screen-scraping, and when you still need parsing.
Show where credentials come from in your code.

phases.name: Embedded, IoT & hardware
phases.aim: Run Python on microcontrollers and single-board computers, and connect devices to services.

resources.name: Welcome to CircuitPython
resources.why: Adafruit's step-by-step guide for boards and sensors

resources.name: MicroPython
resources.why: Python on microcontrollers

resources.name: Raspberry Pi
resources.why: Hardware, GPIO and the operating system

resources.name: Wokwi
resources.why: Simulate microcontrollers and circuits in the browser

resources.name: Eclipse Paho MQTT
resources.why: MQTT client for Python

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: The background for running Python on a board. Work items 0 to 3 first on a real board or in Wokwi, which runs MicroPython in the browser, then 4 to 8 once you have a working sensor loop. Spend about two thirds of the time with code running on the device rather than reading.

items.text: MicroPython and CircuitPython vs CPython: what is missing and why.
items.how: Read the MicroPython differences page, then run one script using json, re and datetime in CPython and on the board through mpremote run. Note every import or method that fails and what replaces it on the board.
items.done: You can name three CPython features missing on your board and say why: flash size, RAM, or no operating system.

items.text: GPIO: digital input and output, pull-up resistors and debouncing.
items.how: Wire a button to a GPIO pin with Pin.PULL_UP and an LED to another pin. Count presses, watch contact bounce produce extra counts, then debounce in software by ignoring changes within 20 ms of the last accepted one.
items.done: Fifty presses give a count of fifty, and you can explain why the pin reads 1 when the button is released.

items.text: PWM, analog input, and reading sensors.
items.how: Fade an LED by stepping the duty cycle of machine.PWM. Then read a potentiometer or light sensor with machine.ADC, convert read_u16() to volts, and average ten samples to reduce noise.
items.done: Turning the potentiometer gives a steady voltage reading within about 0.1 V of a multimeter.

items.text: Buses: I2C, SPI and UART.
items.how: Attach an I2C sensor, run I2C.scan() and match the address to the datasheet, then read one register. Send text between the board and your computer through a USB-serial adapter on UART, reading it with pyserial.
items.done: You can say how many wires I2C, SPI and UART each need, and which you would pick for a sensor, a display and a GPS module.

items.text: Polling vs interrupts, and timing without blocking.
items.how: Blink an LED with time.ticks_ms() and time.ticks_diff() instead of sleep() while also reading a button. Then move the button to Pin.irq() with a handler that only sets a flag, following the interrupt handler rules.
items.done: The LED keeps its blink rate while presses are still caught, and your handler allocates no memory.

items.text: Memory limits: avoiding allocation in loops, and frozen modules.
items.how: Print gc.mem_free() before and after a loop that builds strings each pass, then rewrite it to reuse one bytearray through a memoryview. Read how a manifest freezes a module into the firmware and why that saves RAM.
items.done: The rewritten loop shows flat free memory over 1000 iterations, and you can explain what freezing a module changes.

items.text: MQTT: topics, QoS and retained messages.
items.how: Install the Mosquitto broker locally and use paho-mqtt to publish and subscribe on topics such as home/room1/temp. Try the + and # wildcards, QoS 0 against QoS 1, and a retained message received by a subscriber that connects later.
items.done: You can show a late subscriber receiving a retained message and explain what QoS 1 guarantees and what it does not.

items.text: Power: sleep modes and battery budgets.
items.how: Measure current with a USB power meter while the board idles, uses Wi-Fi, and sits in machine.lightsleep() or machine.deepsleep(), noting that deep sleep restarts from boot. Use the numbers to work out days of runtime on a stated battery.
items.done: You have a written budget: battery mAh divided by average mA, with the wake and sleep duty cycle stated.

items.text: Updating devices in the field safely.
items.how: Design an update that downloads new code to a temporary file, checks its SHA-256 hash with hashlib, and only then renames it into place. Add machine.WDT so an update that hangs gets reset, and keep the previous version to fall back to.
items.done: You can describe what happens if power is cut at each step of the update, and every case leaves runnable code.

sections.title: Build — a connected sensor
sections.guide: One sensor node and one service on your computer. Build in item order: sensor loop, MQTT publishing, the storing service, then network-loss handling. Draw the wiring diagram while you wire, not at the end. Item 3 takes the most time, so leave room for it.

items.text: A board that reads a real sensor on a schedule.
items.how: Pick one sensor (temperature, humidity or light), wire it, and read it every 60 s from a non-blocking loop based on ticks_ms. Print timestamped readings over the serial REPL for an hour before adding any networking.
items.done: An hour of serial output shows 60 readings with sensible values and no gaps.

items.text: Readings published over MQTT to a broker.
items.how: Connect with network.WLAN, then publish each reading as JSON with a device id and timestamp using umqtt.simple (installed with mip) to your local broker. Watch the traffic with mosquitto_sub -v -t 'sensors/#'.
items.done: mosquitto_sub prints one message per reading with the expected topic and a valid JSON payload.

items.text: A service that stores the readings and alerts on a threshold.
items.how: Write a CPython service with paho-mqtt that subscribes, validates each payload and inserts it into SQLite. Alert once when the threshold is crossed and once when it clears, not on every reading. Test it by publishing fake readings with mosquitto_pub.
items.done: Fake readings that cross the threshold twice give two alerts rather than one per reading, and every reading is in the table.

items.text: Handling of network loss without losing readings.
items.how: When a publish fails, append the reading to a file on the board's flash, then send the backlog in order with original timestamps once the connection returns. Give the database a unique key on device and timestamp. Test by stopping the broker for ten minutes.
items.done: After a ten-minute outage the database holds every reading with no duplicates and no gaps.

items.text: A wiring diagram and a parts list in the repository.
items.how: Draw the circuit in Wokwi or Fritzing, or photograph a clear hand drawing, showing every pin number and power rail. Write a parts list with part numbers and quantities in docs/, then check both against the real board.
items.done: Someone with only the diagram and parts list could rebuild the board without asking you.

gate.note: A simulator such as Wokwi counts if you have no hardware.

items.text: Debounce a button and explain why it is needed.
Read a sensor over I2C and explain the addressing.
Show your device recovering from a dropped connection.
Explain how much memory your program uses and where.

phases.name: Security engineering
phases.aim: Build security tooling, secure the software supply chain, and detect and investigate incidents.

resources.name: PortSwigger Web Security Academy
resources.why: Free labs for every major web vulnerability

resources.name: OWASP Threat Modeling
resources.why: Process and techniques for threat models

resources.name: Bandit
resources.why: Static analysis for common Python security issues

resources.name: Semgrep
resources.why: Write your own code-scanning rules

resources.name: pip-audit
resources.why: Scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities

resources.name: Scapy
resources.why: Build and inspect network packets

resources.name: picoCTF
resources.why: Legal capture-the-flag practice

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Defensive security work in Python, all on your own code, logs, network and lab machines. Start with item 0, since the threat model tells you what to scan and log. Then do 1 to 3 on your code, 4 and 5 on your logs, 6 and 7 in your lab. Run item 8 as a weekly session alongside the rest.

items.text: Threat modeling with STRIDE on a system you built.
items.how: Draw a data flow diagram of an app you built in an earlier phase: processes, data stores, external entities and trust boundaries. Walk each element through the six STRIDE categories and write one threat and one mitigation per row.
items.done: You have a table of at least ten threats, each tied to a diagram element and a mitigation or an accepted risk.

items.text: Static analysis with Bandit and custom Semgrep rules.
items.how: Run bandit -r src/ on one of your projects and mark each finding as real or false positive. Then write a Semgrep YAML rule for a pattern in your own code, such as subprocess.run with shell=True, with an annotated test file.
items.done: Your rule passes semgrep --test: it fires on the bad lines and stays silent on the good ones.

items.text: Supply chain: pinning, hashes, pip-audit, SBOMs and signed releases.
items.how: Pin a project with pip-compile --generate-hashes, install with pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt, and run pip-audit. Generate an SBOM with cyclonedx-py and read how PyPI release attestations prove where a package was built.
items.done: Changing one hash in the requirements file makes the install fail, and you can say what an SBOM lists.

items.text: Secrets detection in code and history, and rotation after a leak.
items.how: In a throwaway repo, commit a fake API key, remove it in a later commit, then find it with gitleaks git scanning full history. Write the response steps in order: revoke, issue a new key, check logs for use, then rewrite history.
items.done: The scanner finds a key absent from the latest commit, and you can explain why rotation comes before rewriting history.

items.text: Logging for detection: what to record and what never to record.
items.how: Add structured logging to one of your apps for logins, permission failures and validation failures, with timestamp, user id and source IP. Add a logging.Filter that masks passwords, tokens and card numbers, and a test that proves it.
items.done: A test logs a record containing a token and asserts the token is absent from the output.

items.text: Writing detection rules over logs and testing them with sample data.
items.how: Write detection rules in Python over JSON log lines, such as five failed logins from one IP within 60 s. Build sample files with known attack sequences and normal traffic, and run every rule against both with pytest. Read Sigma rules for how others express the same idea.
items.done: Each rule fires on its attack sample and on none of the normal samples, and the tests show both.

items.text: Packet capture and analysis with Scapy on your own network.
items.how: On your own network or a VM, capture 100 packets with sniff(count=100), save them with wrpcap, and count them by protocol and destination. This needs admin rights; capture only traffic on networks you own. Open the file in Wireshark to check.
items.done: Your script's per-protocol counts match what Wireshark shows for the same pcap file.

items.text: Incident response basics: contain, preserve evidence, investigate, recover.
items.how: Read the NIST incident response guide, then run a tabletop exercise on one scenario, such as a leaked cloud key in your own account. Write how you detect it, contain it, which evidence you copy and hash before changing anything, and how you recover.
items.done: You have a one-page runbook for the scenario and can explain why evidence is preserved before cleanup.

items.text: Capture-the-flag practice on legal platforms.
items.how: Work through picoCTF practice problems one category a week, starting with General Skills and Forensics, and the PortSwigger labs for web topics. Solve with Python scripts where you can and write up each solve.
items.done: You have write-ups for ten solved problems, each stating the flaw and how to defend against it.

sections.title: Build — a security tool
sections.guide: One narrow security tool with tests. Write the scope first, then build the detector against test samples, add SARIF or JSON output, write the documentation, and finish with CI. Spend at least a third of the time on the known-good and known-bad samples.

items.text: A tool that solves one security task: a scanner, a log detector or a secrets finder.
items.how: Write the scope first: what the tool detects, on which input, and what it ignores. Build the core as a pure function from input to findings, then wrap it in an argparse CLI. Point it only at code, logs or repos you own.
items.done: The CLI runs on a real input of yours and prints each finding with its location and reason.

items.text: Tests with known-bad and known-good samples, including false positives.
items.how: Make tests/samples/bad/ with inputs that must be flagged and tests/samples/good/ with look-alikes that must not be, such as a placeholder key in docs or password as a variable name. Parametrise pytest over both folders.
items.done: All samples pass, and the good folder includes at least three inputs an earlier version of the tool wrongly flagged.

items.text: Output in a standard format such as SARIF or JSON.
items.how: Add --format json and --format sarif. For SARIF emit version 2.1.0 with one run, your tool in tool.driver with its rules, and each finding as a result with ruleId, level and location. Validate against the schema.
items.done: The SARIF output validates and a SARIF viewer shows each finding on the right file and line.

items.text: Documentation on scope, limits and safe use.
items.how: Write a README with sections for what the tool detects, what it misses, known false positives, permissions it needs, and where it may be run. State that it is for systems you own or are authorised to test.
items.done: A new user can install it, run it on a sample and name one limitation using only the README.

items.text: Run in CI against a real project.
items.how: Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the tool on every push to one of your real projects and uploads the SARIF with github/codeql-action/upload-sarif. Fail the job on high-severity findings only.
items.done: A push that adds a known-bad sample fails the job, and removing it makes the job pass.

gate.note: Only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

items.text: Present a threat model for one of your services.
Write a Semgrep or Bandit rule that catches a bug class, with tests.
Show your dependency scan, the findings and your decisions.
Complete a set of PortSwigger labs or CTF challenges and write up one.

phases.name: Bots & integrations
phases.aim: Build chat bots and integrations between services that run unattended.

resources.name: discord.py
resources.why: Discord bots with async Python

resources.name: python-telegram-bot
resources.why: Telegram bots

resources.name: Bolt for Python (Slack)
resources.why: Slack apps and bots

resources.name: APScheduler
resources.why: Scheduled jobs inside a Python process

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: How chat bots and service integrations work. Pick one platform (Discord, Telegram or Slack) and do items 0 to 2 on it with a private test server or chat, then 3 to 7. Keep one toy bot and extend it with each item, so every item ends with a working change you can run.

items.text: Bot platforms: tokens, permissions and intents.
items.how: Create a bot in the Discord Developer Portal, Telegram's BotFather or a Slack app, and put the token in an environment variable. Enable only the intents or scopes the bot needs, then run a minimal bot that replies to one message in a private test server.
items.done: The bot replies in your test space, and you can say which intents or scopes it has and why each is needed.

items.text: Commands, events and interactive components.
items.how: Add a slash command that takes and validates an argument, a handler for an event such as a member joining, and a button that edits the original message when pressed. Use app_commands and discord.ui.View, or CommandHandler and CallbackQueryHandler.
items.done: Pressing the button edits the message instead of posting a new one, and a bad argument gets a clear error reply.

items.text: Webhooks vs long polling, and verifying webhook signatures.
items.how: Run your bot once with long polling and once with a webhook through a tunnel such as ngrok. For Slack, verify each request by computing an HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, comparing with hmac.compare_digest, and rejecting timestamps older than five minutes.
items.done: A request with an altered body or an old timestamp is rejected, and a genuine one is processed.

items.text: OAuth flows for acting on behalf of users.
items.how: Implement the authorisation code flow for Slack or Discord: redirect the user with a random state, check it on the callback, exchange the code for a token on the server, and store the token encrypted. Request the smallest set of scopes.
items.done: A second account can install the app, and a callback with a wrong state value is rejected.

items.text: Rate limits and retry-after headers.
items.how: Read your platform's rate-limit page, then wrap raw HTTP calls so a 429 waits the seconds given in Retry-After, retries up to a fixed limit and logs each wait. Libraries like discord.py already do this; write it yourself once to see how.
items.done: You can explain per-route and global limits, and your wrapper waits the advertised time before retrying.

items.text: Scheduled jobs and idempotent task handling.
items.how: Add a daily job with APScheduler or discord.ext.tasks. Give each run an id such as the date, record it in the database with a unique constraint, and skip the send when the id already exists, so a restart does not post twice.
items.done: Restarting the bot straight after the job runs does not repeat the job's message.

items.text: Storing state per user or per server.
items.how: Store settings in SQLite keyed by guild id or chat id rather than in global variables. Write a /settings command that reads and changes them, then check that two test servers keep separate values across a restart.
items.done: Two test servers show different settings after the bot restarts.

items.text: Deploying a long-running process and restarting it on failure.
items.how: Run the bot as a systemd service with Restart=on-failure, or in Docker with --restart unless-stopped. Log to stdout so journalctl or docker logs keeps the output. Kill the process and watch it come back.
items.done: After kill -9 on the bot process it is back online within a minute, and the restart shows in the logs.

sections.title: Build — a bot people use
sections.guide: A bot that someone else relies on. Agree the task with the group first, then build the command, the scheduled job, the rate-limit tests and the deployment, in that order. The final week is spent running it and reading its logs, so deploy early rather than on the last day.

items.text: A bot for a group you belong to that solves a repeated task.
items.how: Ask the group which task they repeat by hand, such as reminders, a rota or collecting links. Write the task and the commands in one paragraph, get agreement on it, then build the smallest version that does the task.
items.done: At least two group members other than you have used the bot for its task.

items.text: At least one scheduled job and one command.
items.how: Write the command's logic as a plain function you can unit test, and call it from both the command handler and the scheduled job. Log each command call and each job run with the time and result.
items.done: Unit tests cover the shared function, and the job's log lines appear at the scheduled times.

items.text: Rate-limit handling tested with a fake server.
items.how: Point your HTTP client at a local fake server, built with pytest-httpserver or http.server, that returns 429 with Retry-After: 2 for the first requests and then 200. Assert the wait time, the retry count and that no message is lost.
items.done: The test passes, and it fails when you remove the retry logic.

items.text: Secrets from the environment and a documented setup.
items.how: Read every token and id from os.environ, stop at start-up with a clear message if one is missing, and commit a .env.example with placeholders. Add .env to .gitignore and write setup steps in the README from bot creation to first run.
items.done: Someone else sets up a working copy from the README alone, and a secrets scan of the repository finds nothing.

items.text: Deployed and running for a week, with logs you can read.
items.how: Deploy to a small VPS, a home server or a Raspberry Pi using the restart setup from item 7 of the Learn section. Log with levels and timestamps, rotate log files with RotatingFileHandler or journald, and read the logs daily for a week, fixing what you find.
items.done: Seven days of logs show the job ran each day, and you can explain every ERROR line in them.

gate.note: Follow each platform's terms and rate limits.

items.text: Show your bot surviving a restart without losing state.
Explain how you verify that a webhook came from the platform.
Show how your bot behaves when it is rate-limited.
Show a week of logs and one bug you fixed from them.

phases.name: Blockchain tooling
phases.aim: Read chain data, interact with smart contracts, and test them, from Python.

resources.name: Ethereum developer docs
resources.why: Accounts, transactions, gas, smart contracts

resources.name: web3.py
resources.why: Python library for Ethereum

resources.name: Ape
resources.why: Python framework for contract development and testing

resources.name: Solidity documentation
resources.why: The main smart-contract language

sections.title: Learn
sections.guide: Reading and testing Ethereum-style chains from Python. Work items 0 to 3 against a public testnet endpoint or a local chain, read item 4 before creating any key, do 5 and 6 together on a local chain, then 7. Only test networks and test keys are used; no real funds are needed at any point.

items.text: Accounts, keys, transactions, blocks and gas.
items.how: Read the ethereum.org pages on accounts, transactions, blocks and gas. Then open one testnet transaction in a block explorer and name each field: nonce, to, value, gas limit, max fee, priority fee, and gas used from the receipt.
items.done: You can explain from memory how the fee paid is gas used times the effective gas price, and what the base fee part does.

items.text: Connecting to a node over JSON-RPC with web3.py.
items.how: Install web3, connect with Web3(Web3.HTTPProvider(url)) to a testnet endpoint or local node, and call is_connected(), eth.chain_id and eth.block_number. Then send the same eth_blockNumber call as raw JSON-RPC with requests.
items.done: Both methods return the same block number, and you can decode the hex result by hand.

items.text: Reading balances, blocks and contract state.
items.how: Read a balance with eth.get_balance and convert it with Web3.from_wei, fetch a block with eth.get_block and list its transaction hashes, and call a view function such as totalSupply on a deployed testnet contract.
items.done: One script prints a balance, the latest block and a contract value, all matching a block explorer.

items.text: ABIs, calling contract functions, and decoding events.
items.how: Load an ERC-20 ABI, build w3.eth.contract(address=..., abi=...), and call balanceOf and decimals. Fetch Transfer events for a block range with contract.events.Transfer.get_logs() and print the decoded from, to and value.
items.done: Your decoded Transfer list for a block range matches the explorer's list for the same range.

items.text: Key handling: never in code, hardware wallets, and test keys only on testnets.
items.how: Read how web3.py signs locally with eth_account. Create a key for testnet use only, load it from an environment variable or an encrypted keystore file, and add .gitignore entries and a secrets scanner so keys cannot be committed.
items.done: A scan of the repository and its history finds no keys, and you can say why a hardware wallet keeps keys off the computer.

items.text: Writing and testing a contract with Ape and pytest on a local chain.
items.how: Run ape init, install the ape-solidity plugin, and write a small contract in contracts/. Write pytest tests using the accounts and project fixtures to deploy and call it, including one that expects a revert, and run ape test.
items.done: ape test passes, and changing one line of the contract makes a test fail.

items.text: Common contract vulnerabilities: reentrancy, access control, integer issues.
items.how: Write a contract with a reentrant withdraw and an admin function missing its owner check. Write Ape tests on the local chain that attempt each attack and assert it fails, run them against the flawed contract, then fix it.
items.done: The same tests fail on the flawed contract and pass on the fixed one, and you can say what Solidity 0.8 checks on arithmetic.

items.text: Indexing events into a database for queries.
items.how: Fetch logs in fixed block ranges, write each event to a table with a unique key on (tx_hash, log_index), and save the last processed block in the same database transaction. Answer questions with SQL instead of calling the node again.
items.done: Running the indexer twice over the same range leaves the row count unchanged.

sections.title: Build — a chain data tool
sections.guide: An event indexer plus a small contract. Write and test the contract on a local chain first, deploy it to a testnet, then build the indexer, reorg and restart handling, and the report command. Leave the most time for item 1, since restart and reorg bugs are slow to find.

items.text: Index a contract's events from a testnet into SQLite or PostgreSQL.
items.how: Pick a contract on a testnet such as Sepolia, or deploy your own there. Index its events from the deployment block in batches of a few thousand blocks, inserting with INSERT OR IGNORE or ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on (tx_hash, log_index).
items.done: The event count in your database matches the explorer's count for the same block range.

items.text: Handle chain reorganizations and restarts without duplicates.
items.how: Treat blocks as final only after a set number of confirmations or at the finalized block tag. Store each indexed block's hash; on every poll and on restart compare it with the chain, and on a mismatch delete rows from that block onwards and re-index.
items.done: Killing the indexer mid-batch and restarting gives identical rows, and a simulated reorg in a test removes and re-adds rows.

items.text: A small contract with tests on a local chain.
items.how: Write a small contract that emits events your indexer can read, such as a registry emitting Registered. Test it with Ape: normal use, access control, reverts, and that each call emits the expected event with the right arguments.
items.done: ape test passes with at least one test for every public function and every event.

items.text: A command that reports on the indexed data.
items.how: Add a CLI with argparse, such as report --since 2026-01-01 --top 10, that runs SQL over the indexed table and prints totals, the most active addresses and the last indexed block. It must not call the node.
items.done: The report runs with the network off, and its totals match a hand-written SQL query.

items.text: No mainnet keys and no real funds anywhere in the project.
items.how: Use only local chain accounts and testnet keys read from environment variables. Add a start-up check and a CI step that fail if the configured chain id is 1 (Ethereum mainnet), and run a secrets scanner over the repository and its history.
items.done: A config pointing at chain id 1 makes the program and CI stop, and the secrets scan of the full history is clean.

gate.note: Testnets and local chains only.

items.text: Explain what gas is and estimate a transaction's cost.
Decode an event log from its ABI by hand and match your code.
Show a test that catches a reentrancy bug.
Explain how your indexer handles a chain reorganization.

phases.name: Beyond senior
phases.aim: Skills past senior level: judgment, leverage, and work others depend on.

resources.name: Python Enhancement Proposals
resources.why: Read the PEPs behind features you use daily

resources.name: Python Developer's Guide
resources.why: How CPython itself is built and contributed to

resources.name: PEP 8 — style guide
resources.why: The document everyone cites and few have read

resources.name: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
resources.why: Still the best single source on system tradeoffs

sections.title: Technical judgment
sections.guide: Judgement for choosing, scoping and changing systems. Work s0.0 to s0.3 on one real design of your own, then treat s0.4 and s0.7 as reviews of past and planned projects, and s0.5 and s0.6 as hands-on exercises. Give the design doc and the live migration about half the time.

items.text: Choose boring technology deliberately, and be able to defend it.
items.how: Read Choose Boring Technology. List every dependency in your current project and mark each as boring or new. For each new one, write two sentences on what it gives you that a boring option (sqlite3, Postgres, a cron job) cannot.
items.done: You can defend each new technology in your stack in under a minute, or you have replaced it with a boring one.

items.text: Estimate before building: load, storage, cost, and latency budgets.
items.how: For one feature, write a one-page back-of-envelope estimate: peak requests per second, bytes per record times records per year, monthly cost, and a latency budget split across each hop. Then measure the real system and compare.

where.name: Latency numbers every programmer should know

items.done: Your estimates land within a factor of ten of the measured values, and you can explain any that do not.

items.text: Write a design doc that a skeptical reader can attack.
items.how: Write a design doc for a real change: context, goals and non-goals, the design, two rejected alternatives with reasons, and risks. Give it to someone asked to find its weakest point, and record their objections and your answers in the doc.
items.done: The doc survives a hostile review with its main decision intact, or you changed the decision because of the review.

items.text: Identify the one-way doors in a design and slow down at those.
items.how: Go through your design doc and mark each decision as cheap or costly to reverse: data formats, public APIs, the database, anything users store. For each costly one, note the evidence you need before committing and how you would back out.
items.done: You can name the two or three decisions in your design that would take weeks to undo, and say why.

items.text: Kill your own project when the evidence says it isn't working.
items.how: Before your next project, write kill criteria: the measurable result you expect by a date and what you will do if it is missing. Review on that date. Also pick one past project you kept going too long and write down the signal you ignored.
items.done: You have a dated kill-criteria note, acted on it, and did not argue from time already spent.

items.text: Read a large unfamiliar codebase and orient inside a day.
items.how: Clone a large project you have not seen (CPython, Django, pip). In one day: build it, run its tests, find the entry point, trace one command end to end in a debugger, and draw a one-page map of the main modules.

where.name: The Architecture of Open Source Applications

items.done: By the end of the day you can say where a given feature lives, or fix a small bug, without searching blindly.

items.text: Migrate a live system without downtime — expand, migrate, contract.
items.how: In a small app with a database, rename a column with no downtime: add the new column, write to both, backfill, switch reads, stop writing the old one, then drop it. Keep a load script running against the app throughout and log failed requests.
items.done: The load script records zero errors across every step, and each step could be rolled back on its own.

items.text: Reduce scope as a first-class engineering skill.
items.how: Take a planned feature and write three versions of it: full, half, and the smallest that still tests the core assumption. Ship the smallest first. For each part you cut, note what you learned by not building it.
items.done: You shipped a cut-down version sooner than the full plan and can list what you left out on purpose.

sections.title: Operating in production
sections.guide: Running software that other people depend on. Start with instrumentation and SLOs (s1.3, s1.2) on a service you own, then rollout (s1.4) and a backup restore (s1.5), and finish with an incident drill and its postmortem (s1.0, s1.1). Spend most of the time on the running service, not on reading.

items.text: On-call: triage, mitigate first, root-cause after.
items.how: Run a drill: break a service of yours on purpose (fill the disk, stop the database, deploy a bad config) with a timer as the pager. Log every action with a timestamp. Mitigate first by rolling back or failing over; look for the cause only after that.
items.done: Your timeline shows service restored before the root cause was found, within a target time you set in advance.

items.text: Write a blameless postmortem with real action items.
items.how: Take the drill from s1.0 or a public outage. Write a one-page blameless postmortem: timeline, impact, root cause, contributing factors, and three action items, each with an owner, a date and a tracking issue. Prefer actions that remove a class of failure.
items.done: Someone who was not there can follow the timeline and say why it happened, and no sentence blames a person.

items.text: Define SLOs and error budgets for something you own.
items.how: For a service you run, pick two SLIs (share of successful requests, share served under a latency threshold), set an SLO such as 99.5% over 28 days, and work out the error budget in minutes or failed requests. Write a short policy for when the budget runs out.
items.done: You can read the remaining error budget off your own metrics, not estimate it from memory.

items.text: Instrument before you need it — you can't debug what you didn't measure.
items.how: Add structured logs with a request id and the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) to a service you own, using logging and OpenTelemetry. Then inject a fault and diagnose it using only dashboards and logs.
items.done: You located the injected fault from telemetry alone, without adding print statements or redeploying.

items.text: Feature flags, canaries, and progressive rollout.
items.how: Put a new code path behind a flag read at runtime. Roll it out to 1%, 10%, then 100% of requests, comparing error rate and latency between flag-on and flag-off at each step. Then ship a deliberately bad version and roll it back by flipping the flag.
items.done: You rolled back the bad version by changing the flag, with no redeploy, and your metrics showed the gap between the groups.

items.text: Practice a restore from backup. A backup you've never restored isn't one.
items.how: Back up a real database of yours (Connection.backup in sqlite3, or pg_dump). Restore it to a fresh location and check row counts, a checksum of key tables, and that the app starts against it. Time it and write it up as a runbook.
items.done: You have a runbook with a measured restore time, and someone else can follow it to a working copy.

sections.title: Leverage
sections.guide: Work that multiplies your effect on others. Optional and slow: take two or three items a quarter, not all eight. Do s2.0 and s2.1 together, since a project you already use is the easiest route to a merged PR. s2.7 runs in the background for a year.

items.text: Contribute to an open source project you actually use.
items.how: List the libraries your own projects depend on and pick one. Read its CONTRIBUTING file, set up its dev environment and run its tests. Start with a docs fix, a reproducible bug report, or a failing test for an open issue.

where.name: How to contribute to open source

items.done: The project's test suite runs on your machine and you have opened at least one issue or PR on it.

items.text: Get one non-trivial PR reviewed and merged by strangers.
items.how: Choose an issue the maintainers have accepted, say on it that you are taking it, and keep the PR to one change with tests and a changelog entry if the project uses one. Answer review within a few days and rebase when asked.

where.name: How to contribute to open source

items.done: A maintainer you do not know merged it, and it changed behaviour or fixed a bug rather than only docs.

items.text: Publish a package to PyPI with docs, tests, and CI.
items.how: Move a small utility from your own code into a package: pyproject.toml, src layout, pytest tests, a README. Add CI that tests every push and publishes on a tag via trusted publishing. Upload to TestPyPI first.
items.done: pip install of your package works in a fresh virtual environment and CI shows passing.

items.text: Write technical posts explaining something you struggled with.
items.how: Pick something that took you more than a day to understand. Write 800 to 1500 words: the confusion, the wrong model you held, the working model, and a minimal example that runs. Have one person at your earlier level read it before publishing.
items.done: A reader at your earlier level can run the example and explain the idea back to you.

items.text: Review someone else's code and leave comments that teach.
items.how: Read Google's guide on review comments, then review a PR in an open source project or a friend's repository. For each comment state the problem, why it matters and one way to fix it; label nits as nits.

where.name: Google review guide: how to review

items.done: The author changed the code because of your comments without having to ask what you meant.

items.text: Mentor one person through a problem without writing their code.
items.how: Pair with a learner on a bug in their code and stay off the keyboard. Ask what they expected, what happened and what they have ruled out; suggest one experiment at a time. Afterwards write down which questions moved them forward.
items.done: They fixed it themselves and can explain the fix, and you wrote no code in their files.

items.text: Give a talk or a lightning talk at a meetup or online.
items.how: Turn one of your posts into a five-minute lightning talk: one idea, one demo, at most ten slides. Watch a few lightning talks first, rehearse aloud three times against a timer, then submit it to a local Python meetup or an online event.
items.done: You gave the talk within the time limit and answered at least one question from the audience.

items.text: Maintain something long enough to feel the cost of your own decisions.
items.how: Keep one project in use for at least a year: fix issues, upgrade dependencies, and cut releases with semantic version numbers and a changelog. Each time a past decision costs you time, add it to a decisions log with the cost.
items.done: Your log names at least three past choices you would now make differently, with what each cost you.

sections.title: Staying current after 2027
sections.guide: A standing routine for after the course. Set calendar reminders: release notes each October when a new CPython ships, one codebase per quarter, re-benchmarks and a rebuild once a year. Keep one notes file that every check-in adds to.

items.text: Follow the CPython release notes each version and try the new features.
items.how: When each CPython version ships, read its What's New page, pick three changes and write a short script that uses each. Run your main project's tests on the new version and note what breaks.
items.done: Your notes have one entry per release with three tried features and your project's test result on it.

items.text: Track the free-threaded build (supported since 3.14) and the JIT (still experimental) as each matures.
items.how: Install the free-threaded build (python3.14t) and time a CPU-bound threaded benchmark on it and on the default build; confirm with sys._is_gil_enabled(). Each year reread the status in PEP 779 and PEP 744 and repeat the run.
items.done: You have a yearly table of timings for both builds and can say whether your own code would gain.

items.text: Re-benchmark your assumptions yearly — the fast library changes.
items.how: Keep a small benchmark suite for choices you rely on: JSON library, HTTP client, dataframe library, serialisation format. Once a year run it with pyperf on current versions and update your notes on which you would pick now.
items.done: You have dated results from at least two years and have changed or confirmed a choice because of them.

items.text: Read one significant codebase a quarter.
items.how: Each quarter pick one well-known codebase (requests, asyncio, SQLite, Redis). Read any architecture notes it has, trace one feature through the code, and write a one-page summary of a technique you could reuse.

where.name: The Architecture of Open Source Applications

items.done: You have four one-page summaries a year, each naming a technique you have since used in your own code.

items.text: Rebuild an old project of yours from scratch and compare.
items.how: Pick a project at least a year old. Without opening the old code, rebuild it from its README. Then compare the two: structure, tests, dependencies, line count, and speed on the same input.
items.done: You have a written comparison with measured differences and a list of habits that changed.

gate.note: Each needs evidence.

items.text: Ship a design doc that changed a decision.
Have code you wrote merged into a project you don't own.
Run a migration on a live system with zero data loss.
Debug a production incident you did not cause, using telemetry alone.
Teach a topic well enough that someone else ships with it.
Say no to a technically interesting idea for a correct reason.

phases.name: Final-boss ladder
phases.aim: Build the kind of systems other software is built on, without a predefined project.

resources.name: Build your own X
resources.why: From-scratch guides for every kind of system

resources.name: CodeCrafters
resources.why: Test-driven from-scratch challenges: Redis, Git, shells

resources.name: Advent of Code
resources.why: Messy inputs and rising difficulty

sections.title: The ladder — in order
sections.guide: Six projects, each harder than the last and each able to reuse the one before: the task platform can sit behind your HTTP server and keep state in your database. Do them in order and expect four to eight weeks each. Run every boss through the protocol in s1 rather than following one tutorial end to end.

items.text: Boss 1 · HTTP server: routing, methods, headers, JSON, static files, middleware, concurrency.
items.how: Order: a raw socket accept loop returning a fixed response; parse the request line and headers; route by method and path; JSON bodies and static files with correct Content-Type and 404s; middleware as wrapped handlers; then threads or asyncio. No http.server.

where.name: CodeCrafters: Build your own HTTP server

items.done: curl and a browser both work against it, tests cover each route, and a load test at 50 concurrent clients shows no errors.

items.text: Boss 2 · Mini database: tables, persistence, CRUD, an index, basic query planning.
items.how: Order: a REPL that parses insert and select; rows serialised into fixed-size pages; a pager writing pages to one file; update and delete; a B-tree index on the key; then a planner that picks index lookup over full scan when a query filters on the key.
items.done: Data survives a restart, tests cover CRUD, and a keyed lookup on 100,000 rows is measurably faster with the index than by full scan.

items.text: Boss 3 · Programming language: lexer, parser, AST, interpreter, functions, loops, errors.
items.how: Work through the tree-walk half of Crafting Interpreters in Python instead of Java: scanner, recursive-descent parser to an AST, evaluator, variables and scopes, control flow, functions and closures. Report errors with line numbers and keep scanning after a syntax error.
items.done: It runs a recursive Fibonacci and a closure-based counter, and bad input gives a line-numbered error, not a Python traceback.

items.text: Boss 4 · Distributed task platform: API, queue, workers, retries, idempotency, observability.
items.how: Order: an HTTP API that accepts jobs with an idempotency key; a queue in Redis or a database table; workers that claim jobs with a lease; retries with exponential backoff, jitter and a dead-letter state; then per-job metrics and traces. Kill a worker mid-job to test recovery.
items.done: After killing workers and resubmitting jobs, each job's effect happens once, and a dashboard shows queue depth and failure rate.

items.text: Boss 5 · AI orchestration platform: agents, tools, retrieval, memory, permissions, evals.
items.how: Order: one model call with a tool-call loop; a tool registry with per-tool permissions and human approval for writes; retrieval over your own documents; memory with a size limit; then an eval set of 30 or more cases scored automatically on every change.

where.name: Your AI product needs evals (Hamel Husain)

items.done: The eval suite runs with one command and prints a score, and a prompt-injection case cannot trigger a write tool without approval.

items.text: Boss 6 · Flagship product: a real problem, shipped, monitored, secured, benchmarked, iterated.
items.how: Pick a problem that someone other than you has. Ship a first version within a month with HTTPS, auth, backups, error tracking and uptime checks. Benchmark the main path, then iterate on what users actually do rather than on guesses.

where.name: SRE book: Reliable Product Launches at Scale

items.done: People other than you use it, monitoring alerts you before they report outages, and you have before-and-after numbers for one change.

sections.title: The unknown-problem protocol
sections.guide: The method for every boss and for any problem without a set answer. Work the steps in order on each project and keep one notes file per project with a heading per step. The first four steps should take days, not weeks; most of the time goes to s1.5 to s1.7.

items.text: Define the problem and its hard constraints in writing.
items.how: Write one page: the problem in two sentences, who has it, what done looks like expressed as a test, and the hard constraints (budget, latency, data size, deadline, what must never happen). Mark which constraints are given and which you assumed.
items.done: Someone else can read the page and say whether a proposed solution meets it.

items.text: List the unknowns and rank them by risk.
items.how: List every question you cannot yet answer: will this library handle the input, how fast must this be, can I get the data. Score each for how likely it is to go wrong and how costly that would be, and sort by the product.
items.done: You have a ranked list and can name the single unknown that would sink the project if it went the wrong way.

items.text: Research only the unknowns that block progress right now.
items.how: Take the top unknown and set a time box, such as two hours. Read only what answers that question: official docs, the source, one issue thread. Write the answer and its source in your notes and stop, even when nearby topics look interesting.
items.done: Each research session ends inside its time box with a written answer to one named question.

items.text: Prototype the riskiest assumption first.
items.how: Write throwaway code, under 200 lines, that tests only the riskiest assumption: can the parser handle the real input, can the queue sustain the target rate. Set the pass or fail threshold before running it, then archive the prototype.
items.done: You have a yes or no answer with a number, recorded next to the threshold you set beforehand.

items.text: Choose the architecture after evidence, not before.
items.how: After the prototypes, write a short decision record: options, evidence from the prototypes, the choice, and what would make you revisit it. Start with the simplest structure the evidence allows, usually one process and one database.
items.done: The decision record cites at least one measured result, and you can say why each rejected option lost.

items.text: Build one thin vertical slice that works end to end.
items.how: Build the thinnest path from input to output through every layer: one route, one table, one worker, one screen, deployed where it will run. Hard-code anything off that path. Widen it only once it runs end to end.
items.done: One real request passes through every component in the deployed environment and returns the right result.

items.text: Add tests, logs, and metrics before adding features.
items.how: Before the second feature, add pytest tests for the slice, structured logs with a request id at each boundary, and counters and timings for the main operation. Run the tests in CI and block merges on failure.
items.done: CI runs on every push, and your metrics can tell you how many requests failed in the last hour.

items.text: Measure to find the bottleneck; never guess.
items.how: Write a repeatable benchmark for the slow path and write down your guess of the bottleneck. Then profile with cProfile or py-spy and compare with the guess. Change one thing at a time and rerun the benchmark after each change.
items.done: You have before-and-after numbers from the same benchmark, and the change targeted the top entry in the profile.

items.text: Refactor when the evidence justifies it.
items.how: Refactor when the same friction shows up twice: a change touching many files, a bug in duplicated logic, a test that is hard to write. Cover the area with tests first, then refactor in small commits with the tests passing after each and behaviour unchanged.
items.done: Tests pass on every commit of the refactor, and the next change in that area touches fewer files than the last one did.

items.text: Write down what you learned before moving on.
items.how: At the end of each project write a one-page retrospective: what worked, what you would change, the numbers you measured, and links to your decision records. Add one line per lesson to a running file and reread it before the next project.
items.done: Before starting the next boss you can name three lessons from the last one and where you will apply them.

sections.title: Portfolio target — twelve months out
sections.guide: A checklist for a year of work, not a separate task. The bosses fill most of it: Bosses 1 to 3 count as serious projects, 4 and 5 as production-style systems, 6 as the flagship. Review the list once a month and fill gaps with small tools and one package.

items.text: 10–20 small exercises and tools.
items.how: Keep a list of small tools that fix your own irritations: a file renamer, a log summariser, a CLI for an API you use. Time-box each to a weekend and give it a README and at least one test. Advent of Code solutions count towards the exercises.
items.done: Your GitHub has at least ten small repositories, or one collection repository, each with a README that says how to run it.

items.text: 5+ serious portfolio projects with real READMEs.
items.how: Pick five projects, for example Bosses 1 to 3 and two others, and bring each to a state a stranger can use: a README with purpose, install steps, a usage example, design notes and known limits; tests in CI; a tagged release.
items.done: A stranger can clone each one, follow its README, and run it and its tests in under ten minutes.

items.text: 2–3 production-style systems.
items.how: Give two or three projects (Bosses 4 and 5 fit) the production basics: configuration from the environment, health checks, structured logs, metrics, bounded retries, a container or deploy script, and a runbook.
items.done: Each system deploys from scratch with one documented command and recovers from a killed process without manual steps.

items.text: 1 flagship project you'd put your name on publicly.
items.how: Choose the project you could discuss for an hour in an interview, usually Boss 6. Write a case study: the problem, the architecture, the hardest bug, the measured numbers, and what you would do next. Link it from your profile README.
items.done: You can walk someone through the case study and answer why each major decision was made.

items.text: At least one reusable package published.
items.how: Pick code you have already copied between two of your own projects, since that proves it is reusable. Package it with pyproject.toml, tests, docs and CI, and publish to PyPI with trusted publishing, trying TestPyPI first.
items.done: At least one of your own projects installs it from PyPI instead of carrying a copy of the code.

items.text: At least one deployment serving real traffic.
items.how: Deploy one project to a public host with a domain and HTTPS, add uptime monitoring and error tracking, and put it in front of real users: a tool for a club, a public API, a site friends use. Keep request logs so you can count traffic.
items.done: Your logs show requests from people other than you across at least a month, and you have tested that an outage triggers an alert.

items.text: At least one documented performance optimization with numbers.
items.how: Pick a slow operation in one project. Benchmark it with pyperf or timeit, profile, fix the top cause and measure again. Write it up: setup, hardware, before and after numbers with variance, and what you tried that did not help.
items.done: The write-up includes reproducible commands, and someone rerunning them gets numbers close to yours.

items.text: A written record of your architecture decisions.
items.how: Add a docs/adr folder to each serious project. For each significant choice write a short numbered record: context, decision, status, consequences. Write it when you decide, and supersede old records rather than editing them.
items.done: Each serious project has numbered decision records from which a newcomer can learn why the stack looks as it does.

gate.note: The goal is enough fundamentals and judgment to learn unfamiliar technology quickly.

items.text: Enter an empty folder with an unfamiliar problem and produce a working thin slice within a day.
Ship something strangers use.
Diagnose a production failure from logs and metrics alone.
Teach one of these phases to someone else and have them succeed.

quizzes.name: Git & environment
quizzes.desc: Version control you can recover from.

questions.prompt: You pushed a commit containing an API key, then made three more commits. What is the correct first move?
choices: Revoke the key, then purge it from history
Purge it with git filter-repo, then force-push
Delete the file in a new commit and push it
Revert the commit that added the key and push
questions.explain: Anyone who fetched, forked or cached the repository already holds the key, and no edit to your history reaches their copies. Only revoking it at the provider makes the leaked value useless; filter-repo and a force-push are the clean-up afterwards.
explain_choice: Rewriting your history does not touch clones, forks or caches that already have the key, so it must be revoked first.
Deleting the file changes only the latest snapshot; every earlier commit still contains the key.
revert adds an inverse commit, so the key stays readable in the original commit for anyone who looks.

questions.prompt: What does `git revert <sha>` do?
choices: Restores the working files to that commit's state
Removes that commit and its changes from the branch's history
Moves the branch pointer back to that commit
Adds a new commit that undoes that commit's changes
questions.explain: History is never rewritten: git computes the inverse of the named commit's diff and records it as a new commit on top. That is why revert is safe on a shared branch and reset is not, since everyone else's clone still agrees with yours.
explain_choice: Restoring files from a commit is git restore --source; it does not create a commit.
That describes rewriting history; revert leaves the original commit in place and adds another.
Moving the branch pointer is what git reset does, which rewrites history.

questions.prompt: You are mid-change on a feature branch and must fix something on main now. What keeps your uncommitted work safe?
choices: Run git restore . for a clean tree, then switch
Stash it, switch, and pop the stash when you return
Just switch; uncommitted edits stay on their branch
Reset --hard; the reflog keeps the discarded edits
questions.explain: Uncommitted changes belong to the working tree, not to any branch, so switching either carries them along or refuses. Stash records them as commits on a separate ref, so they survive the switch and can be reapplied. restore and reset --hard discard them, and the reflog only tracks commits.
explain_choice: restore overwrites the working files, so the unsaved edits are gone for good.
Uncommitted edits are not attached to a branch; they follow you to main or block the switch.
The reflog records commits HEAD pointed at, not uncommitted edits, so reset --hard loses them.

questions.prompt: What is the practical difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
choices: fetch downloads one branch; pull downloads every branch
fetch updates your branch; pull also updates the files
fetch moves only origin/* refs; pull also merges or rebases
fetch only reports new commits; pull downloads them
questions.explain: fetch downloads objects and moves only remote-tracking refs such as origin/main, so nothing you are working on changes. pull runs that fetch and then merges or rebases your current branch onto the result, which is the step that can conflict.
explain_choice: Both fetch every configured branch by default; the difference is the integration step, not the scope.
fetch never moves your local branch; only the integration step in pull does that.
fetch does download the commits; it just stores them under remote-tracking refs instead of your branch.

questions.prompt: Your branch looks 'lost' after a bad `git reset --hard`. What recovers it?
choices: git checkout HEAD~1 to step back before it
Nothing: reset --hard deletes the commits
git reflog, then reset to the SHA it lists
git revert HEAD to undo the reset itself
questions.explain: reset moves the branch pointer but leaves the commits in the object store, and every move of HEAD is logged in the reflog. HEAD@{1} is where you were before the reset; HEAD~1 is the parent commit, which is a different thing. Commits the reflog still points at survive for 30 days by default.
explain_choice: HEAD~1 is the parent in the commit graph, not where HEAD was before; that is HEAD@{1}.
reset only moves a pointer; the commits stay in the object store until garbage collection, weeks later.
revert undoes a commit's changes; a reset is not a commit, so there is nothing for revert to invert.

questions.prompt: Why is a src-layout package preferred over a flat layout?
choices: Relative imports need the package to be inside src/ to work
Tests import the installed package, not the checkout
pip and uv refuse to build a flat-layout project
Python finds modules in src/ faster at import time
questions.explain: In a flat layout the project root is on sys.path when tests run, so `import mypkg` can pick up the source folder even if packaging is broken. Moving the package under src/ takes it off that path, so tests pass only against what was actually installed, missing data files and entry points included.
explain_choice: Relative imports depend on being inside a package, not on where that package sits in the repo.
Build tools handle flat layouts fine; the benefit is what your tests end up importing.
Import speed does not depend on the folder name; the layout changes which copy gets imported.

questions.prompt: What does `uv run script.py` do that `python script.py` doesn't?
choices: Installs whatever the script imports, as it hits them
Compiles the script ahead of time so it starts faster
Activates .venv for the rest of your shell session
Syncs the project's environment, then runs inside it
questions.explain: uv run checks the lockfile and .venv against pyproject.toml, installs whatever is missing or out of date, and runs the command inside that environment for that one process. Dependencies come from the project's declaration, never from scanning imports, and nothing stays activated afterwards.
explain_choice: uv installs what pyproject.toml or inline script metadata declares; it does not watch imports.
The script still runs on the normal interpreter; uv's work is preparing the environment.
The environment applies to that one child process; your shell is left as it was.

questions.prompt: A merge stops with `<<<<<<< HEAD` markers in a file. What do they mean?
choices: Both sides changed these lines; you choose the result
The merge failed, so it must be aborted with --abort and retried
The lines below ======= are your current branch's
Git merged both versions and marks lines to review
questions.explain: A three-way merge compares both tips with their common ancestor; where both changed the same region it cannot choose, so it writes both. Above ======= is HEAD, your current branch; below is the incoming side. Edit to the intended result, delete the markers, then git add the file to mark it resolved.
explain_choice: The merge is paused, not failed; resolving the file and committing completes it.
HEAD, your current branch, is the part above =======; the incoming branch is below it.
Git did not combine these lines; it left both versions for you to reconcile.

quizzes.name: Python foundations
quizzes.desc: The behaviours that trip everyone up early.

questions.prompt: What does `def f(x, items=[])` do wrong?
choices: A new empty list is built on each call, wasting time
One list is made at def time and shared by every call
The default is read-only, so appending raises an error
Nothing, unless two threads call f at the same time
questions.explain: Defaults are evaluated once, when the def statement runs, and stored on the function object in f.__defaults__. Every call that omits items gets that same list, so appends pile up across calls. Default to None and create the list inside the body.
explain_choice: If a fresh list were built per call there would be no bug; the default is evaluated only once.
A list default is an ordinary mutable list, so appending works and silently persists.
One thread is enough: sequential calls already share and mutate the same list.

questions.prompt: `a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a; b.append(4)`. What is `a` now?
choices: [1, 2, 3, 4], because a and b name one list
[1, 2, 3], as its ints are immutable
[1, 2, 3], because b = a made a copy
[1, 2, 3], because append returns a new list
questions.explain: Assignment binds a name to an existing object; it never copies. After b = a both names refer to one list, and append mutates that list in place. Use a.copy(), list(a) or a[:] when you need an independent shallow copy.
explain_choice: The ints are immutable, but the list holding them is not, and that is what changed.
