Touching widgets from another thread can crash or corrupt the UI.
A mutex does not make widget code thread-safe; Qt requires the GUI thread.

questions.prompt: Why use a model/view table for 100,000 rows instead of one widget per cell?
choices: Plain widgets cannot display numeric values at all
The view draws only visible rows and asks the model
Qt limits every window to a thousand child widgets
Only model/view tables support sorting by a column
questions.explain: A model answers questions like row count and data at (row, column). The view draws only what is on screen, so memory and start-up time stay small.
explain_choice: Widgets can show numbers; the cost is creating so many of them.
There is no such limit; the problem is memory and speed.
Sorting can be done either way; the difference is scale.

questions.prompt: Where should an app store its settings on Windows?
choices: In the Windows system directory for safety
In the current working directory at start-up
In a folder under `%APPDATA%`
Next to the executable in Program Files
questions.explain: Program Files is not writable by normal users, and the working directory changes. Per-user data belongs in the platform's standard location, such as `%APPDATA%` on Windows.
explain_choice: The Windows directory is for the operating system.
The working directory depends on how the app was launched.
Program Files needs administrator rights to write and is shared by all users.

questions.prompt: What does PyInstaller produce?
choices: An installer that downloads Python the first time it runs
Your code, its libraries and a Python interpreter
A compiled machine-code version of your Python source
A browser-based version of the same desktop application
questions.explain: PyInstaller collects the interpreter, your modules and libraries into a folder or single file that runs without Python installed. The code is still interpreted.
explain_choice: Nothing is downloaded; the interpreter is included.
It does not compile Python to machine code; it bundles the interpreter.
It targets desktop operating systems, not browsers.

questions.prompt: How should app logic be tested in a GUI project?
choices: Click through the whole app by hand before each release
Test it only by comparing screenshots of the window
Skip tests, since code inside a GUI cannot be tested
Keep it in plain classes tested without widgets
questions.explain: Logic separated from widgets can be tested quickly with pytest and no display. A few GUI-level tests can then cover the wiring.
explain_choice: Manual checks are slow and miss regressions.
Screenshots are brittle and slow as the main test method.
Logic can be tested once it is separated from the widgets.

questions.prompt: Why does code signing matter for a distributed desktop app?
choices: Unsigned applications are not allowed to read files
Signing encrypts the source code inside the bundle
The system warns about or blocks unsigned apps
Signed applications start up and run faster
questions.explain: Windows SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper treat unsigned downloads as untrusted. Signing proves who published the build and that it was not altered.
explain_choice: File access is not affected by signing.
Signing does not encrypt anything; it attaches a verifiable signature.
Signing has no effect on speed.

questions.prompt: A long task has a Cancel button. How should the worker handle cancellation?
choices: Check a cancel flag between steps and stop cleanly
Kill the worker thread from the GUI straight away
Close the main window, which ends the task with it
Ignore the button until the task has finished anyway
questions.explain: Threads cannot be killed safely in Python. The worker checks a flag at safe points, cleans up and reports that it stopped.
explain_choice: Python has no safe way to kill a thread; resources can be left broken.
Closing the window can leave the worker running or corrupt data.
Ignoring cancel makes the button pointless.

questions.prompt: Where should a CLI write its error messages?
choices: To a log file, and nowhere else at all
To stdout, with each line prefixed by ERROR
To stderr, with a non-zero exit code
To stdout, followed by an exit code of 0
questions.explain: Keeping errors on stderr means a pipe like `tool | other` passes only real output. The exit code tells scripts that it failed.
explain_choice: A log file alone hides errors from the person running the command.
Errors on stdout end up in the next program's input.
Exit code 0 tells scripts the command succeeded.

questions.prompt: What does exit code 2 usually mean for a command-line tool?
choices: The command was used incorrectly
The command was interrupted by the user
The command succeeded but printed warnings
The command ran out of memory and stopped
questions.explain: By convention, and in argparse, 2 means a usage error such as a bad option. 0 is success and 1 is a general failure.
explain_choice: Ctrl+C usually gives 130.
Success is 0, with or without warnings.
Out-of-memory kills are reported by the system, often as 137.

questions.prompt: A setting can come from a flag, an environment variable and a config file. Which usually wins?
choices: The environment variable
The flag
Whichever source was set most recently
The config file
questions.explain: The most specific source wins: a flag applies to this run only, the environment to the session, the config file to every run.
explain_choice: The environment is overridden by an explicit flag.
Tools do not track when each source was set.
The config file is the broadest and usually the lowest-priority source after defaults.

questions.prompt: Why add a `--json` output option?
choices: So the printed output is shorter than a table
Because terminals cannot display plain text
So the tool finishes its work more quickly
So other programs can parse the output
questions.explain: Human-formatted tables change and break parsers. A stable JSON format gives scripts a contract.
explain_choice: JSON is often longer than a formatted table.
Terminals show plain text fine.
Output format does not change speed meaningfully.

questions.prompt: What does an entry point in `pyproject.toml` do?
choices: Creates a command that calls your function
Marks the first line of the program to run
Lists the source files to include in the package
Sets the minimum Python version for the tool
questions.explain: `[project.scripts] mytool = "mypkg.cli:main"` makes the installer create a `mytool` command that imports and calls `main`.
explain_choice: Python starts from the called function, not a marked line.
File inclusion is configured separately.
The Python version is `requires-python`.

questions.prompt: Why install command-line tools with pipx?
choices: pipx is required to publish a tool to PyPI
Each tool gets its own isolated environment
pipx installs packages much faster than pip
pipx compiles each tool into machine code
questions.explain: pipx creates an isolated virtual environment per tool and puts its command on PATH, so two tools needing different library versions both work.
explain_choice: Publishing uses build and upload tools, not pipx.
Speed is not the point; isolation is.
pipx does not compile anything.

questions.prompt: A tool prints a progress bar. What should it do when its output is piped to a file?
choices: Write the progress bar into the file
Print the progress bar to stdout twice
Refuse to run when output is redirected
Turn the progress bar off
questions.explain: Progress bars use control characters meant for terminals. Check `sys.stdout.isatty()` and skip the bar when output is not a terminal.
explain_choice: The file fills with control characters.
Repeating the bar makes the output worse.
Piping output is a normal use and must work.

questions.prompt: What should a tool do when it reads input from a pipe?
choices: Require a file path argument in every case
Search the whole disk for files that match
Read from stdin, so it works in a pipeline
Wait for the user to press Enter before reading
questions.explain: Reading stdin when no file is given lets the tool combine with others, as in `cat log | tool`.
explain_choice: Requiring a path makes the tool unusable in pipelines.
Scanning the disk has nothing to do with the input stream.
Pipes deliver data without a key press.

questions.prompt: Why multiply movement by delta time?
choices: So the game uses less memory per frame
So speed is the same at any frame rate
So collisions are checked less often
So sprites are drawn in the right order
questions.explain: Without delta time, an object moves a fixed amount per frame, so it moves twice as fast at 120 fps as at 60 fps.
explain_choice: Delta time does not affect memory.
Collision frequency depends on the loop, not on scaling movement.
Draw order is a separate concern.

questions.prompt: What are the three steps of a basic game loop?
choices: Load the assets, save the game, then quit
Render, sleep for a while, render again
Update, compile the scene, update again
Read input, update the state, render
questions.explain: Each frame reads input, advances the simulation, then draws the result. Keeping the steps separate makes the game easier to reason about.
explain_choice: Loading and saving happen outside the per-frame loop.
Rendering without updating shows a frozen game.
Nothing is compiled per frame.

questions.prompt: A fast bullet passes through a thin wall between frames. What is this called?
choices: Z-fighting
Screen tearing
Tunnelling
Aliasing
questions.explain: When an object moves further than an obstacle's thickness in one step, a check at each frame's position misses the overlap. Sweep tests or smaller steps fix it.
explain_choice: Z-fighting is flicker between surfaces at the same depth.
Tearing is a display sync issue.
Aliasing is a sampling artefact in images or signals.

questions.prompt: Why use a state machine for menus, gameplay and pause?
choices: Each state owns its input and drawing
It removes the need for a game loop at all
It lets the game run on more platforms
pygame requires a state machine to start
questions.explain: Explicit states stop bugs like pausing from the menu or dying while paused. Each transition is one clear rule.
explain_choice: The loop still runs; the state decides what it does.
Portability does not depend on this structure.
pygame does not require any particular structure.

questions.prompt: How many milliseconds per frame does 60 fps allow?
choices: About 60
About 6
About 16.7
About 100
questions.explain: 1000 ms divided by 60 frames is 16.7 ms. Input, update and rendering all have to fit in that budget.
explain_choice: 60 ms per frame is about 16 fps.
6 ms per frame is about 166 fps.
100 ms per frame is 10 fps.

questions.prompt: Why load images and sounds once instead of every frame?
choices: Disk reads are slow and would stall frames
Loading once a frame keeps the files smaller
pygame can hold only one asset in memory at a time
Loaded assets expire after they are drawn once
questions.explain: Disk reads and decoding take far longer than a frame. Load at start or level change and keep the objects in memory.
explain_choice: Loading does not change file sizes.
pygame can hold many assets at once.
Loaded surfaces stay valid until you discard them.

questions.prompt: Many objects need collision checks against each other. What reduces the cost?
choices: Draw the objects smaller on the screen
Partition space so only nearby pairs are checked
Check every pair of objects twice for safety
Check for collisions only once per second
questions.explain: Checking every pair is O(n^2). A grid or quadtree limits checks to objects in the same or neighbouring cells.
explain_choice: Drawing size does not change how many checks run.
Checking twice doubles the work.
Checking rarely misses collisions.

questions.prompt: What is a sprite sheet?
choices: A list of every sprite's current position
A spreadsheet of the game's statistics
A single file bundling all sound effects
One image holding many animation frames
questions.explain: Packing frames into one image means one load and one texture. Animation draws a different rectangle of the sheet each frame.
explain_choice: Positions are game state, not a sheet.
Statistics are unrelated to sprites.
Sounds are stored separately.

questions.prompt: How should you compare two computed floats for equality?
choices: Check they are within a tolerance
Compare them with `is` instead of with `==`
Round both to the nearest integer, then compare them
Compare them with `==` after converting both to strings
questions.explain: Floating-point rounding means mathematically equal results can differ in the last bits. A relative and absolute tolerance expresses what equal means for your problem.
explain_choice: `is` checks object identity, not value.
Rounding to integers throws away all the precision you computed.
String conversion keeps the same rounding differences.

questions.prompt: Subtracting two nearly equal large numbers loses accuracy. What is this called?
choices: Underflow to infinity
Stack overflow
Catastrophic cancellation
Integer overflow
questions.explain: The leading digits cancel and the result keeps only the least accurate ones. Rearranging the formula often avoids it.
explain_choice: Underflow goes towards zero, not infinity.
Stack overflow is deep recursion.
Python integers do not overflow.

questions.prompt: You halve the step size of a first-order method. What happens to the error, roughly?
choices: It stays the same
It halves
It doubles
It quarters
questions.explain: First-order methods such as forward Euler have error proportional to the step size. Halving the step halves the error; a second-order method would quarter it.
explain_choice: The error depends on step size, so it changes.
Smaller steps reduce the error for a stable method.
Quartering is the behaviour of a second-order method.

questions.prompt: What does `scipy.optimize.minimize` return for a non-convex function?
choices: The global minimum, whatever the shape
A list of every minimum of the function
The maximum of the function instead
A local minimum near the starting point
questions.explain: Local methods follow the slope downhill from the starting point. For non-convex problems, try several starting points or a global method.
explain_choice: Local solvers cannot guarantee a global minimum.
It returns one solution, not all of them.
It minimizes; maximize by minimizing the negative.

questions.prompt: Why set a random seed in a Monte Carlo simulation?
choices: So the numbers are more random
So the simulation runs faster
So the results are more accurate
So the results can be reproduced
questions.explain: A fixed seed gives the same random sequence each run, so a result can be checked and debugged. Accuracy comes from the number of samples.
explain_choice: A seed makes the sequence repeatable, not more random.
Seeding has no effect on speed.
Accuracy depends on sample count, not the seed.

questions.prompt: When is Numba most useful?
choices: Numeric loops that NumPy cannot vectorize
Code already written as vectorized NumPy operations
Code that spends its time waiting on the network
Programs dominated by string parsing and formatting
questions.explain: Numba compiles numeric Python functions, so explicit loops run near C speed. Vectorized NumPy code is already compiled, and I/O-bound code does not benefit.
explain_choice: Vectorized NumPy already runs in compiled loops.
Waiting on the network is not a CPU problem.
Numba targets numeric code, not general strings.

questions.prompt: A delivery company must choose routes that minimize distance under capacity limits. Which tool fits?
choices: A Fourier transform of the delivery schedule
A linear regression over past delivery times
A routing or integer programming solver
A hash table lookup of the shortest known route
questions.explain: Vehicle routing is a combinatorial optimization problem. Solvers search the space with guarantees or good heuristics.
explain_choice: Fourier transforms analyse frequencies.
Regression predicts values; it does not choose routes.
A lookup cannot search over route combinations.

questions.prompt: What makes a computational result reproducible?
choices: Saving the final notebook together with all its outputs
Pinned dependencies and a script that rebuilds everything
Running the whole analysis again on a faster machine
Writing up the results in a long and detailed report
questions.explain: Someone else must be able to rerun the whole path from raw data to figures and get the same numbers.
explain_choice: A saved notebook shows outputs but may depend on cells run out of order.
Hardware speed does not affect reproducibility.
A report describes results; it does not regenerate them.

quizzes.name: Quantitative finance
quizzes.desc: Returns, bias in backtests, and risk.

questions.prompt: A backtest uses the day's closing price to decide a trade at that day's open. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing is wrong, provided the data is accurate
Survivorship bias: it ignores delisted stocks
Lookahead bias: it uses unknown information
Overfitting: the model has too many parameters
questions.explain: At the open, the close has not happened. Any signal must use only data available at decision time, or the results are fiction.
explain_choice: Accurate data does not fix using it before it exists.
Survivorship bias is about which assets are in the data.
Overfitting is a separate problem about fitting noise.

questions.prompt: Why use `Decimal` for account balances?
choices: Floats cannot store most decimal amounts exactly
Decimal values take up less memory than floats
Decimal arithmetic runs faster than float arithmetic
Floats cannot hold negative account balances
questions.explain: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so float sums drift by fractions of a cent. Decimal stores base-10 digits exactly.
explain_choice: Decimal objects use more memory.
Decimal is slower than float.
Floats store negatives fine.

questions.prompt: A portfolio goes from 100 to 150 to 90. What is the maximum drawdown?
questions.explain: Drawdown is measured from the running peak: from 150 to 90 is a fall of 60, which is 40% of 150.
explain_choice: 10% compares 90 with the starting value 100, not the peak.
33% would be 50/150, the rise, not the fall.
60 is the absolute fall, not a percentage of the peak.

questions.prompt: Why must a backtest include fees and slippage?
choices: They remove lookahead bias from the results
Regulators require them in every backtest
They make the backtest code run faster
They can make a winning strategy lose
questions.explain: Strategies that trade often pay costs on every trade. Small edges disappear once realistic costs are included.
explain_choice: Costs and lookahead are separate problems.
It is about realism, not a legal rule for research code.
Costs do not affect speed.

questions.prompt: Why are random train/test splits a problem for time series?
choices: Random splits are too slow on large datasets
pandas cannot shuffle a time-indexed DataFrame
A random split leaves the test set empty
Training can use data from after the test period
questions.explain: Shuffling lets the model learn from later data and predict earlier data, which leaks the future. Split by time and use walk-forward testing.
explain_choice: Speed is not the issue.
pandas can shuffle any DataFrame.
A random split produces a test set of the requested size.

questions.prompt: What does the Sharpe ratio measure?
choices: The share of trades that made money
Excess return per unit of volatility
The largest loss from a previous peak
Total return over the whole period
questions.explain: It divides the return above a risk-free rate by the standard deviation of returns, so two strategies with different risk can be compared.
explain_choice: Win rate ignores the size of wins and losses.
That is maximum drawdown.
Total return ignores risk.

questions.prompt: A dataset contains only stocks listed today. What bias does a backtest on it have?
choices: Rounding bias
Parameter selection bias
Survivorship bias
Lookahead bias
questions.explain: Companies that failed or were delisted are missing, so the historical universe looks better than it was.
explain_choice: Rounding does not explain a missing set of companies.
Parameter selection is overfitting, a different issue.
Lookahead is using future information in a decision.

questions.prompt: Prices must be adjusted before computing long-term returns. Why?
choices: Splits and dividends move the price, not the value
Exchanges round their published prices every day
Adjusted prices are smaller and easier to store
Older prices were quoted in a different currency
questions.explain: A 2-for-1 split halves the price overnight. Without adjustment it looks like a 50% loss.
explain_choice: Rounding is tiny compared with a split.
Size of the number is irrelevant.
Currency is not the usual reason.

questions.prompt: Why do convolutional layers suit images?
choices: One small filter is shared across all positions
They turn each whole image into a single number
They work well without any training data at all
They sort the pixels of the image by brightness
questions.explain: A feature such as an edge can appear anywhere. Sharing one filter across the image detects it at every position with few parameters.
explain_choice: Convolutions produce feature maps, not one number.
The filters are learned from data.
They combine neighbouring pixels; they do not sort them.

questions.prompt: Two boxes of area 4 overlap in an area of 2. What is their IoU?
questions.explain: The union is 4 + 4 - 2 = 6, and 2 / 6 = 1/3.
explain_choice: 1/4 divides by the sum of both areas plus the overlap.
1/2 divides by one box's area instead of the union.
IoU is a ratio between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: What is transfer learning in vision?
choices: Copying images from one dataset into another
Training two separate models and averaging them
Fine-tuning a model pretrained on a large dataset
Converting a trained model to run on a phone
questions.explain: Early layers of a pretrained network already detect general features. Fine-tuning them needs far less data than training from scratch.
explain_choice: Moving images does not transfer learned features.
Averaging models is ensembling.
Conversion for devices is deployment, not transfer learning.

questions.prompt: Which augmentation can change the correct label?
choices: Adding a little noise to a photo of a dog
Flipping an image of a left-pointing arrow
Cropping a few pixels from the edge of a car photo
Slightly changing the brightness of a cat photo
questions.explain: If the label depends on direction, a flip turns left into right. Choose augmentations that keep the label true.
explain_choice: Mild noise does not change what the photo shows.
A small crop keeps the car in view.
A cat is still a cat at a different brightness.

questions.prompt: An OpenCV image loads with its colours looking wrong in Matplotlib. Why?
choices: OpenCV uses BGR order; Matplotlib expects RGB
Matplotlib cannot display colour images at all
OpenCV stores every loaded image as a string
The image file was saved with the wrong extension
questions.explain: Red and blue are swapped between the two. Convert with `cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)`.
explain_choice: Matplotlib displays colour images.
OpenCV returns NumPy arrays.
The extension does not change channel order in memory.

questions.prompt: Your model scores 98% on validation but fails on camera images in production. What is the likely cause?
choices: Validation accuracy is misleading in general
The learning rate during training was too low
The model does not have enough layers
Validation data does not match production
questions.explain: Different lighting, angles or cameras shift the data distribution. Evaluate on data collected the way it will be used.
explain_choice: Validation is useful when it matches deployment.
Training speed does not explain a domain mismatch.
Depth is not the likely cause of a gap between domains.

questions.prompt: What does mAP summarise for an object detector?
choices: The model's speed in frames per second
Precision across recall levels, averaged
The number of objects found in each image
The average size of the detected boxes
questions.explain: Mean average precision combines how precise the detector is at every recall level, for each class, at a chosen IoU threshold.
explain_choice: Speed is measured separately.
Object count describes the data, not the model.
Box size is not a quality metric.

questions.prompt: How can a model keep up with real-time video on limited hardware?
choices: Run each frame through the model twice
Save each frame as a PNG file before running
Process every second or third frame
Increase the resolution of each input frame
questions.explain: Skipping frames, batching and smaller inputs trade a little accuracy for speed. Objects rarely change much between consecutive frames.
explain_choice: Running twice doubles the cost.
Writing files adds disk time.
Higher resolution makes each frame slower.

questions.prompt: Why do modern language models use subword tokens?
choices: Unknown words can be built from known pieces
Subword tokens remove the need to train a model
Whole words cannot be stored in a vocabulary
Subword sequences are shorter than word sequences
questions.explain: A fixed word vocabulary cannot cover rare words, names and typos. Subwords split them into pieces the model has seen.
explain_choice: Tokenization does not replace training.
Word vocabularies exist; they cannot cover everything.
Subword sequences are usually longer than word sequences.

questions.prompt: A spam dataset is 95% not-spam. A model predicts not-spam for everything. What is its accuracy?
choices: 50%, as each class is equally likely
It cannot be computed for this model
0%, since it never finds any spam
95%, though it catches no spam
questions.explain: Accuracy counts correct predictions overall, so the majority class dominates. Recall on spam is 0, which shows the real problem.
explain_choice: 50% would need balanced classes.
Accuracy is computable; it is misleading here.
It is right on every not-spam message.

questions.prompt: Why build a TF-IDF baseline before a transformer?
choices: Tokenization cannot run without a TF-IDF step first
Transformers need TF-IDF vectors as their input
It shows whether the bigger model is worth it
TF-IDF is more accurate than transformers on any task
questions.explain: A fast linear model on TF-IDF is often close. If the transformer gains little, the simpler model may be the right choice.
explain_choice: Tokenization does not depend on TF-IDF.
Transformers use their own tokenizer and embeddings.
Transformers often win; the point is measuring by how much.

questions.prompt: What does IDF reduce the weight of?
choices: Documents that are longer than average
Words that appear in many documents
Words that appear only once in a document
Words that begin with a capital letter
questions.explain: Inverse document frequency is log(N / df). Words like 'the' appear everywhere, so their idf is near zero.
explain_choice: Document length is handled by term frequency normalization.
Rare words get a high idf.
Case is handled by normalization, not idf.

questions.prompt: What does named entity recognition find?
choices: The grammatical subject of every sentence
The language the text is written in
Spans naming people, places and organizations
The overall sentiment of the whole document
questions.explain: NER labels spans like 'Ada Lovelace' as PERSON or 'London' as a location.
explain_choice: Subjects come from dependency parsing.
Language identification is a separate task.
Sentiment is a classification task.

questions.prompt: Two texts have embeddings with cosine similarity 0.95. What does that suggest?
choices: They share no words with each other
They have similar meaning
They are exactly the same text
They are written in different languages
questions.explain: Embeddings place texts with similar meaning near each other. High similarity does not require identical words.
explain_choice: Similar texts often share words; the score does not show absence.
Different wordings can have very close embeddings.
Similarity says nothing about language by itself.

questions.prompt: Why normalize Unicode before comparing text?
choices: Normalizing makes every text shorter to store
Unicode text cannot be converted to lower case
Normalization translates the text into English
One character can be encoded in several ways
questions.explain: 'é' can be one code point or 'e' plus a combining accent. NFC or NFKC makes them compare equal.
explain_choice: Length may change slightly, but that is not the purpose.
Unicode text can be lowercased.
Normalization does not translate.

questions.prompt: When does a regular expression stop being the right tool for extraction?
choices: When the target depends on meaning, not shape
When the text contains numbers as well as words
When the text runs over more than one line
When the text is written entirely in lower case
questions.explain: Regex handles fixed shapes such as dates and IDs well. Extracting 'the product the customer complained about' needs a model.
explain_choice: Numbers are easy to match.
Regex handles multi-line text.
Case does not limit regex.

quizzes.name: Testing & QA
quizzes.desc: Test design, doubles and flaky tests.

questions.prompt: A module has 100% line coverage but a bug slips through. How is that possible?
choices: Coverage tools do not count function bodies
The bug was hidden inside a code comment
Lines ran, but nothing checked the result
Coverage above 90% turns off the assertions
questions.explain: Coverage shows that code executed, not that its output was checked. Mutation testing finds tests that would not notice a change.
explain_choice: Coverage tools count function bodies like other lines.
Comments cannot contain executable bugs.
Coverage has no effect on assertions.

questions.prompt: When does mocking make a test worse?
choices: When it stands in for a payment provider
When it replaces a slow external service
When it fixes the current time for a test
When it mocks your own logic
questions.explain: Mock at boundaries you do not control. Mocking internal functions ties tests to implementation details and hides real bugs.
explain_choice: A fake payment provider avoids real charges.
Replacing a slow external service is a good use.
A fixed clock makes tests deterministic.

questions.prompt: What does property-based testing check?
choices: That every line of the code has been executed
That a rule holds for many generated inputs
That the output matches a stored snapshot
That the code runs faster than a fixed limit
questions.explain: You state a rule, such as 'decoding an encoded value returns it', and the tool generates inputs, then shrinks any failure to a minimal case.
explain_choice: That is coverage.
That is snapshot testing.
That is performance testing.

questions.prompt: What does mutation testing measure?
choices: Whether tests fail when the code is changed
How many lines of code the tests execute
How long the whole test suite takes to run
How often tests fail for no clear reason
questions.explain: The tool makes small changes, such as `<` to `<=`. A mutant that survives shows behaviour no test checks.
explain_choice: That is coverage.
That is test timing.
That is flakiness.

questions.prompt: A test fails one run in twenty. What is the most common cause?
choices: The test framework itself has a random bug
The computer running the tests has faulty memory
The assertion message is longer than allowed
It depends on timing, order or shared state
questions.explain: Sleeps instead of waiting for conditions, tests that share data, and real clocks cause intermittent failures. Make the dependency explicit and deterministic.
explain_choice: Framework bugs are rare compared with test design problems.
Hardware faults are rarely the cause.
Message length does not affect results.

questions.prompt: Why should a browser test wait for an element instead of sleeping for two seconds?
choices: Waiting for an element makes pages load faster
Timing varies, so a fixed sleep is unreliable
Test frameworks do not allow sleeping at all
Browsers ignore sleeps issued by a test
questions.explain: Waiting for a condition proceeds as soon as it is true and fails clearly when it never becomes true.
explain_choice: Waiting does not change page speed.
Sleeping is allowed; it is just unreliable.
Browsers are unaffected by the test's sleep.

questions.prompt: What does the test pyramid recommend?
choices: Many unit tests, fewer integration, few end-to-end
Manual testing only, for any user interface
Mostly end-to-end tests, as they test everything
The same number of tests at every single level
questions.explain: Lower levels are fast and precise. Higher levels catch wiring problems but are slow and harder to debug.
explain_choice: UI behaviour can be tested automatically.
A suite of mostly end-to-end tests is slow and brittle.
Different levels have different costs, so equal numbers make little sense.

questions.prompt: Two services are developed by different teams. What catches a breaking API change before deployment?
choices: Unit tests inside each of the two services
Manual testing by both teams after release
Contract tests against a shared agreement
A code style checker run on both codebases
questions.explain: A contract states requests and responses. The consumer tests its expectations and the provider verifies it still meets them.
explain_choice: Unit tests do not see the other service.
After release is too late.
Style checkers do not check behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why prefer structured data from an API over parsing show-command text?
choices: Show commands cannot be run from Python
Structured data always uses less bandwidth
Text output changes and breaks parsers
APIs are quicker to type at the terminal
questions.explain: Screen output is meant for humans and changes format. NETCONF, RESTCONF or vendor APIs return data with a schema.
explain_choice: Show commands can be run over SSH from Python.
Bandwidth is rarely the deciding factor.
Typing speed is not the concern.

questions.prompt: What should a network change tool show before applying anything?
choices: The line count of the running configuration
The list of devices it failed to reach
The current speed of each interface
A diff of the configuration it will change
questions.explain: A reviewed diff catches mistakes before they reach a device. NAPALM's compare_config provides one.
explain_choice: Line count says nothing about what will change.
Unreachable devices matter, but the diff is what shows the change.
Interface speed is unrelated to the change.

questions.prompt: Why render device configuration from templates and data?
choices: One source of truth gives consistent configs
Devices accept only templated configuration
Templates make network devices boot faster
Templates encrypt the configuration they produce
questions.explain: The template holds the structure and the data holds per-device values, so changes are made once and applied everywhere.
explain_choice: Devices accept any valid configuration.
Boot time is unaffected.
Templates do not encrypt anything.

questions.prompt: What does Nornir add over a loop with Netmiko?
choices: A graphical interface for devices
An inventory and concurrent tasks
Support for devices with no SSH
Automatic hardware upgrades on schedule
questions.explain: Nornir manages hosts and groups and runs tasks in parallel, collecting results per device.
explain_choice: Nornir is a Python framework without a GUI.
It uses connection plugins; it does not remove the need for a transport.
It does not upgrade hardware.

questions.prompt: Where should device credentials come from in automation code?
choices: The Git commit message that added the device
A comment next to each host in the inventory
An environment variable or a secrets vault
A constant at the top of the automation script
questions.explain: Credentials in code end up in version control. Load them at run time from the environment or a vault.
explain_choice: Commit messages are permanent and shared.
Comments are still in the file and repository.
Constants in scripts get committed.

questions.prompt: What should happen when post-change checks fail?
choices: Delete the inventory to stop further runs
Roll back to the previous configuration
Ignore the failure and carry on
Reboot the device to clear the change
questions.explain: Pre- and post-checks with automatic rollback limit the impact of a bad change.
explain_choice: Deleting the inventory helps nothing.
Continuing spreads the failure.
A reboot does not undo a saved configuration change.

questions.prompt: What does TextFSM do?
choices: Monitors interface counters over time
Generates configuration from YAML data
Encrypts the SSH session to a device
Parses command output into records
questions.explain: A TextFSM template describes the text layout, and the parser returns a table of values.
explain_choice: Monitoring uses SNMP or telemetry.
Generation is Jinja2's role.
SSH handles encryption.

questions.prompt: What is a dry run in network automation?
choices: Showing changes without applying them
Running the script late at night instead
Running on a device that has no traffic
Testing with the network cable unplugged
questions.explain: A dry run produces the diff and checks, then stops before committing anything.
explain_choice: Timing is a change window, not a dry run.
Traffic level does not make a change safe to test.
An unplugged device cannot receive the connection.

questions.prompt: Why does a button need debouncing?
choices: The microcontroller reads buttons too slowly
Buttons need a firmware update before use
Debouncing reduces the board's battery use
The contacts bounce between on and off
questions.explain: Metal contacts make and break contact for a few milliseconds, which looks like several presses. Wait for a stable reading.
explain_choice: Reading fast is why the bounces are seen.
Buttons have no software.
Battery use is not the reason.

questions.prompt: What is a pull-up resistor for on an input pin?
choices: It protects the board from static discharge
It raises the clock speed of the processor
It holds an undriven pin at a high level
It increases the current flowing to an LED
questions.explain: An unconnected input floats and reads random values. A pull-up gives it a default state that a button can pull low.
explain_choice: Static protection uses other parts.
Resistors do not change clock speed.
LED current is set by a series resistor.

questions.prompt: Several sensors share two wires and each has an address. Which bus is this?
choices: I2C
UART
PWM
Analog input
questions.explain: I2C uses a data and a clock line shared by devices, each selected by address.
explain_choice: UART is point-to-point between two devices.
PWM is a signal type, not a bus.
An analog input reads one voltage.

questions.prompt: Why avoid creating new objects inside a fast loop in MicroPython?
choices: MicroPython does not support creating objects
RAM is small and allocation causes GC pauses
Creating objects makes the source code longer
Objects made inside loops are deleted at once
questions.explain: Microcontrollers have kilobytes of RAM. Frequent allocation fragments it and causes collection pauses at unpredictable times.
explain_choice: MicroPython supports objects.
Code length is not the concern.
Objects live until collected, which is the problem.

questions.prompt: What does MQTT QoS 1 guarantee?
choices: Encryption of each message
Delivery at least once
Delivery exactly once
Delivery within one second
questions.explain: QoS 1 retries until acknowledged, so duplicates are possible. QoS 2 gives exactly-once at higher cost.
explain_choice: Encryption comes from TLS, not QoS.
Exactly once is QoS 2.
QoS makes no timing promise.

questions.prompt: When is an interrupt better than polling a pin?
choices: When the pin's value never changes
When the design should use more power
When the device has no hardware timer
When a brief event must not be missed
questions.explain: An interrupt runs a handler as soon as the pin changes, so a short pulse is not missed between polls. Keep the handler very short.
explain_choice: A pin that never changes needs neither.
Interrupts usually save power by allowing sleep.
Interrupts do not depend on having a timer.

questions.prompt: A battery sensor sends one reading per hour. What saves the most power?
choices: Adding a larger colour display
Keeping Wi-Fi connected all day
Deep sleep between readings
Polling the sensor more often
questions.explain: Most power goes to staying awake and connected. Deep sleep between readings can extend battery life from days to months.
explain_choice: A display adds consumption.
Wi-Fi is one of the largest power costs.
Faster polling uses more power.

questions.prompt: The network drops for an hour. What should a well-designed sensor do?
choices: Buffer readings and send them later
Stop reading the sensor until reconnected
Reboot the device once every minute
Discard readings until the network returns
questions.explain: A bounded local buffer keeps data through outages. When it fills, drop the oldest and count what was lost.
explain_choice: Stopping readings loses data too.
Rebooting does not fix a network outage.
Discarding loses the data the device exists to collect.

quizzes.name: Security engineering
quizzes.desc: Threat models, supply chain and detection.

questions.prompt: What is a threat model for?
choices: Measuring how fast the application responds
Counting the lines of code in each service
Mapping attackers, entry points and defences
Choosing the programming language to use
questions.explain: It connects assets, attackers and entry points to controls, so security work goes where the risk is.
explain_choice: Speed is a performance question.
Code size does not identify threats.
Language choice is a separate decision.

questions.prompt: A secret was committed to Git and then removed in the next commit. What must you do?
choices: Nothing, since the latest version no longer has it
Rotate the secret; the history still has it
Make the repository private and leave it there
Delete only the most recent commit from the branch
questions.explain: Anyone with the history, including forks and clones, still has it. Revoke and replace the secret; rewriting history alone is not enough.
explain_choice: History keeps the secret.
Existing clones already have it.
The secret is in the earlier commit.

questions.prompt: Why compare signatures with `hmac.compare_digest` instead of `==`?
choices: It supports much longer input strings
It handles Unicode strings more correctly
It runs faster than the `==` operator
Its time does not depend on the match
questions.explain: `==` stops at the first difference, so response time leaks how much of a guess was right.
explain_choice: Both work on any length.
Unicode handling is not the point.
Constant time is not faster.

questions.prompt: What does an SBOM list?
choices: Every component and version in the software
Every user account in the organization
Every open network port on the servers
Every known attacker and their methods
questions.explain: A software bill of materials lets you answer 'are we affected?' when a new vulnerability is published.
explain_choice: Accounts come from an identity system.
Ports come from a network scan.
Attackers are not listed in software metadata.

questions.prompt: What must security logs not contain?
choices: User IDs of the actor
Source IP addresses
Timestamps of events
Passwords and tokens
questions.explain: Logs are copied widely. Record who did what and when, never the secrets themselves.
explain_choice: User IDs identify the actor.
Source IPs help investigations.
Timestamps are essential.

questions.prompt: A detection rule fires 500 times a day, and nearly all are harmless. What is the problem?
choices: The logs are too small
Too many false positives
The rule runs too fast
Too many false negatives
questions.explain: Alert fatigue makes responders stop reading alerts. Tune rules with known-good data until most alerts matter.
explain_choice: High alert counts suggest the opposite.
Speed is not the issue.
False negatives are missed attacks, not noisy alerts.

questions.prompt: What is the first step when you find an active intrusion?
choices: Announce it publicly straight away
Delete old logs to free up space
Contain it and preserve evidence
Wipe the affected machines at once
questions.explain: Containment limits damage. Evidence such as memory, disks and logs is needed to understand what happened.
explain_choice: Public disclosure comes later, through the right process.
Logs are evidence.
Wiping destroys evidence.

questions.prompt: What does `pip-audit` check?
choices: Installed packages against known advisories
Whether each package is correctly licensed
Your own code for SQL injection patterns
How long each package takes to install
questions.explain: It compares dependency versions with published advisories. Static analysis tools check your own code.
explain_choice: License checks are a different tool.
That is static analysis, such as Bandit or Semgrep.
Install speed is irrelevant.

quizzes.name: Bots & integrations
quizzes.desc: Webhooks, rate limits and unattended processes.

questions.prompt: How do you confirm a webhook request came from the platform?
choices: Check that it arrived over the internet
Reply and wait for a confirmation
Check the User-Agent header value
Verify its signature with the secret
questions.explain: Anyone can send a request to your URL. A signature over the body with a shared secret proves the sender knew the secret.
explain_choice: Every request arrives over the internet.
Webhooks are not confirmed by reply.
User-Agent can be set to anything.

questions.prompt: A platform returns HTTP 429 with `Retry-After: 30`. What should the bot do?
choices: Drop the message and move on
Retry the request immediately
Wait 30 seconds, then retry
Switch to a different bot token
questions.explain: 429 means too many requests. Respect Retry-After, or the platform may block the bot.
explain_choice: The message can be sent after waiting.
Immediate retries worsen the rate limit.
Rotating tokens to evade limits can break the platform's terms.

questions.prompt: Why include a timestamp in a signed webhook?
choices: To make the signature longer
To reject replayed old requests
To sort the requests by arrival
To measure the network latency
questions.explain: A captured valid request could be sent again later. Rejecting old timestamps limits replay attacks.
explain_choice: Signature length does not depend on the timestamp.
Sorting is not a security measure.
It is not used for measuring speed.

questions.prompt: When is long polling better than webhooks for a bot?
choices: When the bot has no public URL
When the platform sends many events
When the bot needs lower latency
When the bot is hosted in the cloud
questions.explain: Webhooks need the platform to reach your server. Long polling lets a bot behind a firewall fetch updates instead.
explain_choice: High volume favours webhooks.
Webhooks usually have lower latency.
Cloud hosts can usually receive webhooks.

questions.prompt: Why must a scheduled job be idempotent?
choices: Idempotent jobs finish faster than others
It may run twice without repeating effects
Schedulers refuse to run any other kind of job
It makes the job's output easier to log
questions.explain: Restarts, retries and overlapping schedules can run a job again. Designing it to have the same effect twice prevents duplicates.
explain_choice: Speed is not the reason.
Schedulers accept any job.
Logging is unrelated.

questions.prompt: Where should a bot token be stored?
choices: An environment variable or secret store
A constant in the bot's source code
The project's public README file
A pinned message in the bot's channel
questions.explain: A leaked token lets anyone control the bot. Keep it out of the repository.
explain_choice: Source code is committed and shared.
A README is public.
Messages are visible to others.

questions.prompt: What does OAuth let an integration do?
choices: Get around the platform's rate limits
Host the bot on the platform for free
Encrypt every message from end to end
Act for a user without their password
questions.explain: The user grants a scoped token. The integration never sees the password, and the token can be revoked.
explain_choice: Rate limits still apply.
Hosting is unrelated.
OAuth is about authorization, not message encryption.

questions.prompt: A bot crashes overnight. What makes it recover without you?
choices: More debug output printed to the log
Two copies running with the same token
A process manager plus state on disk
A longer timeout value in the code
questions.explain: systemd, Docker restart policies or a platform supervisor restart the process. Persisted state means nothing is lost.
explain_choice: Debug output does not restart anything.
Two copies with one token often conflict.
Timeouts do not restart a crashed process.

questions.prompt: What is gas on Ethereum?
choices: Payment for the computation a transaction uses
A type of wallet that holds several accounts
The name of Ethereum's native currency unit
The consensus algorithm that orders blocks
questions.explain: Each operation costs gas; the fee is gas used times the price per gas. It stops programs from running forever for free.
explain_choice: Wallets hold keys.
The currency is ether.
Consensus is proof of stake.

questions.prompt: Why must amounts in wei be handled as integers?
choices: Contracts accept amounts only as strings
Floats cannot hold large amounts exactly
Python cannot store integers that large
Amounts in wei are always less than one
questions.explain: 1 ether is 10**18 wei. Floats have about 16 significant digits, so large amounts lose precision.
explain_choice: Contracts take integers for amounts.
Python integers have arbitrary size.
Wei is the smallest unit; amounts are whole numbers of wei.

questions.prompt: What does a contract's ABI describe?
choices: The gas price to use for each transaction
The full Solidity source code of the contract
The functions, arguments and events of a contract
The private key of the contract's owner
questions.explain: The ABI is the interface. web3.py uses it to encode calls and decode return values and event logs.
explain_choice: Gas price is set per transaction.
Source code is separate; the ABI is derived from it.
Private keys never belong in an ABI.

questions.prompt: What is a chain reorganization?
choices: A deployed contract is upgraded in place
The network doubles its maximum block size
A wallet switches to a different address
Recent blocks are replaced by other blocks
questions.explain: Recent blocks can be replaced before they are final. Indexers must be able to undo data from replaced blocks.
explain_choice: Contract upgrades are a separate pattern.
Block size changes are protocol upgrades.
Addresses come from keys.

questions.prompt: What is a reentrancy attack?
choices: The same transaction is sent twice
The network is flooded with transactions
A callee calls back in before state updates
An attacker guesses a user's private key
questions.explain: If a contract sends funds before updating a balance, the receiver can call back and withdraw again. Update state first.
explain_choice: Duplicate transactions are prevented by nonces.
Flooding is a denial-of-service attempt.
Guessing keys is not feasible.

questions.prompt: Where should keys for a development project be kept?
choices: In the project README for the whole team
Test keys only, loaded from the environment
In the repository, next to the contract code
In a comment at the top of the contract
questions.explain: A key in a repository can be found by anyone who sees it. Use throwaway test keys and a hardware wallet for real funds.
explain_choice: A README is public.
Repositories are shared and scanned for keys.
Contract code is public on the chain.

questions.prompt: Why index contract events into a database?
choices: Node queries over long history are slow
A database makes each transaction cheaper
Events are deleted from the chain after a day
Nodes are unable to return event logs
questions.explain: Nodes answer simple log queries. Analytics across many blocks needs a local, indexed copy.
explain_choice: Indexing does not affect transaction costs.
Events stay on the chain.
Nodes return logs; they are slow for large queries.

questions.prompt: Under EIP-1559, what does a transaction pay per gas?
choices: Only the tip, because the base fee is free
A fixed price the network sets each day
Whatever the sender writes in the data field
The lower of max fee and base fee plus tip
questions.explain: The base fee is burned and the tip goes to the validator. The max fee caps the total per gas.
explain_choice: The base fee is paid and burned.
The base fee changes every block.
The data field carries call data, not the price.

certs.name: CS50P — Introduction to Programming with Python
certs.what: The best-taught beginner Python course that exists. Nine problem sets and a final project.
certs.worth: High. Strong teaching and problem sets. The free certificate is from Harvard.

certs.name: Python Programming MOOC
certs.what: Text-based, brutally exercise-heavy, 5+5 ECTS. Covers OOP, testing, and databases.
certs.worth: High if you learn by doing. Many exercises.

certs.name: Scientific Computing with Python
certs.what: Five graded projects: arithmetic formatter, time calculator, budget app, polygon area, probability calculator.
certs.worth: High. The projects are public and verifiable.

certs.name: Python Essentials 1
certs.what: Syntax through functions, collections, and exceptions. Prepares for the PCEP exam.
certs.worth: Medium. Fast and structured. The badge is free.

certs.name: Python Essentials 2
certs.what: Modules, packages, OOP, exceptions, files, and the standard library. Prepares for PCAP.
certs.worth: Medium. Solid intermediate coverage at zero cost.

certs.name: PCEP — Certified Entry-Level Python Programmer
certs.what: Vendor-neutral entry certification. Take it after Python Essentials 1 if you want the credential.
certs.worth: Low-medium. Recognized, but a portfolio counts for more. Take it only if an employer asks for it.

certs.name: PCAP — Certified Associate in Python Programming
certs.what: Modules, OOP, exceptions, file handling, and standard library depth.
certs.worth: Low-medium. Same as PCEP, at a higher price. Only if a job requires it.

certs.name: HackerRank Skills Certification — Python
certs.what: A timed coding assessment. Pass and you get a shareable certificate.
certs.worth: Medium. Cheap, and useful as a timed self-check.

certs.name: Kaggle Learn micro-courses
certs.what: Python, pandas, intro ML, intermediate ML, feature engineering, deep learning.
certs.worth: Medium-high for data work. Short and practical.

certs.name: Data Analysis with Python
certs.what: NumPy, pandas, and five analysis projects.
certs.worth: Medium-high. Good structure for the data half of the roadmap.

certs.name: Machine Learning with Python
certs.what: TensorFlow-based ML with five graded projects.
certs.worth: Medium. For depth, use Karpathy and fast.ai. Take this for the certificate.

certs.name: Hugging Face AI Agents Course
certs.what: smolagents, LlamaIndex, and LangGraph side by side, ending in a benchmarked capstone.
certs.worth: High for agent work. The certificate requires working code.

certs.name: Hugging Face LLM Course
certs.what: Transformers, fine-tuning, and the Hugging Face stack across 12 chapters.
certs.worth: High if you work with models beyond API calls.

certs.name: Hugging Face MCP Course
certs.what: Model Context Protocol — how tools and context get wired into models.
certs.worth: Medium-high. Agent tooling is standardizing on MCP.

certs.name: Anthropic Academy
certs.what: Building with the Claude API, Claude Code, MCP, and prompt engineering.
certs.worth: High if you're building on Claude specifically.

certs.name: Machine Learning Crash Course
certs.what: Regression, classification, data handling, and productionizing models.
certs.worth: High as a foundation. Short and well written.

certs.name: MIT 6.S191 — Introduction to Deep Learning
certs.what: University-grade deep learning, refreshed every year, with Colab labs.
certs.worth: High. Updated every year.

certs.name: CS50 AI with Python
certs.what: Search, knowledge, uncertainty, optimization, learning, neural nets, language.
certs.worth: High. Covers the classical AI that many LLM courses skip.

certs.name: CS50 Web Programming with Python and JavaScript
certs.what: Django, SQL, JavaScript, front ends, testing, and deployment.
certs.worth: Medium-high if you want the full-stack half.

certs.name: Google IT Automation with Python
certs.what: Six courses: Python, Git, Linux, troubleshooting, configuration management.
certs.worth: Medium-high. A well-known brand. Financial aid is available.

certs.name: Python for Everybody
certs.what: The gentlest credible on-ramp, with free materials and autograders.
certs.worth: Medium. Use it only if CS50P moves too fast for you.

certs.name: ML Zoomcamp
certs.what: Regression through deployment, with peer-reviewed projects.
certs.worth: High. Cohort deadlines keep you on schedule.

certs.name: Data Engineering Zoomcamp
certs.what: Docker, Terraform, workflow orchestration, warehouse, dbt, Spark, Kafka.
certs.worth: High. The most complete free data engineering course.

certs.name: 6.0001 — Intro to CS and Programming in Python
certs.what: Computational thinking, algorithms, and complexity, taught as computer science.
certs.worth: Medium-high. Pairs well with CS50x for the CS phase.
